This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the true ground state can be represented within a specific function space, we establish that the convergence rate of the generalization error is influenced by the non-uniformity of the eigenvalue spectrum. This research relies heavily on the theory of function spaces and spectral theory, offering a comprehensive analysis of the generalization performance in a $d$-dimensional setting. Moreover, our results reveal that the convergence rate can be represented as an exponential function in one dimension, a polynomial function in two dimensions, and a logarithmic function in three dimensions. To validate our theoretical findings, we experimentally verify the predicted convergence rates in both 2D and 3D scenarios. Additionally, our study demonstrates that the ground states of the true and neural network-induced eigenfunctions converge exponentially to each other within the function space where the true ground state resides. This research is the first to theoretically examine the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks in a $d$-dimensional setting and its experimental findings align with the theoretical predictions. Furthermore, our study showcases the capabilities of two-layer neural networks in efficiently calculating the ground state of the Schrödinger equation in high-dimensional settings. To this effect, our study modifies the architecture of two-layer neural networks by incorporating a new type of neuron that allows for efficient representation of the ground state within the specified function space. This research is akin to (Cohen et al., 2019) in that both studies are founded upon the concept of self-similarity at multiple scales. This theory is uniquely incorporated into the framework of two-layer neural networks within our study, demonstrating the distinction from (Cohen et al., 2019) through the utilization of the Schrödinger equation as the governing physics. This research is also distinct due to its theoretical and experimental validation of the generalization performance in high-dimensional settings. This study is also an extension of (Lee and Ghattas, 2013), (Lee and Ghattas, 2015), and (Cohen et al., 2019) in that all these studies are built upon the theories of spectral theory and the conjugate gradient method. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.31 ± 0.18. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Our observation of right ascension symmetry in nearby galactic cosmic rays offers support to the idea that the galactic cosmic-ray distribution is uniform, and also helps to limit magnetic-field at the galactic scale to fall off at a rate of 1/R^n, with n ≥ 0.6. We detail our analysis methodology and simulate the detection of cosmic rays using simulated data, verifying that our observed patterns match expectations. We cannot rule out the possibility that our observed anisotropy patterns result, at least in part, from the detection of a single extremely energetic source, and highlight the significance of continuing close collaboration with other experiments, such as the HiRes and the Telescope Array, in resolving this issue. Furthermore, our study reveals that detection strategies relying solely on in situ observation may be insufficient in uncovering and comprehensively interpreting anisotropy patterns in extremely energetic cosmic rays. We propose an alternative approach, integrating data from ground-based experiments with satellite data to chart galactic magnetic field at scales of tens of gigaparsecs. Homogenization outcomes for thin films, reduced by dimensional reduction, were derived 
under periodic or almost periodic hypotheses in film mid-plane energies. In this note, 
we discuss thin films, resulting from cross-sections of periodic mediums, with incommensurate 
mid-planes - containing no period other than zero - and demonstrate a generalized 
homogenization outcome via geometric, almost periodic reasoning. As a result, the 
microscopic gradient in the mid-plane can be eliminated in the expanded model. This 
generalizes previous studies on thin films with periodic or almost periodic mid-planes. 
Additionally, we discuss the applicability of this model to thin films with "chiral" 
structures, often encountered in nano-science, and propose an ongoing research question. 
Lastly, we provide an almost periodic example illustrating that the regularity of the 
expanded model's right-hand side may not be optimal. Overall, this note focuses on the 
theoretical foundations and proofs are delayed until a subsequent work.

We establish the existence of long-term solutions, starting with minimal initial conditions, for a semilinear equation governing the behavior of half-spin particles within a Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that solutions persist for any magnitude of initial conditions, given the satisfaction of a specified condition known as the Lochak-Majorana condition. As time progresses indefinitely, the solutions asymptotically converge to a state of free particles. When compared to a similar model in a flat spacetime, it is revealed that the curvature of spacetime has a negligible effect on the long-term solutions, provided the total energy is zero. Additionally, it is shown that long-distance solutions in spacetime have a comparable behavior to their counterparts in a spacetime with zero curvature. However, it is noted that long-distance solutions in a spacetime with non-zero curvature may actually violate the Lochak-Majorana condition, resulting in unstable behavior over long distances in time. Finally, it is shown that the long-term solutions for particles with negative energy are either absent or asymptotically converge to a state of free particles. In particular, it is proven that long-term solutions for particles with negative energy either do not exist (or converge to a state of free particles). A key step in this proof involves the use of Sobolev inequality to show that solutions for particles with negative energy either do not exist (or converge to a state of free particles). In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with multiple clients representing diverse datasets, we compared the performance of centralised training methods. Our results indicate that federated learning can produce models with comparable or slightly lower accuracy compared to centrally stored data, but with the benefits of conserving privacy and preventing data hoarding. Additionally, to account for potential statistical variations in training, we employed a novel evaluation method involving repeated training simulations with shuffled data. Our findings also highlight the importance of model architecture and training parameters in achieving successful FL outcomes. With optimal configurations, federated learning can yield performance indistinguishable from local training methods. Furthermore, to investigate the generalisability of FL-trained models across unseen clients, we developed a novel metric known as cross-entity applicability, which assesses a model's ability to handle client populations with which it was not initially trained. Our study demonstrates that with sufficient training iterations, federated learning can yield a model with satisfactory cross-entity applicability and strong overall accuracy. Our research provides a foundation for future research into the application and limitations of federated learning in medical image analysis. With continued development, federated learning could become a practical tool for training models to accurately detect and analyse sensitive medical information while maintaining privacy and conserving computational resources. Cavity magnomechanics provides a unique setting for exploring the physical properties of magnetic materials in response to light, and also offers a tool for manipulating these materials on an extremely small scale. Utilizing a setup consisting of a photonic cavity, two gold mirrors, and a thin, ultra-low friction sheet made of magnetic material, researchers studied the transfer of photon states to mechanical motion states. Numerical simulations revealed how changes in material types and dimensions impact this transfer. Cavity decay times were found to be in the range of milliseconds. Research findings indicate that this system can effectively be used for small-scale magnomechanics and may hold potential for advancements in quantum information technology. Research on this setup may also lead to a deeper understanding of fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics. Recently, a more efficient approach to controlling quadrupedal robots has been developed through reinforcement learning (RL). This method can automatically generate skill-specific controllers without manual input, which is particularly important given the complexity of nonlinear dynamics involved. However, RL struggles with reward sparsity and quadrupedal robots' challenging dynamics, such as maintaining balance on a balance beam. Our novel RL-based approach integrates an evolving generator to create diverse motion patterns for the quadrupedal robot. This allows RL to learn policy adaptations for different ground or link trajectories, resulting in enhanced sample efficiency. Our two tests of this system demonstrate successful policy learning: first, a standard RL approach fails to develop a balanced policy when attempting to navigate a balance beam, but our approach succeeds in both the beam and a more complex 3D terrain challenge. Without prior knowledge of the environment dynamics, our method successfully adapts to generate effective policies in novel conditions. This capability is further demonstrated by cross-testing the generated policy on a different robot model, which yields a high success rate in transferring the learned policy to a distinct quadrupedal model. Our method's results surpass those of state-of-the-art RL and optimization-based controllers in both tests. This groundbreaking research presents an entirely new approach to controlling quadrupedal robots for executing complex tasks in intricate environments. Our method's public availability at https://github.com/SMUAutoML/RLEEG allows for replicating the study's findings. Additional assets, including videos and data, can be found at https://smu-automl.github.io/RLEEG/. This research was partially supported by funding from ONR and NSA. The behavior of super-massive black holes in their lifetime is primarily dominated by a relatively low level of accretion well below the Eddington limit, indicating they appear as low-luminosity active galactic nuclei.  A crucial aspect of these objects is the prediction by various black hole theories and simulations that they often emit hot winds. This is now playing an essential role in large-scale simulations that study galaxy evolution, but direct proof has been hard to find. This paper verifies that specific emission lines present in high-resolution Chandra X-ray spectra from the low-luminosity AGN within a relatively close spiral galaxy named NGC\,7213, is actually driven by a black hole, as earlier research indicated. We see the hot plasma it produces has a speed of approximately 1,100 km per second, indicating a bi-modal distribution consisting of plasma temperatures of 0.2 and 0.5 keV. This hot plasma is powered by the hot wind theory, specifically attributing it to either that or a alternative explanation, which suggests the hot plasma could also result from a confined sub-relativistic outflow. Further investigation is necessary to distinguish between these two possibilities, but we do know the hot plasma has to originate from the AGN itself, as other factors would not produce the required amount of high-energy photons. This confirmation of hot winds from low-luminosity AGN has significant implications, as it means they play a role in the gas rates and chemical composition within galaxies. This research has a potential to impact larger-scale simulations studying galaxy evolution by incorporating hot winds, which were previously unknown. As a result, we propose continued observation of the AGN in NGC\,7213 for a total of 4 Megoseconds to further clarify its wind properties, resolve existing ambiguities and confirm whether the hot wind is in fact the primary source of its high-energy photons. Moreover, we recommend incorporating additional AGN systems into the sample for similar high-resolution X-ray spectroscopic analysis to confirm hot winds in other low-luminosity AGN, ultimately establishing whether hot winds are a common occurrence across the spectrum of AGN. This in turn will allow us to model more accurately how they affect galaxy evolution. In the meantime, we have estimated that a 4 Megasecond observation of NGC\,7213 using the International X-ray Observatory will be able to detect the hot wind's emission, regardless of its orientation relative to our line of sight. Fortunately, reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to optimizing model-free nonlinear controller designs with favorable results. Nonetheless, the current methods suffer from several limitations, including the computational intensity of their offline training processes, the challenge of generalizing to different system configurations, and the risk of local optima traps. In the case of linear systems, these issues can be mitigated to some extent. However, the linear approximation method used in many cases breaks down when subjected to significant deviations from the linear operating point. In this research, a model-free reinforcement learning design is proposed to optimize nonlinear controller performance. By splitting the reinforcement learning process into two distinct parts, the algorithm is made more computationally efficient and capable of handling significant system nonlinearities. Additionally, the research demonstrates that the two-step reinforcement learning design can be effectively applied to optimal regulator problems, yielding improved closed-loop performance and faster convergence rates, all without requiring any prior knowledge of the system's dynamics. In fact, the research shows that the lowest possible frequency of the closed-loop system's Nyquist diagram can be optimized in real-time using the proposed approach, resulting in improved robust stability and performance properties. Extensive simulation results, obtained using a high-fidelity digital twin of a power converter unit, demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the two-step reinforcement learning design, showcasing its capabilities in optimizing nonlinear controller performance for a diverse range of systems configurations, including systems with significant nonlinearities that extend beyond linear operating points. In fact, the research shows that the two-step reinforcement learning design is capable of generalizing to a 70% larger scope of system configurations than other model-free reinforcement learning designs, all while achieving superior performance and reducing training time by two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the research shows that the two-step reinforcement learning design is capable of learning across multiple related systems, also known as meta-learning, thereby enabling the design of adaptable controllers that can be effectively applied to a range of related systems without the need for significant retraining. Existing methods focusing on spatio-temporal anomalies, which are often based on roads or grids, can result in data scarcity issues and compromised detection results. This paper introduces a novel approach that tackles these challenges. An unsupervised anomaly detection framework called ReAD is proposed, which divides the city into regions dynamically based on mobility patterns. This approach ensures consistent data availability across all areas. If a significant discrepancy is found within a region using road network topology, the area is split into smaller sections to pinpoint the anomaly more precisely. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this method. Comparison analysis with other detection methods reveals superior performance of ReAD in terms of precision, recall, F1-score, and processing speed. This research enables the development of more effective anomaly detection methods that are adaptable to various urban mobility patterns. This study evaluates several theoretical pion vector form factor models in an effort to determine the most suitable match for two-pion distribution amplitudes. Additionally, using the most favored model, we calculate the contribution of the rescattering process in the light-by-light contribution of the muon $g-2$. Our findings indicate that while the oblique contribution is significant at low momentum transfer, it can be adequately described by several standard models at higher momentum ranges. Conversely, the direct contribution exhibits a distinctive peak at around 1 GeV and differs notably between various models, suggesting the need for a precise calculation. Furthermore, we show that by incorporating the complete two-pion distribution amplitude, the integral of the light-by-light contribution within the momentum range of 0-1 GeV is increased by about 3 in the axial gauge. This correction enhances the total light-by-light contribution by about 0.9$\times 10^{-10}$. Ultimately, while the full theoretical calculation still falls short of the experimental result by a factor of about 3 in the axial gauge, our analysis indicates that the full theoretical calculation is in better agreement with the experimental result than previously estimated in the dimensional regularization-EPA method. Most importantly, our findings underscore the significance of the high-momentum transfer region in the pion vector form factor in understanding the muon $g-2$. As such, this problem remains unresolved and warrants further investigation. If successfully addressed, this study makes progress towards reconciling the theoretical and experimental results of the muon $g-2$. Conversely, our analysis highlights an unresolved issue in particle physics. Furthermore, we have conceived an experiment to test the pion vector form factor in the relevant momentum range using the J-Park (KEK) electron collider. Our proposed experiment aims to provide crucial insights into the mechanism governing the pion vector form factor at low momentum ranges. This study is crucial not only in resolving the muon $g-2$ anomaly but also in enhancing our understanding of the strong interaction at low momentum ranges. Most importantly, our proposed experiment is well within the capabilities of existing facilities, such as J-Park (KEK), and can be completed within one experimental campaign utilizing the electron collider currently under development at J-Park (KEK). Developing models from source code necessitates access to an abundance of labeled data. However, training models on a single domain typically renders them ineffective on another domain. This challenge is not confined to software development; it affects natural language models as well (e.g., self-supervised image representation). Three primary issues arise in learning universal representations for code: (1) preserving domain-specific details while eliminating redundant information, (2) ensuring representations are applicable to various downstream tasks, and (3) determining effective methods for obtaining high-quality labeled data.

  To address these challenges, this research proposes a novel pre-training approach called UnRep. UnRep relies on the task-agnostic aspect of program execution to extract program semantics. Three distinct components comprise UnRep: a dynamic instruction extractor, a context encoder, and a context-aware embedding space. The context-aware embedding space embeds contextual information into an embedding space using multi-head attention. When paired with a task-specific decoder, it enables downstream training with labeled code datasets. With minimal computational resources, UnRep was trained on public execution datasets and demonstrated effectiveness on six benchmark tasks across three domains (Java, Python, C++/C). UnRep outperforms existing methods in nearly all cases and maintains excellent generalizability across diverse domains.

  Two supplementary approaches were developed to compare with UnRep: Rep-Java and Rep-Py, which tailor the representation to specific domains using multi-task pre-training based on random program sampling. Although they excel within their respective domains, they fall short when applied to foreign domains. Notably, Rep-Java was unable to perform satisfactorily on Python tasks due to its reliance on Java syntax; conversely, Rep-Py failed to impress in C++/C tasks because it was trained using Python syntax. These experiments underscored the difficulty of developing universal representations for code. In an effort to facilitate further research in this area, the source code and associated datasets will be made publicly available. Additionally, six benchmark tasks were devised to assess representation quality and provide a framework for comparison with existing methods. These benchmark tasks were chosen from popular code benchmarks and are available at <https://github.com/danielpdunstan/universal-code-representations>. They encompass a broad range of program execution domains, including concurrent programs, object-oriented programs, and embedded systems, as well as natural language-based programs. In conclusion, this research has successfully developed the first pre-trained, task-agnostic and universal representation of code, making significant contributions to the field of program embedding while addressing long-standing challenges in this

To overcome the limitations of traditional methods, two new techniques were developed and successfully tested with synthetic data. These tests involved mimicking the atmosphere's aerosol optical properties with models, then using the photometry data to back-calculate the aerosol characteristics. The two techniques, referred to as the CMSS and PA algorithms, were applied to photometry data from the CLIO telescope at the Concordia Station and yielded accurate results. The PA algorithm, in particular, demonstrated exceptional performance, producing very accurate results even when a key assumption is relaxed. The test results indicate that both algorithms are highly capable of providing precise aerosol data when combined with other atmospheric observations. The PA algorithm's flexibility, however, makes it particularly suitable for processing photometry data in conjunction with other techniques. The research on these two PA algorithms revealed several beneficial aspects of using photometry data: it can supplement existing observations: even with sparse photometry data, accurate aerosol characteristics can be determined; and certain problematic atmospheric conditions can be effectively mitigated. Overall, the research indicates a positive outlook for utilizing photometry data in operations like ATLAS, which may significantly improve the accuracy of aerosol measurements even when data is scarce. The PA algorithm has been successfully integrated into the ATLAS system and is set to significantly enhance its performance. The research on the PA algorithm also led to advancements in model testing, data processing, and data fusion, ultimately contributing to the development of the CLIO4.0 telescope, which is currently undergoing testing at Concordia. The PA algorithm has since been instrumental in obtaining remarkable aerosol measurements during the ATLAS Antarctic campaign. Further research using the PA algorithm is ongoing to explore its capabilities in conjunction with other techniques. The PA algorithm has been successfully used in numerous analyses, including accurately tracking the aerosol optical depth and depth distribution, as well as its angular dispersion and phase function. The research on these aerosol characteristics has led to a better understanding of aerosols and cloud interactions, ultimately providing valuable input for global climate models. The PA algorithm's accuracy was validated through comparisons with ground-based measurements, satellite data, and model simulations. We generated theoretical forecasts for the cm-wavelength free-free emission produced by two distinct disk models, tailored to the TW Hydrae young stellar object, and analyzed how photoevaporation affects this phenomenon. According to our analysis, the high-energy photons from the star in this system can drive disk photoevaporation and create a gap in the dust emission as observed by ALMA. By applying the CFD model, we determined the extent of the disk photoevaporation, achieving a match with the observed 1.3 mm dust continuum map. Additionally, we predicted the appearance of photoevaporation and MHD wind-driven disk models at higher angular resolutions using the ATCA and ALMA arrays. Our findings indicate that the presence of photoevaporation is key in explaining the observed disk structure, particularly in the case of the inner disk, and predict free-free emission that could be distinguished from free-free emission originating from the disk if able to be resolved at around 30 mas. This would be indicative of the presence of a photoevaporation gap. Moreover, our analysis suggests that the magnetic wind model may produce structures at relatively larger radii than the hydrodynamical photoevaporation model, and predicts the development of a more gradual disk structure as the magnetic wind model extends to larger radii. This could potentially be observed using the ATCA and ALMA arrays at higher angular resolutions. Based on our simulations, we estimate a required integration time of around 10,000 hours to observe the predicted structures at an angular resolution of about 30 mas, using the ATCA and ALMA arrays at 7 mm for both models. This could be achieved in about 4.3 months with the ATCA and about 500 days with ALMA using 50 antennas. Furthermore, we simulate observations using the VLA band 6 at an angular resolution of about 30 mas, and estimate a required integration time of around 200 days. Finally, we propose that future high dynamic range and high angular resolution radio observations at wavelengths of about 3 cm could reveal the disk structure at even greater distances from the star than observed at 7 mm using the ATCA and ALMA arrays at an angular resolution of about 30 mas. This could be achieved in about 400 days with the VLA. This would be indicative of the presence of photoevaporation. Moreover, we predict to observe structures at an angular resolution of around 8.8 mas with the VLA and also with the NOEMA using the B2 band at an angular resolution of about 10 mas

For speech processing applications, tasks such as speech voicing, fundamental frequency estimation, and dynamic pitch tracking are essential components that require efficient algorithms to accomplish. To meet this need, we have developed a novel algorithm that integrates these subtasks into a single unified procedure, allowing it to effectively handle pre-recorded speech with significant background noise levels. The algorithm utilizes a set of established metrics, like the zero-crossing rate, to create an unsupervised voicing classification system, and a hybrid approach based on autocorrelation is used to calculate pitch values. To improve the accuracy of pitch tracking, we suggest utilizing a forward-backward Kalman filter to refine the estimated pitch trajectory. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing, cutting-edge pitch detection techniques. By evaluating complete one-loop corrections to the Higgs boson masses, with full momentum dependence in a combined on-shell-DR renormalization scheme, with and without including sfermion mixing, the loop-corrected Higgs sector is accurately reconstructed. The role of neural architecture search (NAS) has escalated within the deep learning community in recent years, however its full potential is constrained by most current approaches, which explore a tiny portion of the vast neural architecture search space. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes novel techniques that facilitate NAS within a more extensive search space. This is achieved by adopting a more condensed search space that incorporates abstract program properties, where similar architectures exhibit similar performance. As a result, NAS can be conducted more efficiently. To facilitate this process, the research also develops a novel and efficient synthesis method for generating neural architectures based on the desired program properties. This approach, unlike previous methods, allows for program modification without gradient-based optimization. Empirical evaluations using the ResNet, MobileNet, DenseNet, TransNet architectures on various datasets have demonstrated that the proposed method outperforms existing solutions by a considerable margin. Specifically, it takes only 27 hours to find a top-performing model for ResNet54 on ImageNet, whereas current approaches necessitate several days, weeks, or even months. Furthermore, the research has successfully applied the neural architecture search technique to vision-language tasks such as generating NLP models with vision capabilities. To demonstrate the method's capabilities, the research has presented over 700 neural architectures, including models that have been shown to be highly effective in specific task scenarios and those that have been demonstrated to be highly versatile and adaptable across different tasks. To conclude, the research has showcased that NAS can be both efficient and capable of discovering top-performing models through a series of empirical evaluations. The proposed approach, termed Program Guided Synthesis (PGS), has been compared to other existing methods, including evolution, reinforcement learning, and gradient-based search. Notably, PGS has outperformed all other methods by a considerable margin in a thorough evaluation. Specifically, it has been found that PGS makes significantly more accurate predictions about model performance based on program properties, whereas other methods have been found to be consistently off-target. The advantages and limitations of hybrid precoding systems for multi-group multicasting in millimeter-wave technology are explored through simulation-based comprehension of their performance characteristics. Specifically, we compare the performance of conventional and digitally assisted hybrid precoding methods in terms of total transmitted power and effective signal strength at each user. Our findings indicate that while hybrid precoding reduces the complexity of baseband processing, it also introduces non-negligible performance degradation compared to fully digital precoding. Moreover, despite efforts to minimize power consumption, there often exists a significant power gap between hybrid and fully digital precoding schemes. Ultimately, we conclude that although hybrid precoding holds promise for reducing hardware costs, its suitability is highly dependent on the specific constraints of the communication system. In particular, if the number of phased shifters and phase shifter quantization bits are relatively large, hybrid precoding can indeed yield considerable cost savings; otherwise, the performance difference from fully digital precoding may become the dominant consideration. Our research also reveals that multi-mode transmit beamforming can yield better performance than traditional unicasting and multicasting approaches, and points to the potential for hybrid precoding to improve this performance even further. Ultimately, we have identified areas for potential improvement in the design of hybrid precoders. Specifically, by combining multicasting and hybrid precoding design, as well as exploring the use of alternative optimization methods such as suboptimal and semi-definite relaxation techniques, there may be room for enhanced performance and reduced complexity of hybrid precoders. Additionally, the effects of phase quantization in multigroup multicasting systems present an area for further research and analysis. Federated Learning adoption has been hindered by communication challenges. A new Federated Learning paradigm, Federated Distillation, has been proposed due to its superior communication efficiency. However, the current FD protocol has limitations in practical use cases because it requires the transmission of pre-processed distilled models. This can lead to long waiting times for slower devices. To address this issue, a new approach called Communication-Efficient Federated Distillation is presented. The approach involves separating model updates from model architecture, allowing for the transmission of minimal client-specific update tensors instead of entire models. This leads to a substantial reduction in communication overhead without compromising accuracy, making it possible to achieve fast convergence. The approach also enables the efficient handling of model complexity and uneven client computational capabilities. Experimental results confirm that this new approach matches the accuracy of traditional Federated Learning, but with significantly improved communication efficiency and runtime. The code can be found on GitHub at the link below: https://github.com/ericwu1230/CEFD. The federated distillation kit allows for easy deployment of CEFD on mobile and cloud platforms. The code also includes a detailed tutorial on implementation, which can be found in the report attached. CEFD can be scaled up to handle very large FL datasets and models, as shown in the results. The approach is also robust against data heterogeneity and adversarial attacks. The current implementation of CEFD is in Python 3, with support for PyTorch 1.9, TensorFlow 2, and Mixture of Experts models. The future direction of this research will be to explore other forms of Federated Distillation and generalize the approach to other FL paradigms. The book chapter will be based on the initial report, with new results and extensions to be included. The current research has been presented at NeurIPS 2021, with a video available on YouTube. The research will also be presented at CVPR 2022, with a video available on YouTube. The research has been featured in an interview by the Computer Vision Foundation, with a blog available online. The research has been used by 10+ new datasets, with a total of 100+ participants in the implementation of Federated Distillation. The research will be open-sourced soon, with the code and tutorials to be made available. The research has been discussed by the FL community on the Google ML Kit forum, with feedback and suggestions from 100+ participants. The research has been cited by 10+ papers, with a total of 500+ participants.

A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to support future-proof services on large networks of interconnected computers. Our study examines how to effectively manage the flow of service requests across an NDN-based network, considering the varying capabilities of each node to process and generate data. Focusing on service workflows with sequential phases, we develop an optimal algorithm for online, distributed decision-making that maximizes the network's overall processing capability. Our proposed Service Orchestration Algorithm (SOA) achieves the best possible results by selectively allowing each request to be processed at a node with the highest overall processing capability in the surrounding area. SOA allows for efficient management of the network's flow of service requests, leading to significant gains in processing efficiency and simplicity in complex networks. Additionally, SOA's design is based on redundant components, making it easy to implement and adapt in a variety of NDN-based computing networks. Our investigation includes a thorough evaluation of SOA, comparing it to alternative strategies in a variety of network settings. Our findings clearly demonstrate the superiority of SOA, showing that online distributed decision-making can significantly boost the network's overall processing capability. In particular, our research reveals that SOA may raise the network's overall processing capability by up to 25% compared to a control strategy. Our study also sheds light on factors that influence the likelihood of SOA outperforming a control approach, with significant gains consistently observed in densely connected networks and those with highly varied processing capabilities at individual nodes. Ultimately, our research through SOA contributes to the ongoing development of NDN-based computing networks by providing an efficient, optimal technique for managing the flow of service requests and maximising the network's overall processing capability. SOA's design and distribution-based online decision-making process make it a versatile solution compatible with a variety of NDN-based computing networks featuring sequential workflow patterns. Furthermore, our study through SOA initiates a comprehensive examination of the potential processing gains in NDN-based computing networks, influenced by online distributed decision-making in the decision-making process. By analysing the distinct parameters of network processing capability and workflow patterns, our research provides valuable insight and a thorough classification of the potential processing capability in NDN-based computing networks under distributed decision-making. In conclusion, our study through SOA significantly contributes to the advancement of NDN-based computing networks by introducing an efficient, optimal technique for managing the flow of service requests and maximising the network's overall processing capability, achieved through online distributed decision-making. Additionally, our study provides a comprehensive examination of the potential processing gains

The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes predetermined utility functions or ranks solutions based on predefined criteria. In real-world problems, defining utility functions is challenging and time-consuming, especially in scenarios where no guidelines are available. Furthermore, ignoring the learning process may result in suboptimal solutions and decreased reliability. To address these issues, our proposed utility function learning method generates accurate utility functions efficiently, even without prior knowledge, while adapting to available objective functions. Additionally, to enhance performance, our approach integrates prior knowledge, such as domain experts' feedback, if available. Experimental results demonstrate that utility function learning significantly improves the quality of resulting solutions across diverse multi-objective problems. Importantly, our utility function learning method is adaptable to various optimization algorithms and can be applied to different domains with minimal modifications. Consequently, this method can be deployed directly in practical optimization scenarios. Implementation details are available online for public use. Structural information, such as the tree structure of Wasmond et al.'s utility function, is also learned automatically. Experimental results show that utility function learning significantly improves the quality of resulting solutions in multi-objective problems. Implementation details are available online for public use.

Yet, standard weighted arithmetic mean aggregation in current DML systems may lead to considerable inaccuracies and slow convergence speeds over fluctuating networks. In this paper, we introduce a new family of nonlinear aggregation functions to improve DML efficiency in networks subject to change. Our concept, based on discontinuous nonlinear functions, uses multiple linear functions with varying weights to combine local machine learning model updates. By implementing just a few linear functions instead of numerous fine-grained updates, we boost efficiency and precision in changing networks. Results show that our solution outperforms existing aggregation methods in applications involving nonlinear regression and matrix factorization, achieving up to 100% improvement in convergence speed and 30% improvement in accuracy. The research combines theoretical foundations and practical experimentation to demonstrate that the novel aggregation function can effectively handle variable networks and complex machine learning tasks. A publicly available code and model configurations are available at github.com/Tal-Aissar/dmllib-aggregation, including the Python implementation of the new aggregation function. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structural properties, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, a novel problem of inferring non-trivial, homogenous polymers composed of two to six distinct monomers, while adhering to given property targets, has been defined and shown to be solvable through a proposed method combining linear regression and mixed integer programming. This new method has been trialled and proven effective in a range of computational tests. Finally, a feasible approach to inferring heterogeneous polymers with diverse monomers has been identified. These contributions have enabled the development of a versatile and efficient system for polymer inference, setting the stage for applications in diverse fields such as drug discovery and materials science. Preliminary analyses suggest that the resulting polymers could exhibit promising properties in areas like UV absorption and reflectance. As such, this research is poised to make a significant positive impact in these domains. A detailed explanation of the method, along with all employed code and tested compounds, is available at https://github.com/polyinf/polyinf/blob/main/docs/Methodology.md. This research has also been documented in a paper, available at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2207.07363. Both the methodology and the code can be accessed through https://polyinf.github.io. In the context of high-dimensional linear regression, our analysis centers on the Bayesian approach using data-driven priors derived from [1]. These specific priors exhibit beneficial properties such as minimal Bayes factor and posterior contraction characteristics, all while relying solely on the consistency of traditional least squares estimators. Building upon this foundation, we establish more sophisticated posterior contraction results, accommodating cases with unknown error variances and high-dimensional sparsity under specific regularization methods. Our analysis also extends to the analysis of test statistics and confidence sets within a Bayesian framework, all ultimately demonstrating a more than adequate rate of contraction. In contrast, the traditional frequentist approaches often exhibit slower contraction rates, often at the rate of $n^{-1/4}$, $n^{-1/2}$, or even $n^{-1/2}\log n$, rendering our results significantly improved. To achieve these enhanced outcomes, we leverage a unique combination of previous works, along with the utilization of tailored random matrix theories, such as the improved Charlier correlation inequality introduced in [2], which provides an enhanced understanding of the behavior of Charlier correlations. Our paper ultimately demonstrates that the application of the Charlier correlation inequality allows for the accurate evaluation of posterior concentration, even under challenging conditions characterized by high-dimensional data, non-Gaussian errors, and unknown error variances. Additionally, our analysis includes the derivation of optimal bounds for tail probabilities of spectral norms and eigenvalues of band matrices, all while adhering to the framework of [3]. Our results are further exemplified through simulations, illustrating the effectiveness of the proposed Bayesian approach in identifying the underlying sparse structures of high-dimensional linear regression models. Our simulation data reveal that the prior-induced Bayesian methods exhibit enhanced sparsity and more precise parameter estimations when compared to traditional frequentist methods. To address the pressing concern of low carbon emissions and efficient manufacturing, researchers examined the impact of machining variables on energy consumption and surface quality using a Bayesian analysis and evolutionary optimization approach. A meta-model based on the Kriging algorithm was created to simulate energy consumption and surface quality, and compared to historical data, revealed that Bayesian analysis accurately predicted both outcomes. This research introduces three indices for characterizing online signature templates based on distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability. 
Distinctiveness is evaluated through statistical analysis and a random signature assumption on a set of user signature examples.
Complexity is determined by examining the features of user signature examples.
Reliability, on the other hand, is estimated by assessing a validation set of user signature examples.
These three indices serve as indicators for measuring the performance of online verification systems against both random and intentional forgeries as well as the performance of genuine users providing valid signature examples.
Through experiments using different verification algorithms and three online signature datasets plus one keystroke dataset, the validity of these measures and their applications have been verified and demonstrated. 
As a result, these three indices can provide valuable insights for designers, researchers, and developers of online verification systems on how to enhance their systems against both malicious and legitimate attacks. 
Additionally, these results may suggest new approaches for enhancing user authentication security based on signature patterns. 
The proposed indices have been further integrated into an extended version of the well-established FERET challenge by CMC, including three additional datasets. 
The modified challenge is now available at https://feret3.dmi.unipg.it/feret/feret.html. 
The code used for conducting the experiments and generating the results can be accessed at https://github.com/ferruccio-ammanita/Online-Verify-Validation/tree/main/feret_extension.

We investigated four-point amplitude calculations in the most fundamental string theory examples featuring T-fold backgrounds with six supersymmetries in four dimensions. These theories are represented as two asymmetric orbifold versions, one of order two and the other of order three. We demonstrated that the perturbative spectrum and the amplitudes are preserved under a symplectic group with Hurwitz and Eisenstein quaternions. Furthermore, we established the constraints on supersymmetric couplings in the effective theory and speculated about the non-perturbative properties, such as the completion of six-derivative couplings through the integration of Ramond-Nicolai states. Multilingual individuals frequently code-switch between different languages within a single sentence, often depending on the audience, purpose, and context. This Code-Mixing phenomenon is widespread across the globe, creating a unique linguistic characteristic that is rarely acknowledged in Natural Language Processing models. Our paper explores the implications of code-switching for NLP and highlights its significant role in the daily lives of multilingual communities. We demonstrate code-switching through various forms and offer an analysis of its practical applications and future directions within NLP. We hope this study will spark important discussions among sociolinguists, computational linguists, and development experts to tackle the practical concerns and limitations of NLP for multilingual societies. We invite readers to share their views and expertise through comments on this preprint. We will compile the responses to create a comprehensive list of considerations, challenges, and potential solutions, to be shared publicly on a dedicated website. We plan to incorporate these insights into an upcoming article outlining specific technical contributions and implementations. We expect this collaborative effort to contribute positively to future NLP research and development. We hope this preprint will serve as a starting point for a virtual and public discussion. Please visit https://github.com/cstm-lab/Code-Mixing-NLP-for-Multilingual-Societies for the preprint and comments. We look forward to hearing from you soon!

This study reveals that sharing images online can compromise one's privacy, prompting the development of Graph Privacy Advisor - an image privacy classifier. This classifier leverages visual details and the number of objects in an image to predict its privacy level, by adapting a sophisticated model, reducing its complexity and improving performance through feature refinement. In particular, the classifier identifies the most relevant image characteristics to use for privacy evaluation and replaces complex, high-dimensional image data with simplified features, thus reducing its complexity. Moreover, the classifier tackles the issue of preconceived biases by modeling the likelihood of objects appearing together, rather than the frequency of individual objects within each class. As a result, the classifier performs better than established methods, such as ImageNet, while being more efficient than more advanced models, such as DeepLab, in classifying image privacy. Following a detailed evaluation, the study demonstrates the feasibility of the classifier in real-world applications by integrating it into an online photo-sharing platform, thereby empowering users to control the privacy of their images. The study also releases a comprehensive dataset of processed images for future research on visual privacy. This release enables the research community to build upon this work, further adapting and refining the image privacy classifier to suit diverse applications. Moreover, the study provides a versatile approach to image privacy, extending beyond the current method of classifying images as purely private or public. Rather, the classifier assigns a confidence value to the privacy status of each image, thereby facilitating more nuanced control over image sharing. To sum up, this study addresses the critical issue of online image privacy, introducing a practical solution - the Graph Privacy Advisor. This classifier offers a balanced approach to learning image privacy, comprising efficient models, a refined feature set, and a performance benchmark. This work also contributes valuable knowledge and resources to the research community, including a processed dataset and a platform for fine-tuning the classifier. Finally, the study releases a platform for controlling image privacy, based on the classifier, thereby empowering internet users to safeguard the privacy of their images. This research will ultimately contribute to improving the resilience of visual data privacy in the online environment. The research code is publicly available at https://github.com/jbtran/Graph-Privacy-Advisor. The released dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/jbtran/Graph-Privacy-Advisor/blob/main/ImagePrivacyDataset.json. The online platform for fine-tuning the classifier can be accessed at https://graph-privacy-advisor.herokuapp.com/. These quantum radiation models are based on the assumption that pure quantum states correspond to thermal states at zero temperature. We propose two models of hidden purity, each of which relies on different mathematical constructions to explain the divergence of entropy in physical systems. These constructions involve either embedding pure states within larger spaces of quantum states or visualizing pure states as singular limits within families of mixed states. We examine the possibilities and limitations of both models, as well as their potential applications to understanding quantum thermodynamics and the paradoxes of black holes and cosmic strings. Ultimately, these theoretical models can provide insights into the fundamental nature of pure and mixed quantum states, and the ability of quantum systems to store and release energy over time. We suggest that further research on these models could shed light on the underlying principles of quantum mechanics, and potentially lead to new mathematical generalizations of quantum theory. Additionally, these constructs of hidden purity can be seen as a representation of quantum systems experiencing fluctuations in energy, and may thus find a practical application in the analysis of quantum thermodynamic systems. It is also possible that these models could offer a new perspective on the longstanding thought experiment known as the black hole information paradox, as well as other puzzles related to high entropy and pure quantum states. We explore these possibilities and propose a novel approach to resolving the information paradox, one in which the conversion of pure radiation into thermal states plays a key role in explaining how black holes appear to lose and gain mass in a cycle of growth and decay. This study aims to address this gap by developing a method that combines train- and test-time augmentation to improve social influence prediction. Utilizing a variational graph autoencoder based on variational autoencoders, we show that this approach yields superior results over existing state-of-the-art methods. Through exhaustive experiments on four benchmark datasets, we successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Additionally, we highlight the computational efficiency of our augmentation method, making it more suitable for real-world applications than existing graph augmentation techniques. This research is expected to contribute significantly to the field of social network embedding. The proposed model's test-only inference capability and computational efficiency make it an ideal choice for practical applications. Moreover, we highlight the potential for our study to facilitate responsible AI development by thoroughly examining the characteristics of the social influence network and the ethics of our evaluation strategy. It can also remove unnecessary information from low-resolution cameras by input filtering and leverage high-quality signals from low-resolution cameras by input amplification. The method's performance in real-world scenarios is demonstrated through comprehensive tests. Experimental findings reveal that the method can achieve superior results compared to the current best approaches with the following achievements: the method can achieve an average PSNR of 40.30 in RGB images, 39.69 in YUV images, and 41.35 in grayscale images on the UCID face dataset, which marks a notable improvement of 2.07, 2.03, and 3.63 over the current best approaches with the same number of input cameras; the method can scale efficiently to dual-camera systems with diverse configurations; and the method demonstrates impressive generalization capabilities across various cameras and scenes with minimal calibration required. The researchers also conducted extensive abuse studies to analyze the method's resilience to misuse and the results show that the method remains resilient even when faced with significant perturbations of camera parameters. The study further examines the method's performance in a battery-drain application and the findings suggest that the method can significantly prolong battery life by 13% or 8GB, which demonstrates the method's practical utility. The study's key contributions can be summarized as follows: the method offers an efficient and practical solution to the colorization problem in the most common dual-camera configurations; the method can achieve superior results through effective input filtering, amplification, and learning; the method demonstrates impressive generalization capabilities and resilience to misuse; and the method's performance surpasses that of the current approaches as well as offers a tangible benefit in a real-world application. The proposed method has been made available on the GitHub platform. The study also employs the UCID, PyTORO, and CCV libraries for the experiments and has utilized the TensorFlow and PyTorch frameworks for the method's implementation. The study also conducts abuse studies by utilizing the OpenCV library to manipulate image properties. The study also utilizes the Synology DS918+ and DS720+ dual-camera systems for the battery-drain application. The study also utilizes the DS718+ dual-camera system for the battery-drain application. The study also utilizes the DSM 6.2 and DSM 6.

The advent of online collaboration tools like GitHub has made it easy for software developers to share and reuse code across various repositories, often employing clone-and-own or forking techniques. As a result, it has become crucial to effectively maintain these shared files, especially in keeping them updated to the most recent version of the reused code. This contrasts with previous approaches, where the focus was on identifying the most suitable version of a file for update, and thus implementing maintenance strategies. To address this new paradigm, we introduce the concept of meta-maintenance, which revolves around managing the diverse versions of a single file across multiple repositories, and propose a method to achieve this. Our analysis of a sample of 18 GitHub repositories reveals that a significant portion of software development involves meta-maintenance, and demonstrates the feasibility of this approach through a manual validation process. Furthermore, we introduce an automated system to assist in meta-maintaining these shared files, and showcase the results of its application on the sampled repositories. Taken together, our findings underscore the importance of meta-maintenance in the maintenance of software development, and suggest that a automated system such as the one we introduced could be deployed to great effect. Additionally, we make available our code, as well as a package tailored to support meta-maintenance operations, for the convenience of the GitHub community. These resources can be accessed at: \url{https://github.com/eriksolerg/diff-maintenance}. Additionally, the following repositories contain the data required to replicate our analysis: \url{https://github.com/eriksolerg/replication-materials}. Furthermore, we have prepared a document that provides a detailed explanation of our approach, as well as the underlying theoretical and practical frameworks that guide our work: \url{https://eriksolerg.github.io/papernotes/diff-maintenance}. We invite the GitHub community to build upon our findings and utilize our proposed solutions to address the complex challenges of meta-maintenance across shared repositories. In particular, we identify and outline two promising research avenues in our appendix (Appendix A and B). We believe that by tackling these research questions, we can create a more autonomous and effective maintenance strategy, and ultimately make software development more efficient and productive. In the end, we aim to devise innovative methods to address the critical issue of maintaining shared software files across different repositories, and demonstrate the feasibility of these solutions through practical applications. This is reflected in the presence of significant radial velocity differences and irregular patterns. Furthermore, time series photometry taken in different seasons have uncovered unusual features and oscillations. One of these features, consisting of an irregular and variable minimum brightness level, can be explained by the presence of a small third component or uneven distribution of the primary star's disk. The primary star in BD And appears to be experiencing unusual oscillations given its size, and it displays characteristics similar to those of the gamma Doradus variable stars, although it does not exhibit the expected long period phenomenon. These features can be attributed to BD A's unusual evolution path or it may be experiencing unusual stellar activity. To confirm whether BD A is a gamma Doradus variable or not, further observations are required. Observations of the BD And system are recommended until season 3, as it aligns with the northern hemisphere's best viewing period. This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved introducing a Yamabe flow based on fractional curvature and demonstrating the existence of mild solutions. In the current study, we examine the long-term consequences of this Yamabe flow. Under the constraint of non-negative scalar curvature for complete non-compact manifolds, we show that solutions obtained from initial data within our specified class converge over time to a steady state. In contrast, when the scalar curvature is restricted to be non-positive, we find that the solutions converge to the universal Riemann metric. In both scenarios, we find that the key to convergence relies on the growth rate of the metric's distance from the Euclidean metric. In addition, we establish an important inequality that relates the fractional curvature to the metric's distance. This inequality, in conjunction with standard elliptic estimate techniques, plays a crucial role in our analysis. In particular, we note that our argument does not rely on any compactness or boundary conditions, thereby allowing the metric to degenerate at possibly singular points. In this context, we also discuss the implications of our results on the $L^2$ norm of the metric's Laplacian. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least two domains with sufficient data and are unable to learn comprehensive aspect preferences. To address this, a new framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) is proposed, which can handle multiple sparse domains and collaborates with each other through enhanced training of aspect preference across multiple domains. Theoretical analysis confirms that using multiple domains is more beneficial than using just one or two domains in terms of improving recommendation performance. Theoretical findings are substantiated by experimental results, showing that MSDCR achieves state-of-the-art results on winerecomm and movielens-20m datasets. The source code of the framework is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/ChenKai12138/MSDCR. MSDCR has the potential to significantly impact the cross-domain recommendation arena with its innovative framework. The system requires Windows 10 or later to operate, and can be executed using the provided code which takes about 10 minutes to complete a run. The computed results are then posted on this GitHub page. The parameter values used in the experiments are predefined and documented in the code. The empirical evaluation of MSDCR is comprehensive, encompassing three diverse scenarios in which the performance of MSDCR is consistently compared with top 9 CDR approaches across two domains. The computational complexity of the framework is analytically derived and shown to be acceptable for real-world implementation. The experimentally obtained AUC values validate the framework's ability to learn general and discriminative aspect preferences. The winerecomm dataset is further analyzed to illustrate the applicability of MSDCR to real-world problems. To further validate the framework, additional experiments on movielens-20m dataset are conducted while varying the number of available domains and data sparsity levels. The results demonstrate the robustness and reliability of MSDCR across varying dataset configurations. The theoretical and empirical results collectively confirm that MSDCR is a superior choice for cross-domain recommendation in real-world scenarios. To investigate the transportation and yield production of the $J/\psi$, $\psi(2S)$, $B_c$ and X(3872) in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, a kinetic-rate equation is employed and compared with data from the Large Hadron Collider. The rate equation depends on two primary parameters: the equilibrium limit and reaction rate for each state, both influenced by quark fugacities and masses as well as binding energies. The X(3872) is distinct in its approach, incorporating two possible ground-state quark combinations, namely a tetraquark structure resulting from different quark spins, or a diquark-state combination of quarks. In this study, exchange interactions between quarks are used to calculate the binding energies of these states, with the most suitable X(3872) description being the one with a tetraquark structure for collision temperatures above 90 MeV. The study further analyzes the influence of collision conditions, varying temperature, chemical potential and transport coefficients on the yield, distribution and sequential production timing of these states. Moreover, the rate of transport and thermalization is found to significantly differ between $J/\psi$ and X(3872)$, with the latter's rate of transport being lower by an order of magnitude due to its compact nature. A notable observation from this study is the pronounced production of X(3872) in central collisions, exceeding that of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$, indicating its potential as a probe of the ALICE experiment's alleged low-mass muon anomaly. A further investigation into the transport and characteristics of $B_c$ and X(3872) in small systems of proton-proton and proton-lead collisions is also conducted, revealing that X(3872) exhibits a notable nose-shaped pattern in its transverse momentum distribution when colliding with protons, coinciding with its anticipated tetraquark structure and possibly related to mechanisms involving nucleon-nucleon collisions. This study provides a foundation for the utilization of these states as sensitive probes of the QCD theory and its quark-gluon plasma, thereby furthering our comprehension of quantum chromodynamics and its applications in heavy-ion collisions. All code used to generate the figures and data for this study has been shared at a public repository for reproduction and verification. Moreover, a public version of the transport model has been made available for the $B_c$ and X(3872) states. This study does not address X(3872) production

Robots that learn from observations in real-world environments using inverse reinforcement learning can face challenges when they encounter situations involving human intervention. Their ability to distinguish between the robot's original goals and human actions is limited, as both involve changes to the environment. This causes issues in RL algorithms, making it difficult to achieve consistent results. To address this problem, we developed a new hierarchical Bayesian model that incorporates two main components: one that identifies achievable goals and another that predicts likely states based on these goals and past observations. This model enables the robot to learn its original goals and achieve better outcomes compared to existing methods. Our results, shown in simulations using mujoco environments, reveal substantial improvements in both policy convergence and reward optimization. Additionally, our approach exhibits greater adaptability and flexibility in the face of human intervention. A significant benefit of this model is its capacity to generalize goals across multiple tasks and learn autonomous ly in partially-observable environments. Deep reinforcement learning has made notable strides in resolving control issues, but its current state approaches are primarily tailored to handling compact control problems. When it comes to solving more complex problems, for instance those involving the control of geometrically intricate objects or multi-body systems, the policies learned through deep reinforcement learning tend to lack coherence, often resulting in unrealistic representations of the control strategy. To address this limitation, we propose a multi-phased approach that leverages both short-term and long-term planning to achieve a deeper understanding of the control issues at play. This methodology comprises two distinct stages: the first involves training a short-term controller using deep reinforcement learning to focus on immediate goals, while the second utilizes a long-term planner to generate policies that incorporate planning coherence, using the estimated dynamics from the short-term controller. To make this approach scalable for large problems, we have also developed a method that allows the transfer of knowledge across related tasks. We evaluate our proposed methodology by applying it to a diverse range of controlled physical simulations, successfully demonstrating its ability to improve the coherence of the control strategies and reduce the complexity of the learning process. Furthermore, we show that the transfer of knowledge across related tasks can be effectively harnessed to accelerate the resolution of novel, unseen control issues. Our research introduces a groundbreaking two-staged approach that combines short-term and long-term planning to solve complex control problems, marking a significant advancement in the field of deep reinforcement learning. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. In this article, we outline our theory pipeline, specifically designed for PDF fitting, which incorporates the input of various ENSEMBLE groups and utilizes the LUNDHEP tool to handle parton shower outputs through the DGLAP code, SHATTO. By providing access to precomputed parton distributions, both on and off shell, our pipeline facilitates the comparison of different PDF candidates across a range of scales. In addition to its primary function, our pipeline also serves as a platform for publishing and downloading ensemble members of PDF sets, as demonstrated by our inclusion of NNPDF data sets. Moreover, we discuss the potential applications of our pipeline in conjunction with other tools, such as PDF GRIFF, for navigating and selecting suitable ensemble members based on specific criteria. By showcasing two example runs, one with top-quark data and another with top-quark data supplemented by top-side data, we highlight the pipeline's capability to handle novel data while applying conventional PDF constraints, thereby illustrating its potential for addressing a range of theoretical and experimental concerns in the future. Ultimately, with its integrated theory component, our pipeline is designed to enable and augment existing PDF fitting groups, as well as future initiatives focused on fitting PDFs, in their efforts to incorporate a wide range of theoretical and experimental data into their analyses. In particular, we anticipate this pipeline to be particularly useful for groups working with top-quark cross-section data but also applicable to groups focused on other processes, as it allows for precomputed PDF distributions to be used as input in future studies. In this spirit, we make the pipeline and all of its components publicly available at <https://github.com/ueeany/pdf_fitting_pipeline>, as well as through SHATTO, LUNDHEP and PDF GRIFF, as a resource for the PDF fitting community. In the long term, we envision this pipeline to be integrated into existing PDF fitting

For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact and adaptable representation is required, making implicit neural representations an attractive option due to their ability to model complex 3D shapes. However, their application to generating entire cell shapes has been limited by the difficulty of training them on a single point in 3D space. Researchers in neuroscience hypothesize the brain utilizes diverse coordinate systems, such as body-centric, world-based, and others, to represent 3D environments. Conversely, advancements in reinforcement learning present a novel approach that might serve as a more plausible model for spatial perception and navigation in biology. Focusing on reinforcement learning methods that encourage agents to achieve target images without creating a 3D map, we examine this type of representation's capability to facilitate spatial tasks involving geometric consistency, like decoding location features. To test this, we developed a hands-on experiment where humans provided snapshots of an object at distinct locations within a structured space. A neural network trained to generate 3D shapes using reinforcement learning was then trained with these images. When asked to predict object positions, networks using snapshot data performed better than those using traditional image datasets. These findings support the idea that task-driven representations might offer a more accurate model for biological spatial representation, paving the way for novel neuroscientific investigations. Additionally, these outcomes present an interesting possibility for future AI systems - utilizing lower-dimensional representations could potentially enable them to handle complex 3D tasks more efficiently. Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent studies suggest that East Pacific El Ni\~no develops in conjunction with weaker and more localized atmospheric responses, as opposed to the central Pacific variant, which is linked to increased regional precipitation and anomalous rainfall patterns in the equatorial Pacific during the season. We aim to build upon previous findings by investigating the distinct impacts of both flavor variations during periods of extremely high or low seasonal precipitation globally. To achieve this, we utilized a high-performance computing system to simulate and analyze the behavior of the tropical Pacific-South America climate system under various ENSO conditions. Our analysis reveals that East Pacific El Ni\~no tends to weaken the rainfall response in the equatorial Pacific, while enhancing precipitation in the Amazon and weakening it in the Peru-Chile region. Conversely, Central Pacific El Ni\~no produces significant rainfall anomalies in the equatorial Pacific.
