In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, a versatile family of global pooling layers can be created. To optimize efficiency, a new, simple and fast pooling layer called the PoolNet has been developed. Compared to other global pooling methods, PoolNet has been shown to achieve better performance on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Additionally, a mathematical analysis of the issue of vanishing gradients in deep neural networks has been provided. Based on this analysis, a new type of neural network called the Unbalanced Optimal Transport Network has been designed. To test its effectiveness, a UOTN model has been trained on the CIFAR-100 dataset. The results show that it surpasses ResNet-18 in terms of performance and demonstrates the capability of deep neural networks to solve the issue of vanishing gradients. The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences based on AGN type. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGN types, to investigate this hypothesis. We conducted an analysis involving multiple linear regression for each Hubble type galaxy subclass, and found a significant variation in the distribution of AGN types within these subclasses. We found the most notable difference being that the suburbs of spiral host galaxies predominantly contain narrow-line region-type AGN, whereas the cores contain broad-line region-type AGN. In contrast, the cores of elliptical host galaxies mainly consist of type "other" AGN. These findings indicate that the environment in which an AGN resides within its host galaxy differs according to its own type. These regional variations hold implications for the accretion of material onto the supermassive black hole. Its availability may be restricted by its proximity to the star-forming region, and by its interaction with other processes within the galaxy. Its rate could also be influenced by the feeding of the black hole and its extension, through the process of gas and dust migration. Its activity may also be regulated by the fed-back energy, through the process of outflow. It is also possible that the long-standing, steady-fed AGN, residing at the centre of the galaxy, is the cause of the radio-emitting, star-forming galaxy. However, our research also reveals potential biases of colour selection based on the type of AGN, particularly in the case of the 'other' type which is heavily contaminated by star-forming galaxies. Our research points out that star-forming galaxies can be falsely classified as narrow-line region-type AGN due to the presence of a high-excitation line-driven outflow. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort and can be labor-intensive due to the cost of accurate annotation. Pre-training with a task other than semantic segmentation, such as classification or depth estimation from a single image, has been shown to expedite the training process and enhance performance. In this research, we evaluate whether depth estimation-based pre-training better promotes speed and performance enhancements in comparison to classification-based pre-training. To achieve this, we conducted an in-depth examination of the influence of pre-training data quantity,, quality, and complexity, along with the selection of convolutional neural network architecture and loss function. Our results demonstrate that pre-training with depth estimation is a more effective approach, and the code is available online at https://github.com/jaychow123/DEP/.

In contrast, we introduce TCube, a breakthrough model capable of describing time-series data in a universal, English language. In our evaluations, TCube surpasses existing methods in both overall quality and consistency, and outperforms a strong baseline model in predicting future time-series data. Furthermore, TCube's time-series forecasting capabilities outshine those of a powerful state-of-the-art model. This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora. Notably, this model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Japanese Newswire Part-of-Speech Task corpus and the Japanese Web Parsing Challenge corpus. Moreover, results indicate that the proposed model exhibits high consistency, demonstrated by repeated training sessions on the same dataset. To validate universality, this study also evaluates the model on a comprehensive corpus compiled from various domains. On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities, where 82.5% of all links are external and 57.0% consist of frequently shared resources. To streamline users' knowledge management, this study delves into the characteristics of these shared links to identify common patterns in external resources that are repeatedly disseminated. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow, where analysis reveals that links to text-based documentation, tutorials, and other reference materials are most often reshared. This leads to observations such as users contributing identical knowledge across multiple posts, users reusing links for promotional purposes, and the issue of links referencing overwhelming amounts of data that can make information retrieval difficult. Our findings offer actionable insights to Stack Overflow moderators and researchers, including the recommendation to implement a centralized knowledge management system for maintaining and updating shared resources to preserve the integrity of the community's collaborative knowledge base. Our study's conclusions and proposed solutions may also hold value for other platforms featuring similar features. A dataset containing all relevant information is available at: https://github.com/quanyinai/Shared-Knowledge-on-Stack-Overflow. (This work is based on the author's master's thesis.)

Galactic rotation curves typically indicate the presence of dark matter, and various solutions have been proposed to explain this phenomenon. Despite significant progress in the field, the underlying nature of dark matter remains poorly understood. We offer an objective review of multiple solutions to the galaxy diversity problem, including their respective strengths and weaknesses. These solutions are compared based on criteria such as reliability, ability to predict, and overall simplicity. While it is unlikely that any single property determines the state of dark matter research, our comprehensive analysis aims to provide a reality-check for researchers working on the topic. By focusing on the most promising approaches, our ultimate goal is to advance the field towards a unified explanation for the galaxy diversity problem. resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes and effects to relevant personal values.

sharing similar values, and that even small amounts of climate information can boost the likelihood of a meaningful conversation.

Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. In particular, autonomous driving poses significant challenges as a supervised learning problem due to dynamic interactions with pedestrians, vehicles, and road conditions. We evaluate the framework using both simulated models of reality and actual video data. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Our findings demonstrate that both temperature and magnetic field strength impact the radius and height of spin-polarized strange quark stars. However, when these parameters are combined, they yield contradictory outcomes, necessitating further experimental and theoretical investigation to clarify these results. Additionally, we observed that the radius of spin-polarized strange quark stars is smaller than that of non-spin-polarized ones, and their maximum mass is comprised of $\sim 1.37 M_\odot$. Our analysis also reveals that temperature and magnetic field both diminish the maximum mass of spin-polarized strange quark stars. It is noteworthy that the effects of temperature and magnetic field are opposite in the radius of spin-polarized strange quark stars. Our study offers an explanation for the phenomenon of small radii observed in ultracompact stars, potentially attributed to the significant influence of magnetic field. Our research may also be applicable to other compact stars comprising free quarks, such as neutron stars. Furthermore, it is conceivable that our findings could be verified using the observation of pulsar PSR J1416-2234, as the resulting analysis of the radius mass-radius relation indicates. Our study positions the stage for exploring the properties of quark stars governed by the interaction of strong magnetic fields and temperature. It is anticipated that future experiments employing the Large Jet Gravitational Wave Detector will uncover the effects of magnetic field and temperature on quark stars, thereby validating our theoretical predictions. Our analysis also underscores the necessity of considering temperature and magnetic effects in the study of compact stars, particularly quark stars, to avoid theoretical inconsistencies. It is expected that our research will contribute to the growth of theoretical understanding of compact stars, paving the way for future research in this area. Our results may also be instrumental in guiding future observations of the Victoria and Large Jet Gravitational Wave Detectors. It is also our hope that future experiments will validate our predictions regarding the radius of small quark stars. Our study offers a theoretical framework that can be utilized to interpret the data collected by these detectors in the future. A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment across a range of platforms, encompassing desktop, mobile, and handheld devices, and even extending to the Chrome OS operating system. A comprehensive evaluation, encompassing scalability, latency, and reliability, as well as a survey of 172 participants, showcase Pando's effectiveness and benefits. Through an empirical study, we have found that to achieve optimal results, a trade-off or balance must be struck between utilising the vast computational resources available on personal devices at lower browser latency levels. Our research has successfully proven that Pando can successfully and efficiently harness the vast computational resources available on personal devices. We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property. Furthermore, we derive formulas for calculating Hausdorff dimensions of levels in these attracting sets and establish a relationship between these dimensions and the Hausdorff dimensions of levels in greedy beta-transformations, thereby generalizing and refining a previous theorem by Briseid-Melby. We also prove that the Hausdorff dimensions of levels in these attracting sets attain their maximum value at the attracting fixed point, a concept referred to as 'Hausdorff optimality.' We also show that the Hausdorff dimensions of levels in these attracting sets exhibit local self-similarity over a compact interval. Additionally, we derive formulas for calculating Hausdorford dimensions of levels in various subsets, including the set of well approximable numbers, the set of poorly approximable numbers, and the set of rational numbers, thus extending a previous result by Fathi-Melby-Melianas. We also show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique periodic and preperiodic properties, thereby generalizing and refining a previous result by Briseid-Melby. We also show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations exhibit a countable number of intersections, thereby generalizing a previous result by Sarig. We also show that the set of numbers which exhibit bad approximation properties exhibits a countable number of intersections, thereby generalizing a previous result by Fathi-Melby-Melianas. We also show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations are winning in Schmidt games, thereby generalizing a previous result by Szelag. We also show that the set of numbers which exhibit good approximation properties exhibits a countable number of intersections, thereby generalizing a previous result by Fathi-Melby-Melianas. Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Our work develops a novel method to gain insight into these models by analyzing how features individually contribute to prediction outcomes. Building on the concept of attribution, our approach, called Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC), offers an intuitive and error-estimation associated with each feature's importance, allowing for better interpretation of these models. DAC's utility is demonstrated through applications to datasets for predicting iodine levels in medical imaging and political votes. Compared to traditional methods, DAC reveals features to be less important than initially reported, and provides a more accurate error estimate, enhancing overall understanding and generalization of these models. DAC's code is available at https://github.com/fortunade/DAC.git. This approach is compatible with model-agnostic explanations and can be applied to various other machine learning models. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation. Moreover, comparative evaluations against 12 distinct baselines demonstrate the superiority of Flatee in overall performance. Furthermore, theoretical analyses and real-world experiments validate the proposed framework's reliability in safeguarding sensitive information, while an open-source implementation based on PyTorch is also made available for continuous community evaluation. The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research presents a novel approach to automated driver testing, utilizing a realistic simulation of hardware peripherals. This solution leverages the LFS (Lightweight Framework for Embedded Systems) testing framework, making it suitable for development within safety-critical and resource-constrained systems. We evaluate the proposed solution by comparing its performance to traditional hardware-based testing, considering aspects like accuracy, efficiency, and computational complexity. The results indicate a substantial reduction in testing time, with a computation complexity of 2.71 for the simulated testing, compared to hardware testing, which has a complexity of 101. To validate the accuracy of our simulation, a code similarity metric is employed, showing a high similarity ratio of 0.95 between the actual and simulated test codes. Moreover, the entire testing process is automated using a Python script, eliminating the need for manual testing. This research contributes simulated test code for I2C, SPI, UART, ADC, and GPIO drivers, as well as a substantial code snippet illustrating how to utilize the LFS testing framework for driver simulations. The source code is publicly available on GitHub. The research highlights that hardware simulation is a feasible and efficient means of testing embedded drivers, thereby reducing costs and the environmental impact of testing. The study also shows that simulated testing can be accurately validated and efficiently automated. Overall, this research offers a solution to the complex testing issues of embedded software development. The solution incorporates a testing framework that can be easily adapted for various driver models, as well as a simulation model that can be extended with more complex hardware components. The latter involves modeling additional hardware complexities using systems of linear equations, as initially proposed in a related study. Utilizing this approach, developers can create their own driver models and test them using the LFS testing framework in conjunction with the provided simulation models. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters, support for common development practices and runtime library usage, by leveraging runtime information. Our experiments with a real-world e-commerce application demonstrate that Timeloops learns a system call policy in under 10 seconds and achieves a 97% accuracy rate, also encompassing new, previously unobserved system calls (4%). Furthermore, we have made Timeloops available to the public as part of the Chase container runtime system. Our evaluation suggests that Timeloops significantly enhances the security of Chase by allowing it to effectively isolate sensitive applications from hazardous system components, while its low-latency and near-real-time decision-making capabilities make it suitable for demanding use cases like financial systems. Overall, Timeloops offers a groundbreaking solution for automating system call filtering in containerized applications, characterized by exceptional accuracy, efficiency, and resilience. Nonetheless, we have identified some limitations in Timeloops, such as potential performance impacts from logging and administration functions, which we plan to address in the future. Our ultimate goal is to develop a fully automated system call filtering tool, also as part of Chase, and make it available to the public. Our research to date indicates that Timeloops significantly outperforms existing system call filtering techniques, such as AppArmour and Google's gVisor. In the near future, we intend to broaden the scope of our research by applying our method to other runtime environments, such as Linux and Windows. We envision a future where Timeloops is integrated into widely used package managers, such as pip for Python and npm for JavaScript, in order to facilitate easy deployment of microservices with built-in system call filtering. Our ultimate vision is to revolutionize the microservices world by making it safe to run multiple untrusted services together, without the need for manual system call filtering. In the future, we will also be researching ways to extend the applicability of Timeloops across a diverse range of domains, such as IoT systems and laptops. Our underlying hypothesis is that Timeloops has immense potential to improve the security and efficiency of software systems. Our ultimate goal is to develop a comprehensive system call filtering method, also as part of Chase, and make it available to the public.

Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification tasks in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments.
To tackle this issue, we've devised an innovative approach to determine if a complex point lies within a defined region of a high-dimensional space with multiple product space components.
To achieve this, we've adapted the concept of Voronoi vertices for multilinear forms and developed algorithms using stochastic gradient descent, affecting both model and embedding parameters.
Empirical evaluations using both synthetic data and real-world scenes showcase the efficiency and accuracy of our method in defining linear boundaries within complex product space structures. 
The associated code can be accessed via our GitHub repository.

Recent studies at the Galactic Center have revealed a diverse population of young stars surrounded by a high-speed globular cluster called Gliese 13. A theoretical analysis from the 1970s predicted that stars orbiting around a supermassive black hole would be evenly distributed if their velocities did not depend on their distance. However, researchers found that the distribution of young stars in Gliese 13 is more concentrated at farther distances and less concentrated at closer distances. A theoretical model developed to explain the strong segregation of stars orbiting around supermassive black holes is being revised to better account for certain effects, which may be responsible for the concentrated distribution of the young stars in Gliese 13. This model considers the possibility of a more detailed analysis of the orbital velocities of the stars as being insufficient and instead uses an average velocity based on past research, taking into account the dynamics of the stars and their three-dimensional distribution. Our simulation of this model shows that the resulting galactic structure can exhibit a concentrated distribution of stars, especially if their orbital velocities are not as varied as they would be if their distances were solely determined by their mass. Our simulation of the strong segregation regime is being used to explain the galactic structure of the concentrated globular cluster called Glausen 2 and the divergent galactic structures of the young stars and the globular cluster in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. Our simulation of the strong segregation regime is also being used to explain why certain stars in various galactic structures are more concentrated in certain areas. A detailed examination of our simulated model reveals that certain characteristics of the galactic structures that we based on past research, such as their shape and size, are actually a result of the varying velocities of the stars, which are dependent on their distance, as predicted by a theoretical analysis from the 1970s. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a square lattice. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes. Depending on the colonizing capabilities of each species, different scenarios of exclusive existence, simultaneous coexistence, or alternative exclusive existences can occur. The application of this model to the invasion biology of biological species reveals that external noise can influence the outcome of competitive interactions. Furthermore, the critical noise level above which exclusive existence prevails can differ depending on the specific parameters of the model. The possible arrangements of species competition observed in the model are species that exclusively exist, two species that never coexist, or one species that always wins and another that never wins. The binary voter model corresponds to a species with limited dispersal that exclusively exists, while the noisy voter model can be seen as a species of unrestricted colonizations that exclusively exists. We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$. This is done by demonstrating the absence of non-zero subalgebras within these regions that are isomorphic to matrix algebras over a finite field. If a subalgebra exists, we show that it must be isomorphic to the algebra of scalar matrices, based on properties of the coordinate function that drives the model's construction. This property implies the existence of certain specialized operator systems within these region algebras, which in turn indicates the infiniteness of the type $II$ classification. This type of investigation is novel in the study of quantum double models and represents a initial step in exploring the intricacies of the algebraic structure of these models through the lens of C*+-algebra and von Neumann algebra theory. Additionally, this study adds another first in the study of quantum double models - a comprehensive comparison of the operator algebras constructed using two different approaches to the double model's abstract algebraic construction, a construction known as the universal C*+-construction and the Lizzi-Samuel-Wen construction. This comparison reveals that the two constructions yield isomorphic algebras, which is a first in the study of quantum double models. Furthermore, this study extends the findings to certain double models based on higher-rank and higher-dimensional systems, constructing a library of reference algebras that encode the intrinsic mathematical structure of these systems through the type of von Neumann algebra theory. Finally, this study proves that the double models can be embedded into a broader class of algebras known as Hopf C*+-algebras, specifically emphasizing the role of a certain mathematical structure known as a 'Himbert-Murphy map' in constructing these algebras, which is a first in the study of quantum double models. To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we develop a model incorporating a coherent feedback loop. This loop, connected to both the cavity and the membrane, enables us to leverage quantum effects to amplify entanglement. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates, specifically those with fixed alignment 
characteristics, to determine their potential in improving resolution beyond 
what's achievable with conventional phase plates. Through mathematical analysis and 
computer simulations, we explore the performance of two designs - a hybrid and a 
multi-aperture phase plate - in enhancing resolution and suppressing inner 
auto-correlation. Our findings indicate that these phase plates can sustain high 
electron currents, thereby preventing sample contamination. However, the phase 
modulations applied to these designs to optimize performance are susceptible to 
temporal fluctuations during actual use. To maintain stability, we recommend 
implementing an control system capable of adjusting the phase shifts based on 
real-time electron energy distributions. Our research also identifies other factors, 
such as electron imaging nonlinearity, electron energy spread, and phase plate 
imperfections, that influence performance, and suggests areas for future research 
and development. Ultimately, we conclude that a programmable hybrid phase plate 
could serve as an effective solution for achieving high-resolution imaging. 

In a supporting role, we also examine the concept of using a hybrid phase plate as 
an 'electronic' objective lens to gain insight into its performance, and explore 
possible designs for an aperture-lens hybrid phase plate. Our analysis indicates 
that these designs can serve as effective tools for high-resolution imaging. 

Our study, while grounded in theoretical considerations and computer simulations, 
may hold significant value for informing the development and design of future 
electrostatic phase plates in transmission electron microscopes. Furthermore, 
by re-examining the underlying physics of phase plate action, our research may 
also contribute to advancements in the design and optimization of electromagnets 
used in scanning transmission electron microscopes. Additionally, our simulation 
method may find applications in other areas of electron optics, such as electron 
spectrometers and electron multipliers. 

We propose that a hybrid phase plate could serve as an efficient and relatively 
simple solution for achieving high-resolution imaging. While there are certain 
design limitations, our analysis suggests that a multi-aperture phase plate could 
also be an effective option. Our study may be seen as an extension of earlier 
research, and we hope that our conclusions will contribute to further 
innovations in this field.

Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper. Ultimately, we reflect on the inherent properties of the fundamental unit of information itself to better comprehend the underlying properties of computational devices. These systems generate speech one segment at a time without considering prior or subsequent segments, resulting in synthesized speech that sounds unnatural when compared to actual speech. To bridge this gap, we propose an approach that leverages a masking strategy in conjunction with a pre-trained audio model. This approach enables the synthesis of high-quality speech that complies with its surrounding environmental context. Specifically, we explore different masking methods and their effect on speech synthesis. Our results reveal that employing a conventional masking strategy successfully encourages the generated speech to conform to its context. Furthermore, our model's code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/Chen-5511/MaskedSpeech. Our model's demo can be accessed via http://speech.nten.org/. Future studies could also investigate other methods for integrating context, such as incorporating sentence-level masking or utilizing pre-trained language models. Additionally, the potential for integrating context in other modalities, such as image description, also presents an interesting area for further research. Our work may also be applicable to other areas of natural language processing, such as text generation, due to its reliance on a trainable transformer model. We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it with established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in accurately selecting variables and recovering relevant structures. Furthermore, the computational time required for our approach is significantly lower than that of existing methods. You can find the implementation of this technique in the R package called <ppc>.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies. Ultimately, this research contributes to the understanding of the spread of conspiracy theories in the context of climate change via social media. Our approach also detects climate-related conspiracy theories and analyzes their transmission, providing insights into their impact on social media discourse. Our research does not, however, explore the causality behind the spread of conspiracy theories and climate discussion. Instead, we identify patterns that warrant further inquiry. Our data collection approach could be applied to other online platforms to gauge the extent to which conspiracy theories entwine with broader public discussions. We envision our work as a foundational aspect of a larger study, aiming to comprehensively examine social media's influence on the dissemination of conspiracy theories. We also envision our data analysis approach as a tool to aid researchers working with limited resources and capacity, as well as social media companies, to gauge the extent to which conspiracy theories pervade online discourse and inform targeted strategies to counteract them. We reveal the underlying assumptions of our approach - that stance detection can accurately capture online attitudes and that a non-paronymous dataset is suitable to analyze the spread of conspiracy theories. We also demonstrate how our data collection and analysis approach can be nuanced by considering factors such as dataset size, variation, and posture coverage, as well as transmission difficulty. We show the results of our experiments, involving variations of Twitter dataset size (from 1.3M to 11.3M tweets), and analyze how these alter our understanding of the dissemination of conspiracy theories. We also examine how our approach changes when we apply it to three distinct climate change stance detection datasets, differing in terms of target (climate change in general, or specific aspects like temperature rise or sea-level increase), variation (six distinct keywords), and posture coverage (four distinct categories). Finally, we investigate how our data collection approach is affected by our stance detection technique and dataset variation, and highlight the implications for further research. We reveal the underlying assumptions of our data analysis approach

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV is reported. Data collected by the CMS experiment during 2016 and 2017, totaling 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, was analyzed. It is hypothesized that dark matter is created through the interaction of a Higgs boson with a top quark or top quark pair. To identify this interaction, signatures from single top quark and top quark pair events were compared to those of standard model processes. It was determined that certain models fail to match the observed data, while others are consistent with the data collected. In particular, it was discovered that the cross section of $t\rightarrow h + \text{DM}$ is likely greater than 1 fb, while $\sigma_{\text{np}}$ of $t\bar{t}$ production with invisible particles is below 1.1 fb. Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has shown that in these systems, the majority of the acquired mass is typically added to the less massive star, resulting in mass equalization.  Yet, young stellar groups are frequently composed of more than two stars that are predicted to exist in a hierarchical setup.  Notwithstanding the significant astrophysical relevance of this issue, little research has been devoted to understanding differential mass acquisition in systems consisting of three or more stars.  We carried out a study aimed at determining whether the trends of mass acquisition predicted for binary systems are applicable to more complex systems consisting of three or more stars.  Utilizing three-dimensional Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics simulations, our research team used the code Phantom to simulate the growth of both binary systems and hierarchical triples within a surrounding disc of gas and dust.  We identified distinct patterns of mass acquisition in systems consisting of three stars and found notable differences between these patterns and those seen in binary systems.  These distinctions are attributed to interactions between the less massive binary in these systems and surrounding disc material.  Notably, our research revealed that in systems consisting of three stars, the less massive binary in these systems accumulates more mass than would be expected in binary systems.  Conversely, the more massive binary in these systems may experience mass loss as the less massive binary in these systems interacts with surrounding disc material.  Additionally, we carried out various variations of our simulations to understand the impact of certain factors on mass acquisition in these systems, specifically the size of the less massive binary, the presence and disappearance of the outer companion in these systems, as well as the breakdown of the disc in these systems.  Our research reveals that in systems consisting of three stars, the less massive binary experiences mass acquisition when its size is relatively large, but experiences mass loss when its size is relatively small. Moreover, the presence of an outer companion in these systems results in a reversal of mass acquisition in the less massive binary, specifically those consisting of three stars. A solar type-I noise storm is created by the rapid movement of charged particles along closed magnetic fields.  These storms are typically found near regions that experience frequent eruions of magnetic field.  This study investigated another aspect of these storms - how they change over time.  To do this, researchers looked at the properties of a particular storm in a region of the solar upper atmosphere called the quiescent chromosphere.  Using data from the Murchison Widefield Array, they analyzed the characteristics of the storm in multiple frequency bands.  As expected, the storm exhibited the typical behavior of increased noise with frequency.  However, the real discovery was that the lower frequency noise decreased at a slower rate than the higher frequency noise.  This implies that the magnetic field dynamics of the storm are controlled by a complex interplay between two different current systems.  This finding is consistent with observations of other solar storms.  Additionally, the data indicated that the storm was triggered by a small but intense energy release, known as a microflare.  This is significant because similar but larger events may be responsible for the eruption of major solar flares. A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity. Furthermore, this design facilitates the integration of a planar atomic clock with a silicon photonic chip, setting the stage for the development of compact, high-performance atomic clocks. Additionally, this design can be adapted for use in portable quantum computers with atomic memory by combining it with a cavity from another material. The optimized parameters for our planar-integrated MOT have been thoroughly discussed, along with the trap's optical and magnetic coherence characteristics. These parameters have enabled the creation of an extremely compact MOT with a small trap volume, capturing a large population of atoms. The implementation of this design using a 2-inch wafer offers the advantage of mass-produced, scalable components for magnetic and optical coherence, ensuring high precision and coherence in the trapped atoms. The optimization of this design for rubidium atoms has potential implications for the development of new atomic clocks and gravigrometers with reduced size and weight, as well as contributions to ongoing research in portable quantum computers with atomic memory. The specific design choices and options for optimization have been explored, along with a plan to integrate this setup with a cavity for use in magnon-based quantum computing. The potential for adaptation to various types of atoms, such as ytterbium, has also been considered, given its potential as a material for large-scale, room-temperature quantum computing due to its long-lived states. The design could be modified to meet specific requirements for any given atom, with a focus on ytterbium as a possible future application. The development of this compact mot represents a significant breakthrough towards the integration of atomic clocks, gravigrometers, and quantum computers using a common platform based on semiconductor technology, offering high precision, coherence, and the potential for mass production. The mot has been designed with the capability for in-housing a single atom, while its potential for use with larger numbers of atoms is also being explored, particularly for room-temperature quantum computing. From a technical perspective, the challenge involved the optimization of the mot's performance, given the limitations imposed by the grating chip and the coil chip

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine the impact of a finite radius of influence. Through both analytical and numerical methods, we study how this influence radius affects accretion rates. We discover that for small non-zero angular momentum, the merging process is divided into three distinct time periods: initially, kinetic energy dominates; in the middle period, potential energy dominates; and finally, the impact of angular momentum becomes significant. The potential energy dominated period determines the overall accretion rate, whereas the momentum influenced period indicates a minor correction. Kinetic and potential energy are in a state of equilibrium at the radius of influence, which helps to understand and verify our findings. Additionally, without angular momentum, the merging rates are lower than those calculated in established studies. Higher angular momentum, however, results in enhanced accretion rates, even changing the order of importance of kinetic and potential energies in the accretion process. Several numerical solutions are developed to illustrate the influence of spin parameters and boundary conditions on accretion rates, revealing that for large values of spin, to the extent that the radius of influence extends to the event horizon, accretion rates are heightened. Consequently, a more precise calculation of accretion rates must take into account both the kinetic characteristics of the cloud and the gravitational influence of the black hole. This research is a development of the study of accretion rates by Gruzinov and Shapiro, and is part of a broader body of work on black hole accretion by the same research group. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys, combined with multi-fiber spectroscopy, allow for a thorough examination of this hypothesis like never before.  By cross-referencing a near-infrared catalogue from the Gaia-ESO survey with a more comprehensive photometric survey, we have identified 28 massive stars located in the less crowded areas surrounding Westerlund 2.  These stars are predominantly early-type luminosity class III.  By comparing the locations of these stars relative to each other, we noticed that none are found in the dense central parts of Westerlund 2, despite extensive search.  Additionally, we noticed a significant absence of O-type stars in the less crowded areas surrounding Westerlund 2, which we attribute to these stars being obscured by dust.  Once we account for dust effects, we found that the distribution of late O- and early B-type stars does not significantly differ from the distribution of these stars in the Gaia catalogue.  By contrast, we found that the distribution of massive B-type luminosity class I stars appears more dispersed than those of luminosity class III.  Our findings suggest that massive stars are less likely to form in less crowded environments, but once they do exist, they can spread out due to dynamic processes.  This is consistent with the notion that massive stars are primarily formed in clusters and then move to less crowded areas once they exist.  Further research is required to distinguish between the two hypotheses.  It is also possible that late O- and early B-type stars are consistently formed in clusters of various densities.  If true, then our findings would merely reflect the uneven distribution of these stars across different regions of the Milky Way.  Additional observations in different parts of the galaxy are needed to resolve this issue.  We have also discovered a young moving group centered on Westerlund 2, which consists of roughly 180 stars spanning a radius of 650 pc.  This group appears to contain a significant number of massive stars, primarily in the dense central parts of Westerlund 2, and is predominantly composed of B-type stars.  It is evident that the central parts of Westerlund 2 are a relatively young cluster in the process of dissolving. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly useful in data restoration, allowing historical black and white images to be repurposed for modern color display technologies. While the process is relatively straightforward for straightforward images, it presents significant challenges when addressing complex subjects such as astronomy. In order to produce accurate and scientifically legitimate results, it is essential to incorporate domain-specific knowledge. This research presents a novel, state-of-the-art approach to colorization and upscaling of astronomical images utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks. The proposed model leverages domain knowledge to guide the colorization process through the use of transfer learning and domain-specific corruptions. By assessing a range of methods, this research demonstrates the importance of addressing noise reduction in order to generate visually appealing images. The implemented model was tested on the SDSS dataset consisting of 12,000 images, producing results within reach of contemporary computational capabilities. Furthermore, this research delves into the challenges and limitations of automatic colorization, underscoring the need for further development before this technique can be utilized within the astronomical community. The implemented model, along with pre-trained weights, can be accessed via a user-friendly interface at https://github.com/Chercherry/Astronomical_colorization. Additionally, the following link provides access to the colored and original images utilized in the research: https://doi.org/10.6086/M4EK21.1.

We introduce a pioneering neural network framework that reframes the widely accepted Universal Approximation Theorem in a novel, application-friendly approach. This new paradigm bypasses the traditional challenges of gradient computation, instead employing an iterative process that calculates each neuron's output directly. As a result, the proposed framework significantly reduces computational overhead, striking a desirable balance between efficiency and efficacy. Additionally, our framework enables seamless integration of inherent biases within the neural network architecture, thereby boosting its overall accuracy. Through thorough examinations, the computational benefits of this algorithm were demonstrated through real-world benchmarks on popular datasets (MNIST, FMNIST, and CIFAR-10), showcasing its capability to approximate complex target functions with high precision while minimizing additional computational cost. Moreover, the results revealed that the proposed framework outperformed state-of-the-art models in terms of both computational complexity and numerical accuracy. This breakthrough neural network architecture has immense potential for real-world implementation due to its enhanced efficiency and high approximation capabilities. The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation. It summarizes the results of two large-scale surveys conducted by the panel in 2021, focusing on the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and the needs and interests of young researchers in the ECFA community. It also describes the panel's initiatives to address the challenges faced by young researchers, promote inter-generation networking, and foster a sense of community within the ECFA community. Moving forward, the panel plans to continue to listen to the voices of young researchers, advocate for their interests within the ECFA community, and take proactive actions to address the needs and concerns of this group. It encourages every young researcher to reach out to the panel for support, guidance, or simply a platform to share concerns and ideas, as well as contribute to the panel's efforts by sharing their expertise and knowledge. The panel is happy to hear any suggestion, idea, or concern, please email: ecfa-ecr-panel@cernNOSPAM.ch. common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy. Furthermore, our experimental results reveal that
this strategy not only enhances the models' ability to recognize relationships
between established words but also improves their ability to anticipate unlisted
object nominations, marking a notable advancement in state-of-the-art models.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining a prediction confidence or normalizing the data distribution. This study introduces a novel approach, semi-generative modelling, which integrates discriminative and generative techniques to create a flexible framework for handling various types of covariate shift. Our method employs a deep neural network to model the shared structure between tasks, represented by cause and effect features, to facilitate adaptation without explicit normalization. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on synthetic datasets, real-world hospital-visit datasets, and language-modeling tasks with zero-shot and few-shot settings. Comparative assessments are also conducted with established methods: MLE, reweighting, gradient normalization, and a generative adversarial network. The results show that semi-generative modelling outperforms other methods in all tested scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/shruthig/sgm. Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level. Additionally, we introduce a new geometric structure for attention mechanisms that facilitates the efficient computation of complex dependency graphs in descriptive string sequences. In a real-world application, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in aligning biological sample data under the constraint of shared spatial topology. Overall, our geometric model presents a unified view of deep learning that can be used to develop new architectures with established connections to established geometric theories. A publicly available code repository for our work contains the computational implementations of the geometric structures discussed throughout the study. In particular, we have included a Python package called GeoDL that enables the automatic geometric interpretation of deep learning architectures. With GeoDL, developers can quickly and easily map the geometric structures of deep learning architectures without prior training in geometric theories. Furthermore, GeoDL provides a range of new algorithms for deep learning architecture design, including new variants of GANs based on geometric structures, as well as hyperparameter tuning tools. Furthermore, GeoDL includes a new Python package called GeoDL-RT that enables real-time video rendering based on the geometric structures of deep learning architectures. With GeoDL-RT, developers can create real-time video displays of deep learning-based image denoising, restoration, and super-resolution, among other applications. A demo video illustrating the capabilities of GeoDL-RT is included in the supplementary material. For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together. First, we'll derive a formula describing the extreme Stirling number itself, then use that result to develop a formula connecting two different variations of the number. Finally, we'll explore the mathematical significance of these variations, highlighting their relationships with other, already established formulas. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our data showcases excellent agreement with exact diagonalization results, thereby substantiating the method's robustness and efficiency. Ultimately, this methodology's potential to handle severe sign problems makes it an ideal candidate for tackling intricate many-body phenomena. Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, these studies have pinpointed the masses of binary systems consisting of proto-stars, reaching up to $\sim 0.25$ solar masses per component. To gain a deeper understanding of the formation processes of such systems, we conducted a series of computational simulations based on idealized core fragmentation. Our study focused on how a rotating parental core collapses and fragments when its total mass increases. Key findings from these experiments include the following: (i) Binary systems formed through this process have a mass distribution that closely mirrors that observed in recent astronomical studies, with a power-law slope of $-2.15$; (ii) Most proto-stars have masses below $0.25$ solar masses, with few exceeding this threshold; and (iii) As the mass of the parental core increases, its rotational velocity remains relatively constant, leading to a reversal of mass ratio, favoring lower-mass binaries at higher masses. These discoveries demonstrate that the formation of systems comprising multiple stellar objects is likely a common phenomenon, giving rise to a broad array of binary configurations. Their ultimate survival rates and patterns of rotation remain subjects for further investigation. Mass disparity in binaries may serve as telltale signs of formation mechanisms through core fragmentation. Additionally, as observed in astronomical studies, the resulting distribution of binary system masses is unaffected by the angular momentum of the parental core. This discovery underscores the significance of mass increase in the formation of systems comprising multiple stellar objects, providing insight into their potential for future star formation. Using mass augmentation in simulations of core fragmentation may provide valuable perspective on the formation processes of such multiple stellar object systems as observed today. Our study offers theoretical validation for the patterns of binary configuration and formation that have been recently documented. Furthermore, the theoretical mass dispersion of binary systems in our simulation masses closely mirrors that observed in astronomical studies. Our analysis provides the groundwork for future research into the formation of systems comprising multiple stellar objects, incorporating both mass augmentation and the protostellar population's dynamic properties. Our results offer a preview of the patterns of binary configuration and formation that should be seen as formation proceeds further, drawing from the growing body of observational data for insight. Our study offers the first theoretical  supports for the patterns of binary configuration and formation that have been recently documented. New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the usefulness of the weighted skew-spectrum as an optimal estimator of angular bispectrum amplitude in extracting non-Gaussian information from both galaxy survey data and microwave background data that have been affected by lensing. We compare the sensitivity of the skew-spectrum to three typical bispectrum estimators and find that it outperforms them significantly in terms of Fisher information. Furthermore, we suggest and evaluate the practical implementation of the skew-spectrum across various data sets, including those with varying levels of noise. Our results indicate that using the skew-spectrum to analyze data combinations such as CMB lensing and galaxy clustering can lead to more precise constraints on models of non-Gaussian simulations by at least a factor of four compared to using the bispectrum directly. We also show that using the skew-spectrum on CMB lensing data alone results in more precise constraints on sigma_8 and N_s compared to analysis using the lensing power spectrum alone, demonstrating that incorporating angular bispectrum information into skew-spectrum analysis offers an enhancement of over a factor of two. We expect that the skew-spectrum based approach will play a vital role in the upcoming combination of cosmic surveys. It also presents potential applications in other fields of research, such as galaxy bispectra and primordial non-Gaussianity analysis. Most of the code used to evaluate our approach, including our own extension of the Cosmo-Enzpi package to perform skew-spectrum based analysis, is openly available at https://github.com/PetoUz/CosmoEnzpi-skew-spectrum. Future upgrades are planned to integrate our approach with other codes such as Healpix and Ccl. We are also open to collaborations and suggestions at puzelis@gmail.com. We hope that this tool becomes useful to the research community. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor. Our analysis covered 349 common rumors circulating in China and compared their spread to COVID-19 information accuracy as predicted by experts. Our research aimed to explore the behavior of online rumors in China, equip netizens with fact-checking skills, and provide insights for social media platforms, government agencies, and public health institutions to combat misinformation during crises. Our findings could guide efforts to monitor and mitigate the spread of misinformation through collaboration between technology giants, government agencies, and health institutions. Our data can support the development of rumor detection systems and aid crisis management by identifying high-risk periods for spreading misinformation. Our analysis also underscored the crucial role of social media platforms in containing misinformation and highlighted the necessity for government intervention to prevent harm from online rumors. Our research finally emphasized the importance of individual responsibility in preventing the spread of misinformation. This research investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Through experiments using SPOT-5 hyperspectral data and four relevant land cover categories in Istanbul's Adalar district, we evaluate the accuracy of classifications resulting from different dimensionality reduction methods. Compared to a full 204-band hyperspectral dataset, classifications based on reduced spectral configurations exhibit negligible differences, implying that certain hyperspectral bands convey superfluous information for the specific classification purpose in question. By employing the Akaike information criterion, we identify the optimal spectral configuration for the dataset in question, ultimately consisting of six spectral intervals achieving the best results among the methods examined. Consequently, employing spectral dimensionality reduction can yield computational and data storage benefits without significantly compromising classification performance. Therefore, this technique is advisable for use in hyperspectral image classification tasks involving limited bandwidths and distinct categories. Furthermore, this study highlights the usefulness of hyperspectral remote sensing in urban areas for land cover management, emphasizing the need to tailor dimensionality reduction to the specific requirements of each dataset and application. Future developments of this research will focus on integrating relevant machine learning techniques, such as feature selection and genomic hyperspectral image classification. Additionally, we intend to assess the applicability of spectral dimensionality reduction to other types of hyperspectral datasets and classification methods, including multi-class and kernel-based approaches. Lastly, we plan to utilize the reduced spectral configurations obtained in this research to address problems in the genomics hyperspectral field and evaluate their potential in tackling challenges within genomics hyperspectral remote sensing. Additionally, we will carry out further analysis on urban areas to assess the efficacy of hyperspectral remote sensing in distinguishing between various land cover types, ultimately informing decisions related to dimensionality reduction in genomics hyperspectral remote sensing. Finally, we intend to assess the feasibility of applying the spectral configuration configurations obtained in this research to tasks in genomics hyperspectral remote sensing and provide recommendations on the implementation of dimensionality reduction in genomics hyperspectral remote sensing. Additionally, we will derive lessons from the results of this research and make recommendations on the use of dimensionality reduction techniques in genomics hyperspectral remote sensing. Lastly, we plan to publish our research on the applicable methods for dimensionality reduction in genomics hyperspectral remote sensing, along with the urban examples that informed our choices, and make the related code and datasets publicly available. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same tasks is a viable option to improve network interpretability. In this research, we explore the potential of using sparse networks and network compression through the elimination or modification of redundant or less important parameters. Due to the large number of parameters within many neural network layers, the task is often referred to as 'network pruning' or 'compression.' In this study, we investigated the possible applications and effects of network compression on natural language processing models, specifically focusing on the key parameters within the final linear layer. By selecting and tuning approximately 0.3% of the network parameters, we demonstrated that substantial compression is achievable without compromising task accuracy. The findings also highlighted the significant reduction in inference time that compression allows. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, such as the KL-divergence and pinwheel losses, yield superior outcomes compared to established methods like cross-entropy. These results suggest that future deep learning models should meticulously consider loss function selection to optimize performance. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of training neural networks using the KL-divergence and pinwheel losses for multi-class classification tasks. Additionally, we show that combining these losses yields outstanding results, even when utilizing a simplified model, thus paving the way for future explorations of deep learning with KL-divergence and pinwheel losses. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexvonderwiesche/DeepLearningLossSurvey. Our report has been accepted for publication in the 2022 IEEE International Symposium on Intelligent Automation and Information Systems. We are contributing our research under a liberal license to facilitate widespread use and adaptation. We advocate for transparent research practices, such as clearly disclosing related works, research limitations, and assumptions, as well as openly sharing knowledge to foster a collaborative environment. We also explored other topics, such as the challenges of training deep learning models to withstand attacks and the need for more robust loss functions, but ultimately chose not to include these topics in our final research report. We are engaging in a data-driven research agenda, guided by an outstanding question, namely "What is the impact of loss function variation in deep learning for classification?" Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently heuristic. Within the context of a theoretical framework developed by Kraichnan, a new Hamiltonian-based analysis is applied to parquet's structure in the context of fermionic particles, resulting in a natural formation of the theory's underlying equations through its canonical representation. This approach reveals the inherent connection between the conserving properties of the derived scattering amplitude and the traditional parquet theory. Although the derived amplitude conserves properties at a microscopic level, it does not maintain symmetry. In contrast, the traditional amplitude maintains symmetry but fails to ensure conservation at any point. Ultimately, the decision to use one amplitude over the other is determined by the specific requirements of the system under consideration rather than its adherence to a theoretical ideal. Both amplitudes are capable of accurately describing low-energy characteristics of systems that interact strongly, such as those exhibited by electron gas and certain heavy fermion systems. A corresponding analysis for fermions is compared with an existing bose-based analysis, revealing common practices in the derivation of scattering amplitudes and introducing potential avenues for application in the study of interacting bosonic and fermionic systems. Potential areas of study include but are not limited to: $\cdot$ low-energy electron physics $\cdot$ heavy fermion systems with strong interactions $\cdot$ atomic physics $\cdot$ quark-gluon plasma and other applications of strongly interacting quantum systems. Furthermore, this analysis suggests new paths for investigation in these fields of study. Possibly significant areas of study that were not previously considered are: $\cdot$ low-energy electron physics $\cdot$ heavy fermion systems with strong interactions. Additionally, since the derived amplitude maintains the conserving properties of the scattering amplitude, it may be possible to utilize the derived amplitude in approaches that utilize conservation principles. It is also possible that the traditional amplitude could be utilized in approaches that utilize symmetry principles. Consequently, the choice between conserving and symmetric amplitudes depends on the specific requirements of the system under consideration. The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator. This theoretical approach aims to simulate the exciton condensation using a first-principles method and an infinite-range interaction approximation. By applying this approximation to the electron-electron interaction, our results reveal that TiSe2 exhibits exciton condensation at temperatures below 180 K. Furthermore, the characteristic lattice distortion associated with the (3√2x3√2) superstructure of the excitonic insulator phase is in agreement with experimental findings. Additionally, the current approach can be generalized to model other excitonic insulators. Preliminary calculations of the electron-electron interaction using a more complex approximation of exciton pairs yield comparable results to those obtained with the (3√2x3√2) approximation, underscoring the validity of the approach. However, the pair distribution function reveals subtle deviations between the two approximations that may potentially provide insight into the nature of exciton pairs in materials like TiSe2. By comparing the results of these calculations with the experimentally observed phonon softening in TiSe2, our findings indicate that the charge response to phonons is intact despite the formation of an excitonic state. This suggests that the excitonic insulator phase of TiSe2 can be described through the interaction of electrons with both electron-electron and electron-ion potentials. Consequently, the notion of "electrons in a solid" being transformed into "electron holes and pairs" is an oversimplification, as the ion core continues to exert an influence on the system. Moreover, the presence of uncondensed electrons necessitates the use of more complex mathematical operators to model the excitonic state. By applying the first principles of many-body theory to the problem at hand, our results demonstrate that the resulting mathematical equations for the problem are both self-consistent and controllable. Furthermore, the first-principles approach based on the infinite-range interaction approximation is analogous to methods used in both superconductivity and ultra-cold atom research. Therefore, the excitonic insulator phase of TiSe2 can be viewed as a three-dimensional realization of the phenomenon of exciton condensation that has been observed in two-dimensional systems. Additionally, the phenomenon of exciton condensation in metals represents a fundamental transformation of matter in which the excitonic state emerges from the interaction of electron-electron and electron-ion potentials, and is characterized by both structural and electronic phase transitions. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. This study proposes a novel approach - the Minimax Active Learning algorithm (MAL) - that minimizes the influence of models' uncertainty while maximizing diversity in the selected dataset. By regularly updating its strategy through backpropagation, MAL adapts to ongoing changes in the training dataset and model. Evaluations on four image classification datasets demonstrate that MAL outperforms existing methods in achieving high accuracy with a small number of annotated samples. Additionally, MAL's designed components and individual modules are effectively integrated to achieve superior performance.
