A novel category of stochastic processes, designated'multiple-entry reinforcement processes', is investigated in this study. This class of processes involves a continuous evolution of objects categorized into distinct groups based on specific attributes, where objects belonging to the same category act independently but interactions among different categories are synchronized. The research focuses on modeling dependencies between different data sets by treating them as separate 'entries' of a single data set, where each data set is represented as a collection of independent data points. The study shows that, under certain conditions, this model exhibits asymptotic similarity to a random matrix generated through a process of matrix perturbation. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the'spectral density' of the model converges to a universal distribution as the size of the data sets increases indefinitely, while the distance between this spectral density and the universal distribution converges to zero at a rate proportional to the logarithm of the size of the data sets. The study presents two possible methods for estimating the spectral density from finite data sets, offering theoretical assessments of the convergence rate and bias of these estimation methods. Results show that one method achieves nearly optimal convergence rate, where the rate is solely dependent on the strength of interactions between data sets. A comprehensive mathematical framework is established to support these findings, where a previously established relationship between these estimation methods and a class of polynomial regression models is further generalized and simplified. Furthermore, a systematic approach is presented for deriving uniform convergence bounds of several estimation methods of spectral density. The study demonstrates that many existing spectral density estimators possess an optimal rate of convergence under specific conditions. A comprehensive simulation study is conducted to examine and compare the performance of several estimation methods, where results show that one particular method exhibits nearly optimal convergence and superior practical performance across various scenarios. A novel estimation method, where data sets are artificially expanded using techniques of symmetry and periodicity, is also introduced and shown to offer improvements over existing solutions. The study offers theoretical justification for this expansion method and presents a comprehensive mathematical framework to support its results and findings. Additionally, a comparative study of several existing spectral density estimators is conducted to examine their performance on real-world data sets, where results show that one particular method exhibits nearly optimal convergence and superior practical performance across various datasets. The study offers comprehensive mathematical proofs to support its results, where many key concepts of stochastic processes, polynomial regression models, and random matrices are carefully examined and utilized. A comprehensive mathematical framework is presented to support the results and findings of this study. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework is based on the notions of flow and harmony to describe the interaction of proofs as a form of theatrical exchange. By applying the harmony condition to the realm of proofs, this paper shows that it mimics the behavior of both the inversion and recovery principles. Additionally, by extending the harmony condition to also restrict occurrences of proofs, known as proofs with occurrences, along with their corresponding notions of correctness and harmony with occurrences, this paper is able to reproduce the original three notions. This extension is then demonstrated on two examples, one of which involves the exponential modality and cut-elimination. This reinterpretation offers a new understanding of these concepts and highlights the evidence that the Computational Ludics framework is a versatile tool for analysing the structure of proofs. Furthermore, this paper predicts that the harmony condition should hold for any proof system that is consistent with the principles of natural deduction. Since the concepts of inversion, recovery, and cut-elimination are pivotal in understanding the fundamental structure of proofs, this paper expects that the results will yield significant implications for the fields of proof theory, and that the Computational Ludics framework will serve as a useful tool for explaining and reinterpreting these concepts. Finally, this paper expects that the predicted relationship between harmony and correctness should hold not only for the realm of proofs, but also for the domain of proofs with occurrences. Therefore, this paper is confident that the results will yield new insights and perspectives on the themes of inversion, recovery, and cut-elimination. Ultimately, this paper is an exercise in exploring the creativity of the Computational Ludics framework as a tool for explaining and reinterpreting the fundamental concepts of proof theory. Since the results will yield novel interpretations of the core concepts of proof theory, this paper is confident that the results will be of great importance to the fields of proof theory and the theory of types. Additionally, this paper expects that the results will be of great importance to the fields of programming languages and type inference. Finally, this paper expects that the results will be of great importance to the fields of logic in general and belief change in particular. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Additional benefits include improved robustness to labeling errors and the capability to detect novel states that were not encountered during training. We demonstrate the time efficiency of our approach through comprehensive evaluations on three mujoco tasks. Furthermore, we provide a framework for implementing our methodology on complex vision-based tasks. Through successful application to the AI2 Grader challenges, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach. Our project code is available at https://github.com/AsyaDov/Visual-AACR. Experimental videos are available at https://as Yadov.com/time-efficient-reward-learning.

Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties. While the classical Smyth topological powerspace does preserve core-compact properties, it does not uniformly do so. The Smyth topological space itself preserves local compactness, but this property may be lost in its powerspace. However, the core-compactness of a space's Chawna powerspace does uniformly correspond to the core-compactness of the original space. A key finding here involves a detailed analysis of the relationship between a space's core-compactness and the core-compactness of its Chawna and Smyth powerspaces. Moreover, we show the core-compactness of a right limit of topological spaces implies the core-compactness of their product space, a result that has implications for the continuity of the Smyth topological powerspace functor. Ultimately, this study provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between a space and its powerspaces. Furthermore, it offers a framework for generalising results about core-compact spaces to other classes of spaces with additional structural properties. In doing so, we generalise a result about the continuity of the Smyth topological powerspace functor from a specific class of localic frames to a broader class of localic frames with core-compact covers. We also examine the relationship between a space's core-compactness and the core-compactness of its Chawna and Smyth powerspaces, as well as the relationship between a space and its Eifler powerspace. In particular, we show a space's core-compactness corresponds to the core-compactness of its Eifler powerspace if and only if the space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Eifler powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties. We also show a right limit of topological spaces is core-compact if and only if their product space is core-compact, a result which has implications for the continuity of the Eifler powerspace functor. Ultimately, this study provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between a space and its powerspaces, as well as a framework for generalising results about core-compact spaces to other classes of spaces with additional structural properties. We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points. The study further identifies various geometric and analytic features of the configuration space, ultimately leading to a general method for constructing point vortex loops and related solutions for 2D ideal fluid flows. The study also explores connections to other areas of mathematics and physics, notably linking it to recent research on hyperbolic surface diffeomorphisms. In particular, a specific type of point vortex loop is found to exhibit similar behavior to the Teichmüller line when compared to the modular group for a specific value of the vorticity. The study delves into calculating geometric and analytic properties of these point vortex loops for specific values of vorticity and points, leading to new insights in both the low-regime and ultra-high regime. The study concludes by highlighting remaining open problems and potential areas for further investigation. Alongside the main text, an appendix provides an alternative approach for constructing point vortex loops using a specific type of reference loop and establishes a relationship between this construction and another method for building point vortex loops along curves. Additionally, the study provides a quick construction method for building point vortex loops in specific shapes. Furthermore, the study explores and calculates the length of certain curves within the configuration space under specific geometric and topological considerations. Lastly, the study links a specific type of point vortex loop to a mathematical concept known as a "spin network," a construct commonly used in both physical and mathematical theories. The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, warranting greater theoretical attention in the coming years. Enhanced data sets from Belle-II, as well as LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, will soon provide more concrete insights. If experimental findings confirm the current indications of new physics, it is anticipated that the next generation of physicists will play a crucial role in unraveling the underlying truth. This article serves as a summary of the discussions held during the 13th International Workshop on the CKM Unit (CKM2021), where leading researchers from both theoretical and experimental circles converged to discuss the latest advancements in the field. The primary topics of discussion centered around the underlying new physics responsible for potential violations of lepton flavor universality, as well as the potential for $\tau$ decays to offer breakthroughs into the nature of neutrino mass, dark matter, and baryogenesis. Furthermore, progress in using real-world and fictitious $\tau$ decays to compute QCD parameters was discussed. The critical implications of upcoming $\tau$ experiments for the unperturbed and perturbed Standard Model were also examined. This article is divided into five distinct sections, each delving into specific topics from the workshop. Additional contributions from the workshop participants are gathered at the end. Due to the rapid evolving nature of the field, the content of this article may already be partially outdated, and it is expected to become even more antiquated in the years to come. This article is best considered as a historical snapshot of the state of the art in the field at the workshop. For the most up-to-date information, readers are referred to regularly updated online materials. This article is intended to serve as a starting point or a reminder for young investigators tackling the numerous challenges posed by precision $\tau$ physics. It is expected that the next generation of physicists will make further substantial contributions to the field, helping to bridge theory and experiment. This article is dedicated to the memory of Nick van Eijk. It is our hope that future generations will build upon the ideas presented within its walls, enabling us to finally unlock the full potential hidden within $\tau$ physics. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK. The findings indicate that the proposed method results in more accurate parameter estimations and posterior concentrations. Additionally, a parameter transformation with'm' close to 0.5 exhibits the best characteristics in line with standard asymptotic analysis. This method is made available through our online repository at: https://github.com/tommy-uk/pp_reparamiser. Do not hesitate to contact the author via t.davenport@lancaster.ac.uk for any questions or feedback. This work was funded as part of the PARISE project under grant NE/R004826/1. The data used in this study consists of daily extreme rainfall totals obtained from the Met Office's rainfall database. This project was carried out in collaboration with Professor David J. T. Sumner at Lancaster University. Key words: Bayesian inference, Extreme value, Parameter reparameterisation, Poisson process, Non-homogeneous, Inverse problems, Markov Chain Monte Carlo.

In recent years, various theories proposal the idea that Brownian motion could be driven by quantum fluctuations.  Although these ideas are interesting, they lack a realistic connection to the underlying physical process causing the motion.  Here we develop a model for molecular motors that captures their dynamics through a process involving the sudden transfer of electrons, followed by the relaxation of leftover energy.  We find that this model generates sustained non-reversible movement, and demonstrate how to apply the calculated force and speed to a thermodynamic framework, even in cases where the model's microscopical components are beyond analytical solution.  As an example, we apply our general model to a specific device, verifying that its movement is indeed non-reversible and computing its mechanical and electrical properties.  The model proposed here provides a universal tool for analyzing molecular motors that transfer electrons, and can be used to identify whether such motors are truly non-reversible.  Furthermore, we show that it is possible to tune the motor's speed and force to optimal values by adjusting its electronic structure.  The method used here for calculating the motor's thermodynamic properties can be an independent merit, allowing the use of the model beyond the realm of thermodynamics.  The simulated microscopical process can be studied using advanced techniques such as scanning tunneling spectroscopy, and we outline how to implement this in a real-life experiment.  The suggested methodology can be applied not only to analyze already built molecular motors, but also to guide the development of new, improved motors, and can be particularly useful in devices currently under design where a sneak-circuit archaism could generate undesired consequences.  The sustained movement generated by our model has two forms: continuous non-reversible transfer of charge, and the transfer of a single charge in a series of jumps.  The model based on continuous charge transfer matches results previously calculated using other theories, and our findings for the single charge transfer have similar results to a different theoretical model previously published.  The analysis of how the quantum fluctuations affect the sustained movement generates two different mathematical equations, and solving these gives two different solutions.  One solution matches results previously calculated using other theories, and the other solution gives results for the single charge transfer.  The two different solutions have similar properties, and we outline how to choose the correct solution. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of infectious diseases in enclosed settings. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to other types of enclosed spaces, such as airplanes, theaters, and shopping malls. To facilitate the use of our findings in epidemiological modeling, we also explored the relationship between aerosol transport configurations and the coefficients typical of 'well mixed' models. Additionally, through parameter estimation based on COVID-19 transmission risk assessments, we derived key parameters that influence disease spread and the effectiveness of countermeasures in urban buses. Our analysis highlights the importance of considering the differences between detailed and simplified models to inform public health strategies. By doing so, we contribute to the development of general guidelines that could be applied to urban transportation settings to mitigate the transmission of infectious diseases. Moreover, our study demonstrates that through careful analysis of the underlying physical phenomena, it is possible to reconcile numerical model predictions of low-to-medium Nusselt numbers, which we used to inform urban transportation policy, in an effort to prevent future outbreaks. Ultimately, the differentiation in model types holds implications for epidemic emergencies handled by public health experts, as well as for ongoing research aimed at developing simulation tools for urban transportation to combat the spread of diseases. This work remains relevant today, given the ongoing pandemic and the ongoing efforts to navigate situations of 'low N' and potentially 'no indoor transmission', where a deep understanding of the dynamics at play is essential. To that end, we have based our investigation on numerical simulations that were already completed as of September 2020. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which did not introduce any additional axioms into the system. From these formal proofs, we were able to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code for double-sided auctions. To validate the practical value of our research, we successfully tested the verified code using real market data from an exchange to automatically identify potential program violations. Our research aims to promote the application of formal methods in industry, as well as promote the use of formal techniques in computer science education. We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic. 

In our study, the decay widths of bottom mesons exhibited sensitivity to the cut-off parameter Lambda, with values ranging from approximately 0.25 GeV to 0.35 GeV. These outcomes may be informative for future research seeking to refine these parameters. 

We also compared our calculated mass values of bottom mesons to those predicted by isospin approximation, revealing that while most masses align closely with each other, significant discrepancies exist for certain states (notably the $F_3(1980)$), suggesting the need for additional considerations in terms of isospin approximation. 

Our research also allowed us to assess the domain in which quark potential models may operate by analyzing the domain of quark potential validity. In doing so, we discovered that the domain of quark potential validity in F-wave states lies within a range that is significantly smaller than what is seen in S-wave states. 

Our research on Regge trajectories offered valuable insights into the quark-confinement property of QCD, revealing that for F-wave bottom mesons, the ground-state quark and antiquark both satisfy mass quark convergence (M_q = M_{\bar q}) within a precision of approximately 5%, a finding that holds true across multiple planes. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future research on the quark and antiquark mass convergence. 

Our analysis of bottom mesons also enabled us to examine the quark potential under the influence of the QCD string tension constant (beta), a parameter that significantly affects the quark and antiquark mass relationship. By calculating the ratio of quark to antiquark mass (m_q / m_{\bar q}) as the angular momentum (J) approaches infinity, we were able to refine this calculation, yielding a precise estimate of this ratio.

The dynamic mode decomposition technique is successfully able to extract informative insights from large datasets, however the effectiveness of this method greatly depends on the accuracy of its underlying assumption.  When this assumption is breached, the technique generates meaningless'retained dynamics', leading to a decrease in its overall performance.  In order to mitigate this limitation, we introduce a new method, the Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO), which aims to differentiate between linear and nonlinear system components.  By applying a kernel learning approach, LANDO first identifies the linear system structure while minimizing error, before determining the residual nonlinear component using a kernel dynamic mode decomposition technique.  Through theoretical analysis and various numerical and real-world tests, our findings confirm that LANDO successfully extracts linear system features and accurately detects nonlinear components.  What's more, our research reveals that these linear and nonlinear components can be recombined to obtain the original dataset, thereby providing new insights into the underlying structure of the system. A major benefit of our method is its ability to operate in an offline setting, thereby making it suitable for a wide range of applications. The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe, from casual enthusiasts to competitive masters. Despite rule changes being highly disapproved of in the past, the chess community has come to accept online platforms as a normal part of the game. These platforms, which enable real-time data collection, have made possible the analysis of chess players' opening moves on a massive scale. This study utilizes a massive dataset of one million chess games played online to examine how chess players employ different openings in response to varying circumstances. Our research reveals that, contrary to popular belief, experienced players employ more complex opening strategies consisting of multiple moves, whereas less experienced players tend to utilize simpler openings. By employing advanced algorithms to map chess openings, we demonstrate that there is a distinct hierarchy among them and show how different openings are related to one another. Furthermore, we identify clusters of commonly used openings among casual players that differ from those preferred by experienced players, thus demonstrating how the community data can be used to identify and distinguish chess openings preferred by novice and expert players. Our approach provides a methodological framework for utilizing large-scale datasets to analyze strategic behaviors within any complex system that involves repeated decision-making. Finally, we show how the quantitative metrics developed in this study can be used to create an interactive tool that allows users to explore the distinctions between high- and low-skilled chess strategies in an immersive environment. This research combines computational methods, large-scale datasets, and statistical analysis to gain new insights into the underlying structure of complex decision-making systems, such as chess, thus offering a model that can be applied to the study of other systems as well. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future. By applying a straightforward yet systematic approach, the research demonstrates that each Euler-Lagrange equation corresponds to a corresponding Noether constant of motion, providing a meaningful connection between these two concepts. The study ultimately highlights that the constraints given by the research can offer valuable insights into understanding the dynamic behavior of the models under consideration. Most importantly, the investigation shows that the Euler-Lagrange equation itself is a Noether constant of motion for the corresponding Noether constant of motion, providing a useful relationship between these two concepts that can be advantageously exploited in the study of the models under consideration. In this research, we present an alternative approach by focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As an initial step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a tool to collect and retrieve 3D sketches in VR, gathering the first dataset of $167$ sketches in two categories from ModelNet, developing a novel approach to generate synthetic human-like sketches, and evaluating the performance of different approaches. We observed that in the context of sketch-based retrieval, volumetric point-based methods excel due to the sparsity and abstract nature of VR sketches. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. This new level of accuracy may allow for the detection of subtle gravitational influences on the planet's orbit caused by other celestial bodies in the future. Moreover, the updated ephemeris should facilitate more efficient scheduling of observations using the James Webb Space Telescope by providing predicted transit times with high precision. Our goal is to determine the conditions under which such collapses result in forming black holes or bounce-back scenarios using an approximate analytical method. Initially, we establish a set of ordinary differential equations based on the given equation of state, then transform these equations into a single equation involving the density of the fluid, with the outcome depending on one constant. Next, we analyze the behavior of this constant, determining its influence on both viability and the subsequent forms of the resulting colliding waves. Our analysis reveals two distinct viabilities, thereby expanding upon previously established results in the literature, including those by Calabrese et al. in 1992. Our findings demonstrate that, in the presence of a linear relationship between pressure and density, there are indeed two viable forms of collapsing waves, as opposed to the single form observed in incompressible fluid collapses. Our method also facilitates a deeper understanding of the role of the Eqs. parameter in forming colliding black holes. Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes. Lastly, we have explored the potential for promoting Iyer-Wald perturbations to act as soliton-like solutions during the black hole collapse, which may hold the key to uncovering clues left behind by the black hole's birth. This work represents a significant advancement in the field of extremal black holes and brings us closer to understanding the mysteries surrounding their formation. It is worth noting that our findings are consistent with existing results obtained using alternative approaches. We expect this method to be equally applicable to higher-dimensional black holes and those with additional supersymmetry. The associated code used for these calculations has been openly sourced at https://github.com/ChristopherCagle/IyerWald Corrections/tree/main/KerrNewman.

A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives as an alternative to conventional reward functions. End-effect drives define a desired outcome based on the environment's state, using a target distribution that the agent must replicate. This concept was initially developed for reinforcement learning and is expanded here to motivate improved performance in supervised learning as well. We demonstrate that incorporating end-effect drives into supervised learning protocols enhances the generation of highly realistic training data. This technique is beneficial because it defines an objective that is explicitly decoupled from the choice of policy, allowing the network to focus on replicating the target distribution solely based on the transition model. Our experiments in deep reinforcement learning reveal that end-effect drives can be an effective tool for enhancing performance, and we find similar results when applying this concept to supervised learning. Additionally, end-effect drives offer several advantages over conventional rewards, and we identify key characteristics that contribute to successful learning using end-effect drives. Our research highlights the potential for end-effect drives to serve as a versatile framework for training agents and neural networks. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/alexrame/end_effect_drives.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to a specific image of a scene. To succeed, the agent must remember and use previously encountered images. Current methods often employ random memory retrieval or rely on the agent exploring all possible paths to find its target, making them inefficient. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MemoNav, a novel approach that uses a modular architecture to maintain memories and selectively retrieve them for navigation. By leveraging a novel self-supervised loss function, MemoNav learns to prioritize relevant memories. Our results show that MemoNav outperforms current methods on diverse goal navigation tasks and achieves near perfect performance on some benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/affun/MemoNav. To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have sought unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band, with LAA being the name later assigned by 3GPP. Recent and ongoing LAA deployments, primarily in the US, provide insight into how unlicensed and licensed spectrum interact in practice. This paper summarizes my past, present, and planned research into small cell optimization. Moving forward, I will concentrate on a newly utilized unlicensed band, the 6 GHz frequency, where emerging Wi-Fi and 5G NR technologies are likely to coexist. The initial steps in my planned research are outlined here. The key drivers for a new generation of wireless technology appear to be the increasing demand for data rates, increasing interference due to the growing number of devices, and the unlicensed/licensed spectrum dichotomy. These challenges may be mitigated by higher frequency bands with wider bandwidths. The 6 GHz frequency band, offering 1.25 GHz to 6.42 GHz coverage, is strategically located at the midpoint of the 5 GHz (2.4 GHz) Wi-Fi band, making it an ideal replacement for a portion of the unlicensed spectrum. The 6 GHz frequency band also pairs well with licensed spectrum in the same range. This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to verify factual information and locate supporting evidence within tabular data. The comprehensive dataset encompassed 981 manually crafted tables and an automatically generated collection of 1980 tables, both sourced from scientific publications. This task was designed to promote research on automated fact verification and evidence finding for structured data. We also report the results from the recent 2021 competition, featuring three sub-tasks and 28 participating systems from around the world, showcasing significant progress in the field. In particular, sub-task 1: Single-Table Fact Verification attracted 111 system participants, while sub-task 2: Multi-Table Fact Verification drew entries from 42 competitors and sub-task 3: Evidence Finding received 29 system submissions. Our findings indicate substantial gains in micro-f1 scores of 15.13 for single-table verification, 11.76 for multi-table verification, and 16.28 for evidence finding across all participating systems, highlighting the success of our efforts to advance the state-of-the-art in automated fact verification and evidence finding for structured data. To facilitate future research, we will make the complete dataset, along with the task definition and evaluation criteria, along with the competition results, available for download at our website. Moreover, we have published the winning systems' papers on the SemEval website. Ultimately, we aim to expand our research to encompass a broader range of structured document formats, including graphs and sections, as well as explore the intersection of fact verification and evidence finding, making way for novel applications in data-driven industries, such as finance and industry, to extract insights from large datasets. To this end, we are planning to develop an open-access dataset centered around the structure and content of financial reports. This effort will likely yield significant benefits, not only in industry but also in other data-driven sectors, promoting cross-domain research and fostering collaborations between engineering and biology disciplines. In the long run, we envision a future where machines can seamlessly navigate and understand diverse structured document formats, extracting meaningful insights from them. This capability will enable us to tap into the knowledge and expertise contained within large datasets, thereby promoting informed decision-making across a wide array of domains. These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, there's a brief examination of the transient flow scenario. 

It's worth noting that these equations don't account for factors like vertical flow, multiple aquifers, and varying hydraulic conductivities laterally, which would require a more comprehensive approach. Additionally, these equations don't account for changes in hydraulic conductivity with depth, which may or may not be significant. Furthermore, these equations likely won't be suitable for high-precision modeling needs. 

I hope this review provides a useful reference for others working on similar projects. 

Please note that these equations are intended for instructional purposes only and should not be used for actual hydrological consulting or modeling. 

If you find any errors or inaccuracies, please let me correct them.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporates multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also investigate and demonstrate various simulation architectures for integrating these accelerators, comparing the efficiency gains against conventional sequential simulation approaches. Additionally, they demonstrate the functionality of this platform through a practical example involving a neural network simulation. According to their findings, by distributing tasks across available cores, the simulated neuromorphic system can achieve substantial speed-up in simulations, making it an efficient tool for evaluating and comparing different neural network architectures. Ultimately, this research facilitates comparison of state-of-the-art neural computing architectures and identifies VGGNet as a top contender, surpassing other models in classifying image datasets, such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The authors have open-sourced their simulation environment, known as SCNMC, for the benefit of the research community. Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, overreliance on noisy data, and
unrealistic assumptions underlying the model's construction. In this context,
we present a novel approach to learning under uncertainty. Our method draws
on decision trees, adapting them to handle arguments and counterarguments in
a scenario where uncertainty is quantified. We demonstrate the simplicity
of constructing indecision trees while highlighting potential variations to
improve their accuracy in modeling conflict resolution. Furthermore, we show
how to integrate human judgment into the decision-making process, making our
approach suitable for settings with strict regulations on the use of artificial
intelligence. Our framework, called Indecision Trees, outperforms existing systems
in evaluating the effectiveness of disinformation campaigns, according to expert
assessments. This work aims to inspire a broader exploration of machine
learning that takes into account the inherent uncertainties inherent in many
real-world scenarios. The code for this research is publicly accessible at
https://github.com/jbrc-arag/indecision\_trees.

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's capacity to eliminate unproductive alignments, it was later integrated with early abandoning. A new variant of PrunedDTW, known as EAPrunedDTW, was designed with early abandoning incorporated, and it achieves faster abandoning times compared to previous versions. In experiments, we observed a notable improvement in EAPrunedDTW's computation efficiency during similarity searches on the UCR Suite, and it renders pre-calculated bounds unnecessary. As a direct consequence, EAPrunedDTW outperforms PrunedDTW and other variants in a nearest neighbor search implementation. Furthermore, when combined with a technique eliminating unproductive alignments, EAPrunedDTW demonstrates the potential to significantly reduce the time required to complete a similarity search. In specific cases, we observed this combined approach to yield speeds of up to 4.3 times during similarity searches on the UCR Suite. A simplified version of EAPrunedDTW, referred to as SimplifiedPrunedDTW, was also designed and demonstrated to yield comparable results to the original version. Additionally, both variants demonstrate the ability to successfully complete a neighbor search on the largest dataset in the UCR Suite, which had hitherto been beyond the capabilities of PrunedDTW. Specifically, SimplifiedPrunedDTW successfully completed a neighbor search on the Wikipedia dataset at a speed of 188.2 seconds, a feat that had previously been unachievable. To summarize, EAPrunedDTW represents a breakthrough in the development of DTW-based distances, and it is now the fastest known variant of PrunedDTW. At the same time, it is also significantly more efficient than early abandoning variants combined with pre-calculated bounds, and it is even capable of completing a neighbor search on the largest dataset in the UCR Suite, a feat that had previously been unachievable. As such, we propose SimplifiedPrunedDTW as a efficient solution for time series classification tasks requiring a nearest neighbor search. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback is informative, it can also lead students to rely excessively on the tool, overlooking the lesson of independent testing. Consequently, students may view testing as a task that can be fully automated with educational tools, rather than an essential aspect of software development. As a result, this research aims to address the aforementioned issue by introducing two novel educational testing tools: Inquiry-based Testing Environment and Conceptual Testing Inspector. The first tool provides students with coverage perspectives that encourage them to think critically and independently, while the second tool offers a range of testing strategies and promotes reflective learning through testing concepts. Through an empirical study involving 150 students from two groups of testing students, this research compares the effectiveness of providing students with either coverage insights or testing concepts to encourage independent learning. The results indicate that students who were taught testing concepts using the Conceptual Testing Inspector were more likely to demonstrate independent testing skills and had a deeper understanding of testing concepts than those who received coverage perspectives. Furthermore, students who were taught testing concepts performed better in practical exams and had a more positive attitude towards testing, even when compared to students who were taught testing concepts but did not receive the additional training. The implications of these findings are two-fold. Firstly, educational testing tools should be designed to foster independent student behavior rather than simply providing coverage insights. Secondly, incorporating testing concepts into these tools can improve student learning outcomes, even when the tools are used as they would be in professional development. The findings of this research have been shared with software testing professionals through various channels, as recommended by Krivcuik et al. in their 2019 paper. The shared materials include a report with more detailed results, the testing tools used in this research, and a presentation outlining the key findings. The educational testing tool used in this research is now available at https://github.com/abdulrazzaqkhudhir/IBE and https://github.com/abdulrazzaqkhudhir/CTI. The research has also been presented at ICSE 2020 and published in the Proceedings of the International Conference on Software Engineering, Volume 2: Research Investigations for the 2020 Software Engineering Conference. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in deep neural networks, we instead explore a new method: Utilizing within-DNN concept analysis and subsequent explanation through symbolic generated training data via an (in)constraint engine. This approach is exemplified by an investigation that uses this method to explain and generate new training data for a deep convolutional network configuring CIFAR-10 classifiers. This novel approach, though computationally intensive, showcases potential for a lightweight, symbolic surrogate explanation of deep learning methods. This system is set to be released as a public GitHub repository.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can handle large portfolios and accurately calculate moments of the probability function within seconds. We demonstrate the versatility of these tools in three practical scenarios: calculating the expected return of an optimal portfolio with a fixed risk level, estimating the probability of significant losses in a portfolio, and updating the return distribution after adding new assets to a portfolio. Numerical tests validate the efficacy of our methods, showcasing cases in finance and economics. The proposed methods significantly outperform existing benchmark approaches, yielding substantial time savings without sacrificing precision. We highlight potential avenues for future research and implementation. A companion package, spret, is provided to facilitate the reproduction of our results and enable users to explore the methodology further. This package combines Python code from various libraries, including scipy and numba, to create a seamless computing experience. We also introduce a novel, interactive visualization tool that showcases the return distribution of a portfolio, revealing the symbiotic relationship between risk and potential returns. This tool demonstrates the efficacy of our methods in the context of the Hungarian Stock Exchange. Given its general applicability, it can be employed in diverse fields, such as economics, finance, bioinformatics, and computer science, where the characterization of probability distributions plays a crucial role. This study thus contributes to the advancement of computational probability and modeling, enabling the extension of our approaches to more complex scenarios with multiple underlying random variables. A comprehensive user guide is included to facilitate the application of our methods and tools. Additionally, three appendices provide a deeper mathematical analysis and context to the problem, as well as numerical results obtained through Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. This allows for a broader exploration of the return distribution, even when some portfolio components are subject to incomplete or imperfect valuation. A special case illustrates how our methods can be adapted to accommodate this type of ambiguity, employing Bayesian estimation to determine the expected return of a portfolio with incomplete information. This adaptation highlights the versatility of our approach, making it applicable to a wide range of domains where the calculation of probability distributions is pivotal. This study thus initiates a new direction in computational research. We examine the boundedness of the fractional series operator $T_{\gamma}$, with its given function form $(T_{\gamma}b)(j)$, in the context of $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $\ell^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, a counter-example demonstrates that the operator $T_{\gamma}$ does not yield a bounded mapping from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. Additionally, the operator $T_{\gamma}$ is shown to be bounded from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $\ell^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1$, under the condition that the function $b$ lies within the space $\cap_{\beta < \gamma} B_{\beta}$. Here, $B_{\gamma}$ denotes the set of functions satisfying the condition that the series $(T_{\gamma}f)(j)$, for all $j$, is a polynomial of degree $\gamma$. The connection between the operator $T_{\gamma}$ and the fractional integral operator $I_{\gamma}$, as well as its counterpart in the continuous setting, is also discussed. The present research is an extension of the initial findings reported in 'Fractional operators on Hardy spaces', published in Mathematical Notes of the Australian Mathematical Society. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart based on the maximal element of the Weyl group corresponding to GL(n,ℂ). Key findings include the following. Firstly, we prove that the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function within this specific coordinate system can be decomposed into vertices. Furthermore, combining our result with existing work on generators, we demonstrate that this set of generators constitutes a Gröbner basis under a naturally imposed monomial order. Lastly, applying our analysis under the action of the Weyl group, we derive an inductive decomposition of the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety of type A along with corresponding Frobenius splitting, expanding on earlier published results by Ito-Koshino-Sasaki. In contrast to previously complex calculations of Gröbner bases, our analysis yields an easier-to-compute structure, allowing us to conclude with the explicit expression of the local defining ideal of type A regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties. Additionally, we provide the explicit description of the local defining ideal for types B and C. Moreover, we prove that our obtained result corresponds to a known case of Chow quotient space, previously studied in the context of type A by Tanabe. In contrast, for type B, this relation holds under the assumption of the existence of a positive real number α ≥ 1/2 which might be unnecessary. Finally, we show that our obtained result fits within a broader framework of regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type C. Furthermore, this work is supplemented by a publicly accessible implementation in Mathematica.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently find this information due to their limited ability to accurately understand the context of each question within the paper. Developing effective information-seeking answering tools requires a large collection of questions based on research papers, along with their corresponding answers, to ensure that answering methods are closely tied to the context of each question. In response to this need, we have created a large dataset of 3,557 questions and answers extracted from 142 research papers in the fields of nutrition and disease. This dataset, known as NutInfo, serves as the first information-seeking answering dataset based on scientific research, offering multiple useful features such as multi-sentence questions, multiple relevant answers per document, and the potential for questions to be related to multiple papers. By using NutInfo, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art information-seeking answering systems can be outperformed by a simple transformer model that was trained on this dataset, resulting in a 12.7 percentage point increase in F1 score. This improvement highlights the significance of contextual understanding in answering systems for research papers, thereby paving the way for further development using NutInfo. The NutInfo dataset is available at https://github.com/airtang/nutinfo. It has also been shared with IACMI as part of a competition at https://www.iacmi.org/facm-2022-competition.html. Additional resources, including NutInfo can also be accessed at https://github.com/airtang/nutinfo. In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, only the explosive model exhibited instability behind the shock, attributed to the interaction between particles and neutrinos. This study calculates the characteristics of these instabilities and their potential impact on the development of the supernova event. Results show that in both scenarios, instabilities primarily affect neutrinos with an energy of around 11-24 MeV, and neutrinos with higher energy tend to experience less instability. This research also establishes a requirement for the spatial structure and fluid flow velocity of any instability that may arise. With a minimum threshold of around 0.03 cm/ms, the velocity of any instability is largely independent of the model and neutrino energy. Additionally, it has been determined that any instability that may arise would not significantly influence the development of the supernova event. Rather, it is conjectured that any impact on the thermodynamic properties or fluid dynamics of the supernova event would be minimal and unlikely. Based on these calculations, it is estimated that any resultant fast flavor oscillation-driven flux modulation could only be sustained for a duration of less than 10 ms. Consequently, any impact on the development of the solar puzzle would be unlikely. This research does, however, leave room for future investigation regarding the potential effects of long-lived instabilities. It is possible that if these instabilities were to persist for an extended duration, they could give rise to a distinct flavor composition of neutrinos relative to the initial model, thereby potentially impacting the solar puzzle. Furthermore, it is suggested that future research into the neutrino events would benefit from a division into epochs based on the supernova event's evolution, rather than simply early and late phases. This classification system would allow researchers to discern whether any changes in neutrino flavor are a result of the inherent instability or merely observational bias. It is acknowledged that any conclusion drawn from this research is contingent on simulations of improved accuracy using more advanced numerical methods. Consequently, it is recommended that any investigation into the neutrino flavor composition is based on models with enhanced spatial and temporal resolution. Specifically, at least 1000 grid points in total, and a maximum time step of 0.5 cm/ms, respectively. This would greatly facilitate the analysis into the fast neutrino flavor instability. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. To address this, MadDog is a comprehensive web-based solution that navigates acronym interpretation challenges throughout their entire lifespan - from formation to dissolution. Featuring a user-friendly interface, MadDog offers a range of features including acronym detection, analysis, and disambiguation capabilities, along with options for domain-specific search and exploration. Additionally, it provides detailed results for analysis and research purposes. Developed using modular architecture and components scalable for distributed and parallel processing, MadDog is an efficient and adaptable system that caters to varying user needs and domains. With its intuitive interface and comprehensive functionality, MadDog is an accessible tool for researchers and NLP students to investigate acronym interpretation issues. Furthermore, the system's knowledge base is made available for download, enabling users to integrate its capabilities with external services and systems for acronym identification and disambiguation. A live demonstration of the system is also available for exploration. System information, including source code and documentation, can be found at https://nlp.niu.edu.il/MadDog/. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry. As a result, an electron charge current can be directed from hot to cold or vice versa, and an accompanying heat current is also predicted. These findings can be attributed to a simple and logical physical interpretation. Furthermore, heat rectification can be achieved by combining two quantum Hall systems with distinct filling factors, and this effect can be enhanced through the interference properties of the tunnel junction. These observations open up new avenues for controlling heat flow and may lead to innovative applications in quantum thermodynamics. Additionally, these systems offer a valuable testing ground for refining theoretical understanding of interacting quantum systems. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct hierarchy with its own root object and multiple child objects. Furthermore, our work includes the development of an efficient algorithm for updating deleted objects' contents, involving the use of specialized primers and "sticker" primers to ensure fast, error-free revisions at the root level and below. Ultimately, our approach provides a solid foundation for the creation of complex, hierarchical data structures in DNA storage. However, additional research is needed to address challenges in areas like DNA sequencing and forensic analysis. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space in phononic systems and electrical circuits. Furthermore, it discusses the prospects for controlling non-Hermitian topological phenomena in experimental systems. We also investigate the relationship between topological nodal lines and their representation in momentum space as Weyl points lines, establishing a link between these structures and their occurrence in Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems. Additionally, we examine the experimental verification of topological nodal lines using artificial materials, focusing on the evidence of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space in phononic systems and electrical circuits. We expect that the control of topological nodal lines will lead to significant advancements in the understanding and development of topological technologies. Given the relatively recent realization of topological nodal lines, we anticipate that future research will further diversify the range of materials exhibiting these lines, and ultimately realize the practical application of these materials for experimental purposes. In particular, we expect that the development of topological nodal lines will be utilized in the creation of topological lasers. We also anticipate that the realization of non-Hermitian topological phenomena will facilitate the creation of devices capable of self-cleaning and self-healing functions. We expect these innovations to emerge primarily through advancements in photonic systems, but also through progress in electrical circuits and other technologies. We believe that our review will provide a foundation for these developments to occur. Given the diverse range of topics covered, we hope that this review will serve as a foundation for initiating and guiding topological research in various fields. In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outmoving waves of oscillation, which are commonly found in both biological and chemical systems. For this type of wave to occur, a region generating pacemaker-driven oscillations must be situated next to a region where the oscillatory frequency is lower. There's considerable evidence from both biology and chemistry that active sources, such as cross-reactive enzymes, can generate and sustain this type of wave. This article focuses on determining the distance ($d_f$) from an isolated source that allows it to generate and propel traveling waves in the presence of inhibition. To this end, we develop and test two analytical approximations for $d_f$ across a wide range of parameters, including the rates at the source and around the perimeter. Our results indicate that even when the source operates at the highest possible rate in an uncoupled system, $d_f$ may still be significantly smaller than the system's overall dimensions. Furthermore, for both weakly and highly inhibited systems, $d_f$ is largely determined by the source's operational frequency. However, in systems with intermediate levels of inhibition, $d_f$ is largely affected by the source's operational frequency and the frequency at the system's perimeter. This article also focuses on understanding the relationship between the source's size and this distance, as well as the source's operational frequency. To this end, we develop and test two new analytical approximations for these relationships. Our results indicate that both the source's geometry and its chemical kinetics affect the distance from the source that allows it to generate and propel traveling waves. Moreover, the source's geometry and its chemical kinetics affect the speed at which these waves move. Our results also indicate that even though the source operates at the highest possible rate in an uncoupled system, the system's periodic structure may still limit this distance and the speed at these waves travel. Finally, we expand on previous research regarding the source's size, its operational frequency, and how these factors interact with the system's inhibition to determine both the distance and the speed at these waves travel. Our research suggests that both the source's size and its operational frequency affect these parameters, as well as how these parameters behave in both homogeneous and heterogeneous systems. A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, also serving as a representative problem for studying the complexity of state partitioning in quantum systems. The development of an efficient algorithm for approximating entropy in quantum systems is thus an important area of study. In this research, we introduce two new quantum algorithms for estimating the entropy of a Markov and create a universal scheme applicable to various random distributions. The first algorithm is tailored to Markov systems and shows that, for lists of length n, the expected approximate error probability is proportional to n^-2/3. The second, more adaptable algorithm, is capable of handling a range of distributions beyond Markov systems, while its expected approximate error probability is proportional to n^-1/3. Both algorithms are shown to be feasible using resources within the resources bounds of Shor's algorithm. The findings from these experiments demonstrate that non-deterministic quantum algorithms can solve a long-standing problem more efficiently than any possible deterministic algorithm. In fact, the ratio of the deterministic algorithm's complexity to our universal algorithm's complexity grows exponentially with the problem size (approximately 2^n), while the ratio of the first algorithm to our universal algorithm grows polynomially with the problem size (approximately n^3). The latter result appears to be particularly surprising as it contradicts conventional wisdom that universal algorithms should be at least as efficient as tailored algorithms. The counterintuitive result suggests that there may be more to entropy than meets the entropy. The research presents new non-deterministic algorithms for approximating entropy, where one is a tailored solution and the other a more adaptable universal solution. The findings reveal an efficiency gap between the tailored and universal algorithms, where the latter is not only more adaptable but also more efficient despite being a universal solution. Furthermore, the research reveals an unexpected property of entropy, where the efficiency of its approximation can depend on the system's non-local properties despite being able to predict its local behavior. The research uses entropy as a representative problem to study the efficiency of non-deterministic algorithms. In doing so, the research identifies an important property of entropy, where its approximation can be efficiently predicted in certain Markov systems, a property that may be useful in other areas of quantum physics and computer science. On the other hand, the research also identifies a long-standing limitation of non-deterministic algorithms, where they may fail to efficiently predict certain properties of random distributions, a limitation that may be inherent in quantum systems. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), lack standardization for clinical condition codes, making them difficult to process in an automated manner. To address this challenge, we developed an innovative approach, combining the strengths of supervised and self-supervised learning techniques. We utilized a small, targeted dataset for supervised training, leveraging domain specialist knowledge to associate CTN sections with standard ICD codes. Subsequently, we applied this model to large-scale CTN data for self-supervised fine-tuning. This robust method effectively transferred knowledge across datasets and maintained accuracy without requiring extensive labeling of new data. When evaluated on newly released CTN data, our approach demonstrated superior performance, connecting CTNs to ICD codes with impressive precision and recall percentages. This state-of-the-art results showcases the potential for our semi-self-supervised method to streamline ICD coding, enhancing automated clinical condition detection. With continued evolution, this technology can facilitate seamless clinical condition tracking and data exchange among healthcare professionals, ultimately fostering better patient care. Our findings and algorithms are publicly available, allowing for replication of our results and future development of this research. We intend to explore self-supervised learning applications in other challenging NLP tasks. This work marks the initial exploration of semi-self-supervised learning within clinical NLP. Our model and associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/a0hei0py/ICD-Coding. This research was funded through a grant from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. We appreciate the support and guidance provided by Dr. Justin Whitehill. We conducted thorough experimentation to validate the reliability and generalizability of our approach. Our models and associated clinical text note data for code lookup were successfully shared with research colleagues, yielding a diverse set of questions and scenarios, which led to the determination of our method's efficacy in addressing these research inquiries. The effectiveness of our semi-self-supervised method in maintaining accuracy with minimal labeled data was confirmed through extensive pilot testing. We calculated the average time required for human medical coders to annotate clinical text notes for ICD codes and found that our model surpassed their annotation speed. The strength of our semi-self-supervised model in connecting CTNs to ICD codes was further demonstrated through comparisons with top NLP models. We developed and shared nine clinical text note scenarios, which we used to show the accuracy of our semi-self-supervised method in maintaining performance on diverse datasets. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the computational power of current machines. Quantum computers, with their ability to process complex information, may soon overcome these limitations, enabling the adaptation of machine learning algorithms for quantum use. Researchers have successfully implemented a quantum version of the K-Means algorithm on superconducting quantum processors, comparing its performance to classical versions with similar resources. Additionally, they have developed a novel quantum approach to clustering based on Gaussian Mixture Models and proposed a method to extend supervised learning algorithms like Support Vector Machines for quantum application. These breakthroughs mark the first step in applying machine learning algorithms on quantum processors and may soon reveal additional advantages. Measurement results showed that the quantum algorithm matched the performance of its classical counterparts for specific dataset sizes. However, further investigation is needed to determine the full potential of quantum machine learning. In order to facilitate future research, the source code used in this study has been made publicly available. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, efficiently differentiating rendering algorithms to match this data is often challenging, since they typically involve complex non-differentiable operations like ray-tracing truncation. To address this issue, we introduce an efficient and differentiable shadow rendering algorithm that offers two primary advantages over existing solutions. Firstly, it significantly improves the computational speed of rendering and its derivative by reducing complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^2), making it more suitable for common image resolution ranges (e.g., N=512). Secondly, it offers an order of magnitude increase in performance over previous approaches that also achieve an O(N^2) complexity. We evaluate the proposed algorithm through various experiments, comparing its performance to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in computing image derivatives for unknown light sources. A significant advantage of this algorithm is its ability to offer comparable results with current methods, while doing so at a significantly faster computational speed. The full source code for this project is available at https://github.com/urchadch/ds-shadows. Additionally, a demo video showcasing the algorithm is available at https://dchad.github.io/ds-shadows-demo/. Extensive results and dataset will be made available at https://dchad.github.io/ds-shadows-results/. and will be updated at https://dchad.github.io/ds-shadows-3D. Moreover, a corresponding journal paper has been published at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14466. and is currently under review at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). Essential 3D pre-computed data for this research is available at https://dchad.github.io/ds-shadows-precompute.
