Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this paper develops an innovative framework to estimate the average and statistical relationship of origin-destination demand while considering the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections. The framework also determines the probability distribution of link and path flow along with their costs, with the goal of minimizing overall network congestion cost. Through numerical simulations using small and large networks, the results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method. Moreover, the findings indicate that under certain conditions, the estimated origin-destination demand is positively correlated with path flow, which does not always hold true in all scenarios. Two real-world applications are also considered to demonstrate the practical usability of the proposed methodology. Ultimately, the study's findings provide insights into utilizing traffic data to improve the understanding and prediction of origin-destination demand, enabling more informed transportation system management and planning. A key potential practical application of this research is in the area of home link management, where knowledge of origin-destination demand probability distribution can aid in determining the most cost-effective and efficient home link pricing policy. Similarly, the results have broader implications for general traffic signal control and the signal timing design. Furthermore, the study's findings are likely to be beneficial in addressing various scaling challenges in large-scale transportation systems. In particular, the proposed framework is expected to facilitate the scalable computation of origin-destination demand probability distribution even in complex networks. Additionally, the results are anticipated to be useful in the domain of recurrent routing and transportation planning. By utilizing day-to-day traffic data, the study makes an important contribution to the existing body of knowledge on transportation networks, particularly with regards to supply and demand modeling, where the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow is a pressing research concern. Furthermore, the paper's results are a significant advancement in the field of homotopy method for nonlinear equations and optimization. Specifically, the study's solution builds upon previous research by Kaparis and Lapeyere in 2006, addressing their initially posed problem of finding the probability distribution of origin-destination demand. The Kaparis-Lapeyere problem is a complex optimization issue, and the associated hypothesis about its solvability by the homotopy method is a key research finding, which the study successfully verifies through numerical testing. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms reveals that combining their strengths can greatly reduce overall construction time, resulting in a faster and more efficient method. This new approach can also be applied to generate random spanning trees, extending the capability to exclude specific vertices from the tree. Furthermore, the research explores its potential applications in social network and web analytics, illustrating through example the ability to estimate time-based metrics on spanning sub-trees. This study also opens avenues for investigating random spanning forests and other combinatorial structures. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia data. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our research expands on existing musical notation, combining it with audio synthesis and generated sheet-music images to create a dataset with precise alignments among audio, visual, and text-based components. This aligned MusicTM-Dataset allows for the development of unified representations across multimodal data. Comprising sheet-music images, lyrical text, and synthesized audio, the dataset is comprised of three distinct modalities. Following a detailed evaluation of various deep learning models, our research reveals that a framework incorporating pair-wise canonical correlation analysis produces superior results. Our music dataset and associated pre-trained models are accessible for public use at https://github.com/soudry-group/ MusicTM-Dataset. This research aims to facilitate the creation of robust cross-modal learning techniques, enabling a range of applications in music domain. Three associated papers are published at NeurIPS 2021 and IJCAI 2021. Additional information is available at https://musictm.github.io/. From a technical standpoint, our research introduces three significant contributions - the design of MusicTM-Dataset, the development of sheet-music image-based canonical correlation analysis model 'SMAX-CAN', and the application of our dataset in evaluating the efficacy of cross-modal learning methods. It is noteworthy that MusicTM-Dataset is the first comprehensive dataset to integrate three modalities with precise alignments, making it an invaluable resource for the research community. Moreover, SMAX-CAN is a unique canonical correlation analysis model that utilizes sheet-music images to enhance cross-modal learning performance, showcasing the potential of sheet-music images to capture intricate structural information. This information can then be leveraged to improve the robustness and representation accuracy of cross-modal learning methods, as empirically demonstrated. Experimental results confirm that MusicTM-Dataset surpasses currently available datasets in terms of domain invariance. Moreover, our research reveals that deep learning models trained on MusicTM-Dataset exhibit exceptional cross-modal performance even when faced with challenging out-of-distribution tests. Notably, our results show that sheet-music images can capture structural information, and combining them with lyrical text and synthesized audio yields more robust musical audio recognition. One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the method demonstrates improved results in enhancing user experience during visual data exploration. We present two methodologies: the application of latent semantic analysis to Wikidata entities and properties, and two alternative approaches utilizing positive sampling; these innovations successfully empower users to discover and explore entity properties previously unknown to them. The method has been successfully integrated into the Ontodia diagramming tool and is available online, with further information and technical documentation provided via the linked repository. The associated data and software can be found at https://dx.doi.org/10.5281/zae-5787. Ontodia is freely accessible at http://ontodia.org/. The Wikidata dataset is available at https://dx.doi.org/10.1596/1810-2008.2576. The Ontodia-WSDM-GSA repository contains further information at https://dx.doi.org/10.5281/zae-5787.

We've analyzed the dynamics of one-dimensional optical solitons within the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation, which includes terms for dispersion and cubic interactions. By introducing a small disturbance into the system, we determine the stability based on the behavior of the resulting soliton. Our research reveals that solitons featuring long-wavelength (exponential) decay are stable in the asymptotic sense, characterized by the occurrence of small, damped oscillations. Conversely, solitons exhibiting short-wavelength (algebraic) decay are unstable, losing energy and evolving into radiation waves as time progresses. Notably, the (hyperbolic) soliton is stable under conditions of anomalous dispersion, whereas it exhibits exponential decay and is thus unstable under conditions of normal dispersion. Additionally, we have derived an exact relation for the stability exponent in the case of cubic interactions. Our findings indicate that the overall stability of the soliton depends on a combination of its spectral properties and the characteristics of the disordering force acting upon it. Furthermore, we have explored the implications of including terms for Kerr-type cubic interactions in the full Madelung equation, which describe three-dimensional optical solitons. Our research reveals that, for long-wavelength disturbances, the (plane) soliton is stable in any dimensionality, whereas it exhibits exponential decay and is thus unstable under conditions of short-wavelength disturbances. Our analysis also indicates that the (hyperbolic) soliton is stable in three dimensions, whereas it exhibits exponential decay and is thus unstable in one and two dimensions. Our research offers new insights into the properties of optical solitons, as well as the behavior of (plane) solitons in cubic quantum hydrodynamics. This collaborative approach in visual analytics aims to facilitate seamless interaction between humans and machines, yet implementing systems that intelligently support and structure this collaboration is a complex task. To address this challenge, we developed Lotse: a comprehensive framework for creating guidance in visual analytics environments. Founded on proven concepts from cognitive science and constructivist learning theory, Lotse enables developers to craft tailored guidance by systematically analyzing and interpreting users' interactive behavior within the context of their tasks. Focusing on learning and performance, Lotse incorporates various techniques, such as evaluation metrics, learning algorithms, and adaptive reinforcement learning, to effectively guide users toward optimal behavior. Furthermore, Lotse comprises a modular architecture that allows multiple learning agents to collaborate and exchange knowledge, thereby addressing the inherent distributed nature of interactive visual analytics applications. Through two practical case studies, we demonstrate the versatility and efficacy of Lotse in enhancing learning and performance: a scenario involving guided search in visual analytics and collaborative analysis with shared knowledge. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Results show that the BDDC algorithm consistently outperforms AMG by reducing solution time, and that these improvements are most pronounced when using parallel computing resources. In all cases examined, the BDDC algorithm displays superior scalability to the number of available processors. A substantial advantage in solution timing is observed with BDDC when compared to AMG, with BDDC requiring less time to reach convergence than AMG. Additionally, research shows that by appropriately configuring BDDC, such as by selecting specific degree of freedom options, the size of problems can be effectively partitioned to effectively exploit the availability of computing resources. This capability is highly desirable when solving large-scale cardiac mechanics problems, and facilitates the use of parallel processing to accelerate solution times. Ultimately, research confirms that the BDDC algorithm remains the preferred choice for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems, either alone or in conjunction with parallel computing resources. Details are provided to advise researchers on how to best configure BDDC to effectively exploit parallel processing, while a theoretical analysis for BDDC is developed to explain and extend the algorithm's proven success. This work is of interest to researchers in cardiac mechanics but also to all scientists using parallel computing resources to solve complex, large-scale algebraic problems. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting collaborative knowledge creation and management. Within these systems, users contribute tags to share knowledge and facilitate tagged resource retrieval, yet the tags themselves are often ignored or undervalued. Conversely, this study seeks to uncover the value of tags by examining their cognitive and socio-cognitive underpinnings, including factors such as user-driven knowledge reuse, temporal dynamics, mutual interests, and collaborative activities. Through a combined application of social network analysis and temporal statistics, along with multiple regression and clustering techniques, this research investigates these phenomena in two social tagging systems: Del.icio.us and CiteULike. Our results reveal that users engage in knowledge reuse and retagging over extended periods, share interests through mutual tagging and similar resource marking, and collaborate through shared knowledge and tagging activities. These findings hold implications for future research and system design. By acknowledging the complex interplay of these phenomena, developers can create environments that foster user engagement, knowledge sharing, and participation. Furthermore, this research enables the development of predictive models and performance metrics, facilitating the empirical evaluation of social knowledge management systems. By applying these methods, administrators can optimize their Del.icio.us and CiteULike platforms to encourage users to share knowledge and tag resources in a collective effort. Ultimately, this research seeks to contribute to the broader realm of collaborative knowledge creation and the growing community of user-generated content applications. The accompanying website (http://kwiki.uni-konstanz.de/index.php/Reuse,_Temporal_Dynamics,_Interest_Sharing,_and_Collaboration_in_Social_Tagging_Systems) serves as a central resource for the research, providing additional information and a demonstration of the methods applied. This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ decay rate is given by $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, with any positive integer $l$. Through the application of the time-weighted energy method, we manage to enhance this rate to $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Under the condition that the frequencies are sufficiently low, by incorporating the principles of the Littlewood-Paley theory, we find that the solutions have properties belonging to certain Besov spaces of negative order and establish the most favorable $L^2$ decay rate. Consequently, we show that the solutions obtained are relatively smooth and their behavior falls within the realm of certain Besov spaces of negative order. Moreover, we employ the principles of the Fourier splitting technique to investigate the time-asymptotic behavior of the solutions. Specifically, we demonstrate that the solutions converge to a steady state as time progresses, with their error terms decaying over time. The analysis also reveals that the distance between the solution and the steady state is quantified by a scale that increases rapidly with the frequency. Consequently, we show that the solutions fail to converge in the top part of the frequency spectrum and do not possess properties belonging to $L^1$ or almost every $L^p$ space for $1 \le p < \infty$. Finally, we utilize the principles of the time-weighted energy method to establish a priori estimates of bounded type for the solutions, and show that the $L^2$ decay rate can be further generalized to other $L^p$ spaces for $1 < p < 2$. The analysis is equally applicable to both the compressible FENE dumbbell model and the incompressible FENE dumbbell model. The main reason for this applicability is the fact that the deterministic components of these two models exhibit a high degree of similarity. Consequently, we show that the results obtained are equally applicable to both the compressible and incompressible FENE dumbbell models. The long-term behavior of strong solutions to both the compressible and incompressible FENE dumbbell models has been primarily investigated through the principles of the time-weighted energy method. Specifically, we show that the solutions obtained are uniformly bounded over time, and that the $L^2$ decay rate can be further generalized to other $L^p$ spaces for $1 < p < 2$.

This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity $H^s$ for $s<3/2$. The velocity of these waves accelerates as one moves further away from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions in Gevrey spaces, where a universal bound on travel wave velocities exists. Notably, we are able to demonstrate that the difference between these regularity cases is primarily attributed to the differences in growth rates of certain Bessel functions. Moreover, we leverage this insight to analyze the long-term impacts of initial data located in close proximity to the Couette flow, revealing a scenario in which non-degenerate perturbations lead to an infinite number of oscillations in velocity over time. This behaviour is akin to a quantum mechanical phenomenon known as "resonance", where waves accumulate indefinitely as they approach certain points. This study is part of a broader research aim that seeks to investigate and understand the dynamics of quasi-conserved quantities near Couette flow in 2D Euler equation. In doing so, we are able to identify and classify a "Landau" resonance where quasi-conserved quantities meet and diverge. Ultimately, this study represents a theoretical realization of the resonance phenomenon observed in a recent numerical simulation of the 2D Euler equation. Additionally, it is anticipated that this theoretical result will be translated into the context of real-world fluids in the future. The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions. Public health specialists rely on time-sensitive and accurate data analysis to make informed decisions about how to manage the outbreak. Due to a lack of clinical SARS-CoV-2 testing, South Africa's data was skewed, making accurate analysis of the outbreak difficult. To address this challenge, we utilized available data, combining it with statistical modeling to inform the public health response. Our approach, which involved time-series analysis of testing and mortality data using exponential and linear models, allowed us to demonstrate that non-linear trends are prevalent in both types of data. Interestingly, we observed that the peak of COVID-19-related deaths coincided with the summer solstice, revealing a possible temperature-dependent effect. Our study exposes the need for critical data interpretation, stressing that correlation does not always imply causation. With a multitude of data available, we must utilize statistical modeling to make the most of what we have, especially in cases of limited clinical data. Implementing an informed decision-making strategy based on available data also helps public health institutions to conserve resources during this health emergency. Our research offers a framework that can be applied to other countries to facilitate data-driven strategic decision-making regarding the COVID-19 outbreak. Moreover, the methods employed in this study can be adapted for analysis of other pandemics and crises. It is our hope that this research will contribute positively to the public health discourse in South Africa and beyond. Furthermore, we hope that our statistical models will aid researchers and public health specialists in making the most of the available data to manage the outbreak effectively. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. Furthermore, it's demonstrated that this restriction can't be relaxed to three elements without invoking intricate constructions rooted in higher-order arithmetic. Lastly, a related question regarding the feasibility of finding near-arithmetic progression structures within sumsets is posed. It's suspected that such structures could only exist under the presence of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem's converse. In support of this, it's shown that its absence would allow for the creation of intricate constructions rooted in higher-order arithmetic within sumsets. Consequently, its presence is required for allowing the incorporation of arithmetic progression structures within sumsets. 

Keywords: Freiman's 3k-4 theorem, sumsets, near-arithmetic progression structures, arithmetic progression structures, number theory, Freiman's conjecture, projective near-arithmetic progression structures, projective arithmetic progression structures, projective sumsets, projective number theory.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, validating this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a solution is proposed that uses neural network-based models to detect patterns in X-ray images that forecast severe symptoms. By combining and iteratively updating annotations for lung lesions based on expert medical analysis and computational predictions from the models, large-scale and reliable data can be created for training machine learning algorithms to identify the characteristic features of X-ray images associated with more severe symptoms. Our approach is designed as an open contribution for the medical community to verify the initial hypothesis through a shared data set and set of features. As an initial test, the proposed system was used to analyze a cohort of 210 patients with severe symptoms, producing 98 new annotations for lung lesions. Our results indicate that models trained on the resulting data can accurately identify areas of the lungs from X-ray images with an accuracy of 90% and predict severe symptoms with an accuracy of 87%, indicating a potential link between image characteristics and the likelihood of severe symptoms. Our research offers a framework and tools for the medical community to validate the initial hypothesis and expand our method for use in other clinical applications involving predicting severe symptoms based on image data. To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to representing utterances semantically and clustering them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that enhances the representation of utterances while maintaining independence from target intents. Secondly, we design a new contrastive loss to drive clustering of unlabelled data without manual annotation. Through exhaustive evaluations on three benchmarks, our method excels in detecting novel intents and identifying new intent categories from unlabeled data compared to state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed technique demonstrates particular strength on datasets with few labelled examples per intent and significant differences between labelled and unlabelled data. It is also remarkably efficient, detecting new intents 3.3 times faster and with 14% higher accuracy compared to the next best approach. The code and dataset can be found at https://github.com/Chen-5431/New-ID.

In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups. This exceeds the previous best known upper bounds - $$r^{\frac{\log_2r}{3}+o(\log_2r)}$$ from Montero's work and $$r^{\frac{\log_2r}{2}+o(\log_2r)}$$ from Benbenisht's research. The new finding essentially optimizes the exponent on the logarithm of the group order and validates the conjecture of Shparlinski and Steger with a stronger result. To achieve this, we combined methods of Vaughan and Chen-Iwaniec-Szemerdi's more recent work involving the polynomial van der Waerden type theorem, alongside other techniques from prime number theory, all integrated into a unified approach. Moreover, the analysis reveals a general method for obtaining upper bounds on the sizes of subgroups given certain conditions on their indices, index sets, or cyclic subgroups, which may be useful for other mathematicians. Lastly, we explore the possibility of further refining the upper bound using the concept of twin primes and their connection to subgroups. The research was a collaborative project between multiple students of Princeton University who were enrolled in the 2020-2021 Math 103: Algebra course taught by Martin Horsch and David J. Vreught. We were assigned to investigate the number of subgroups in a finite group and examine the upper bounds on that number, eventually building upon existing research to reach a new and improved result. The project was supervised by Dr. Shixiang Ma. This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0,0 and S1,0. A detailed analysis is provided on the coupled system of these variables in terms of 3D consistency, Lax pair, bilinear form and continuum limits. The analysis reveals that the variable S1,0 itself adheres to a 9-point lattice equation and upon continuum limiting, it is related to the Lax pair's eigenfunction of the Korteweg-de Vries equation. An interesting property of the variable S1,0 is that it is a perfect square of another, lower-consistency variable. This leads to another, continuum-limited variable which follows an 18-point lattice equation. This entire investigation indicates that the variable S1,0 holds a higher degree of structural consistency compared to the continuum-limited variable. Consequently, it is proposed that for equations with direct linear relationships to continuum-limited variables of high structural consistency, it may be advantageous to first identify their counterparts in Cauchy matrix schemes and then develop corresponding continuum models. Moreover, it is shown that the perfect-square property of S1,0 can be generalised to a wider class of lattice equations which include the 3D lattice equation and the H2 equation itself, as well as certain higher-order extensions of these equations. Finally, it is demonstrated that the perfect-square property of S1,0 can be translated into a corresponding feature in the associated continuum model, thereby establishing a direct analogy between the lattice and continuum formulations. Furthermore, it is shown that this translation can be accomplished through various distinct methods, thereby evidencing its existence and uniqueness. In contrast to differential equations, the lattice equations exhibit a unique possibility where a solution can be perfectly reconstructed from its Lax pair's eigenvalues. This unique possibility serves as the underlying rationale for the proposed strategy to first identify solutions in Cauchy matrix schemes and then develop corresponding continuum models, thereby providing a novel and additional interpretation of the established connection between the lattice and continuum formulations. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is crucial for state-of-the-art models. To achieve this, we propose a new framework called Dynamic Graph Message Passing Network (DGMPN), a neural network architecture designed to efficiently model and process complex relationships. By representing attributes and descriptors as nodes on a dynamic graph, DGMPN enables the exchange of information between nodes through an attention-based message passing mechanism. This allows the network to learn and process relationships of varying distances. Notably, our framework consists of multiple stages, each representing a different semantic concept, allowing the network to focus on specific relationships in each stage. Through this structure, DGMPN outperforms existing methods in tasks such as person re-identification, vehicle re-identification, and semantic segmentation. Additionally, our framework's design enables the direct analysis of relationships through node attention, providing interpretable results. Furthermore, our framework can be applied to a wide range of problems beyond the tested tasks. To showcase this, we also demonstrate the effectiveness of DGMPN in tasks such as image level classification and object detection. Specifically, our results reveal that DGMPN achieves superior performance compared to existing methods in person re-identification, with a mean average precision (mAP) of 71.9 on the testing datasets DesiReDB and VehicleViewRDB. The implementation details of our framework are available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/zhousizong/DGMPCN. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. Recent research has focused on reducing the hardware required for MCM implementations, surpassing earlier works. This article builds upon this progress by introducing a new method, based on Optimal Binarization Approach (OBA), which achieves better results while using fewer resources compared to existing solutions. New extensions of OBA are proposed, including one that can handle floating-point operations efficiently. A comprehensive evaluation compares the newly proposed approach with state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its superiority in terms of hardware cost. The article also provides insight into why certain methods are less effective and presents a new rule that can help identify such instances. Finally, a tool is introduced that can automatically generate optimized MCM code for any given integer power and constant value. The proposed approach is expected to benefit a wide range of applications, including digital signal processing and control systems. The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously being separate entities, advancements have revealed that quantum circuits share parallels with artificial neural networks, paving the way for widespread adoption. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way. It also explores the challenges inherent in quantum deep learning research from multiple viewpoints, followed by a discussion of prospective future directions and practical applications. Additionally, the paper outlines relevant quantum computing frameworks for practical application in learning problems. This paper is intended to serve as an informative entry point for readers, including graduate students, who are interested in exploring the rapidly evolving field of quantum deep learning. As such, comprehensive references to the latest research have been included for further study. This material is based on ongoing research projects supported by ANID via the funding agencies FONDEF and BASAL. Additionally, this work has been facilitated by funding received from the University of Santiago de Chile (USACH).

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to be fundamental in 
high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, where significant progress has been 
made over the past decade in advancing the field. This progress has enabled 
injection of more than one particle species into the same accelerator, 
utilized new beam charges, and developed innovative methods for generating and 
delivering RF electrons and magnetic fields. A recent surge in R&D activities 
throughout the RF community has been witnessed. This report outlines the current 
state of R&D progress, future development plans, and the corresponding 
contributions that these developments can make in addressing the challenges posed 
by the Snowmass 2021 report. 

Key R&D Focus Areas:

1. **Multi-Bunch Charge Management**: Achieving successful injection and 
   acceleration of high-intensity proton and ion beams at frequencies higher 
   than 1 GHz.

2. **Coasting and Knock-Out**: Developing the technology to produce long-coasting 
   beams with low-density, high-energy electron beams using RF cavities in 
   conjunction with machine learning and other innovative approaches.

3. **Intelligent and Optimal Beam Delivery**: Utilizing advanced algorithms and real-time 
   digital signal processing to dynamically control RF cavities and deliver beams 
   tailored to the specific requirements of the experiment.

4. **RF Power Source Innovation**: Introducing new, high-performance RF power sources 
   such as inverse cyclotron resonance systems and fast-switching ICR systems to 
   enable innovative low-energy electron beam generation.

5. **Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning**: Applying AI and ML technologies to 
   optimize RF system performance and introduce new R&D pathways.

6. **Hybrid and Monolithic Accelerators**: Developing innovative technologies, such 
   as combined RF/fixed-field and monolithic RF structures, to address the 
   deserialization challenge.

7. **Standardization and Interoperability**: Striving for interoperability among 
   different R&D programs through the use of modular, commercially available RF 
   components and standardized interfaces.

8. **Education and Training**: Implementing a comprehensive educational program 
   and fostering collaborations among young researchers and researchers from 
   diverse backgrounds to address future R&D needs. 

The RF community has identified several key areas to focus on in the short and 
long term to address specific challenges posed by the Snowmass report. The 
identification of these priorities was achieved through an in-depth review and 
evaluation of the relative impact and feasibility of addressing each challenge.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment. It's argued that a Muon Collider can be built with a reasonable level of technical feasibility using existing or near-term Advanced Superconducting Technology. Nevertheless, the unusual characteristics of high-energy muon collisions pose substantial challenges to both the detector and the simulator, particularly with respect to the interpretation of events involving heavy vector bosils and high-rate jet events. This presentation outlines the ongoing R&D initiatives aimed at addressing these difficulties. It's contended that a Muon Collider offers an unparalleled opportunity for in-depth exploration of the Standard Model and its sensitivity to departures from it, potentially serving as a global benchmark for the foreseeable future of particle physics. This presentation will also discuss the scientific advantages and energy reach of different collision options at a Muon Collider. It's also expected to play a pivotal role in the broader global HEP landscape, given its potential to serve as a prototype for the development of future electron-positron colliders. In the long term, a Muon Collider may well be the last major particle-smashing accelerator required to uncover the fundamental truths of Nature. It's also worth noting that a Muon Collider can be built in multiple configurations to address various scientific objectives, ranging from a low-energy, high-luminosity machine suitable for the precise examination of light fermions and rare decays to a high-energy, low-luminosity machine enabling thorough searches for physics beyond the Standard Model. This presentation will also discuss the underlying physics driving these different design options. It's also intended to provide an overview of the collaborative R&D between Fermilab and Cornell, spearheaded by the Muon Collider joint task force. It's noted that a Muon Collider can be built with existing or near-term technology using an iterative approach, where the machine and detector are developed in tandem with ongoing R&D. It's also contended that a Muon Collider offers a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for American particle physicists to play a leading role in a groundbreaking, high-profile project. It's also expected to attract and train a new generation of young researchers from diverse backgrounds.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation would be excessively high compared to observed radiowave signals. Furthermore, the assumption that PMDs emit through processes other than Hawking radiation also fails, as the alternative emission processes don't account for the observed flux. However, if a portion of dark matter exists in the form of these black holes, the Hawking radiation could become a viable explanation for the observed signals. For example, if dark matter constitutes 20% of its hypothetical black hole form, the Hawking radiation would precisely match the observed flux. Moreover, we found that the predicted spectral index ranges from -2.7 to -3.2, which closely aligns with observations. Ultimately, we conclude that the cosmic background of Hawking radiation remains a potential non-primordial explanation for the observed excess radiowave signals. To confirm or refute this theory, we suggest conducting joint analyses of gamma-ray and radiowave data from the IceCube and LOFAR collaborations. If ice cap data yields the same results as the LOFAR dataset, it would support this theoretical explanation, while conflicting results would necessitate an alternative interpretation of the observed signals. For instance, if the spectral index from the ice cap data is 2.01, as reported by the "soft" component, it would contradict our predicted range. Conversely, a spectral index of -3 from the LOFAR dataset would necessitate an alternative explanation of the observed signals. Moreover, we recommend analyzing the stratospheric detector data to verify whether the Hawking radiation hypothesis could be behind these signals. If this hypothesis is confirmed, it would mark a significant breakthrough in fundamental physics, while a refutation would necessitate exploring alternative theories behind these signals. It's possible that these primordial black holes could be detected through a joint analysis of gamma-ray and radiowave data, as their combined cross-correlation might reveal a characteristic "hourglass" shape. Ultimately, we emphasize that these signals serve as a significant test of theories behind these phenomena, as their lack of connection to astrophysical sources strengthens our understanding of these hypotheses. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation without relying on the LP round-up approximation technique from Baker's proof.

This research focuses on CSPs with constraints defined by functions taking non-integer values. For these types of problems, the current state-of-the-art approximation schemes are restricted to using linear programming with integer-valued constraints.

This research proposes a new PTAS for CSPs with constraints defined by functions, maintaining the relaxation of linear programming. The algorithm's efficiency is ensured by limiting the size of the linear programming solution space.

The results are achieved without referring to specifiable parameters. Instead, the specifiability of graph classes is sufficient. The new PTAS applies to, for example, $k$-colorable graphs and $H$-free graphs. The combinatorial technique used in this research is likely to be useful in other problems with similar specifications. The algorithm's time complexity is directly tied to the time it takes to solve the LP, which is $n^{O_t}(poly(k)}$. The number of steps required to solve the LP, $O_t$, doesn't depend on $n$.

The authors also present a new PTAS for $k$-CSP. The algorithm works by first removing vertices that can be optimally either in or out of the solution, which is determined using a special type of LP. The type of LP relies on $k$ being a perfect square. The algorithm then solves an LP problem for the reduced graph. The PTAS achieves $k+1$-approximation for any $\varepsilon > 0$ in $n^{O_t}(1/\varepsilon)^{2O_s})$ time, where the number of steps required to determine which vertices to remove is $O_s$. The algorithm is even more efficient when $\varepsilon$ is small enough and $k$ is large enough. The authors also present a new PTAS for $k$-edge $Q$-color cyclic Neighbourhood. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to define sentences' constituent structures. Furthermore, two experiments testing parsing tasks with limited and no annotated sentences were conducted, demonstrating the superior performance of UPIO in both cases. Additionally, we explored few-shot learning scenarios for parsing in low data conditions, leveraging the strong results of UPIO as a strong baseline. Our findings indicate that incorporating external supervision significantly enhances the performance of UPIO in parsing tasks with limited examples. The code and configuration to reproduce our results are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghadran/upoa. Our best model, UPIO, achieved better performance on the Penn Treebank dataset when compared to the current state-of-the-art unsupervised and few-shot parsing models. Importantly, the results show that enhancing the quality of the constituent structure within the language model leads to better parsing performance in low data conditions. Our findings also indicate that leveraging few-shot learning opportunities can effectively support the adaptation of unsupervised parsing models to new domains with limited examples. High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into a novel application of HSI, leveraging its multi-dimensional spectral data to facilitate weakly-supervised semantic segmentation within the detailed Cityscape dataset. By analyzing the spectral properties of 101 classes in Cityscape, we demonstrate that HSI can effectively discern between diverse categories, even without the need for pixel-level labels. Our proposed method outperforms conventional approaches using conventional RGB images, with comprehensive experimental results and ablation studies provided. Ultimately, this research showcases the significant potential of HSI data, highlighting its capacity to transform computer vision. The corresponding project page is available at https://hypers-pascal.github.io/. For technical contributions and code, please visit the repository at https://github.com/hypers-pascal/HyperPASCAL.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a internal star rotation pattern in KIC 9267653, acquired through 4.5 years of long-baseline mode fitting data from Kepler. We observed a significant and prolonged increase in the star's surface rotation speed over this period, defying typical expectations. Typically, as stars age, their internal rotation accelerates while their surface rotation slows, but in KIC 9267653, internal and surface rotations are surprisingly equivalent. There are two primary theories to explain this unusual rotation pattern: Firstly, the star may have once been part of a multiple star system and as it shrank to its current size, it absorbed one or more companion stars, resulting in the unusual rotation. Alternatively, there may be an abnormal movement of the star's angular momentum, caused by forces other than convection, which is unusual for stars of this type. Further observation is needed to determine the cause of this anomaly. We estimate that if the rotation pattern continues as it is, it may become completely internalized within the next 1.5-4.5 billion years. Additionally, while analyzing KIC 9267653, we discovered other less common variations in the star's movement, as well as various characteristics, including 11-day oscillations, irregular and unexpected variations in the star's contraction, and problems with existing star models. We observed that as the star contracts, its internal heat produces variations in its movement, but current star models fail to accurately predict this behavior, indicating that this star may undergo unusual transformations in the future. To better understand this star, we plan to analyze even longer datasets, thanks to the PLATO mission. We observed over 1 year following the arrival of the PLATO mission and discovered even more variations in the star, but were unable to complete this analysis due to issues with data quality caused by the satellite's malfunction. As a result, we are seeking permission to download and use in-house data from the PLATO mission, acquired through other channels, in order to complete our research and understand this unusual star rotation pattern. Using theoretical equations, we estimated possible variations in the star's movement, as well as its future rotation patterns, based on different and unlikely assumptions about the movement of the star's angular momentum. To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets. This work brings about two important contributions: first, a novel graph construction technique to identify related sessions within a user's historical data, and second, an efficient graph co-training algorithm to produce informative, not artificially sparse, data for training session-based recommendation models. This approach overcomes the problem of data sparsity affecting these models, using a session-based graph to enhance the quality of these models. Specifically, it improves the recall of top-20 recommendations by up to 7.4% compared to baseline supervised models, without using external data. Additionally, it outperforms existing supervised models that use labeled data, achieving better performance across multiple benchmark datasets. Moreover, it compares favorably to various strong baselines, consisting of supervised and unsupervised models, on three large-scale real-world datasets. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-trivial homology classes in the graph complex, which is the graph space with edges removed, connected by graph metrics. Ultimately, we propose an interpretation of motivic Feynman integrals as periods of this graph complex. The relationship between graph period integrals and multiple zeta values remains to be fully explored. The integration of these forms also provides an alternative proof of the feasibility of the Feichtinger, Gakker, and Matthes conjecture concerning graph zeta functions. The used techniques are analytical, whereas the proof of the feasibility involves the study of metrised complexes of graphs. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Notably, although our findings are based on object categorization, the underlying processing mechanisms may be applicable to a broader range of tasks.  This research also sets the stage for future investigations of factorial bias in recurrent neural networks.

We investigate the effect of correlations on the topological characteristics of non-Hermitian 1D systems. Specifically, we analyze how correlations influence the topological number of a non-Hermitian system with a point-gap topology. Our results demonstrate that correlations modify the topological number, rendering it dependent on the correlation strength. Moreover, we find that in the absence of correlations, the topological number is robust against interactions. However, correlations can drastically alter the point-gap topology, leading to the emergence of extended zero-mode states. Moreover, we show that correlations can shift the position of zero-modes within the gap. Our findings indicate that correlations offer a novel means of controlling and modifying the topological properties of non-Hermitian systems. Nonetheless, we also observe potential limitations in the practical manipulation of zero-modes due to their potential fragility under interactions. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of correlations in determining the topological properties of non-Hermitian systems, particularly in 1D systems where correlations can drastically alter the point-gap topology.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few instances of 97x97, while a proof shows the non-existence of a 97x97 GCM quadruple with a certain property. Furthermore, this study explores the relationship between GCMs and Golay complementary matrices, establishing the necessary and sufficient conditions for extending a GCM to a GCM quadruple. Using these findings, several new 4D GCM quadruples are constructed and it is proven that there is no 5D GCM quadruple. Lastly, a theoretical investigation into finding the largest possible size for a 4D GCM quadruple is initiated. To confirm the conjecture about the largest possible size for a 4D GCM quadruple and to gain insights into this theory, the authors analyzed the properties of Hamming graphs. Several new 78x78 and 97x97 GCM quadruples were also constructed using the Hamming graph approach. Furthermore, this study presents an alternative proof that there is no 5D GCM quadruple and demonstrates that any 4D GCM quadruple can be transformed into a 3D GCM quadruple under specific conditions. Finally, a novel method based on the Hamming graphs is presented for constructing 4D GCM quadruples that are also Golay complementary arrays. This approach utilizes the graph's automorphisms to build the GCM quadruples. Several new 78x78 and 97x97 GCM quadruples were constructed using this method. Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previous experiments from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 35.9 inverse femtobarns of luminosity. The four-lepton final state is examined, allowing for the measurement of the Higgs boson's width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By analyzing Higgs boson production near and away from its resonance, constraints are obtained on theoretical models beyond the Standard Model. In one such analysis, the Higgs boson's width is bound by the Standard Model, while in another, the HVV coupling is measured with precision. For the beyond Standard Model analysis, consideration is given to a variety of alternatives, including a type-I two Higgs doublet model, a heavy vector triplet model, and a low mass scalar model. In these alternative models, the Higgs boson's width and HVV coupling deviate significantly from their Standard Model values. To this end, a fit to these measurements, along with other Higgs boson production and decay data, yields a global 95% confidence level upper limit on additional production in the range of 11-20 GeV. Furthermore, a type-I two Higgs doublet model is shown to be ruled out by these experiments up to a mass of 550 GeV and 680 GeV for the Fermi Constant and electroweak parameters, S and T, respectively. Finally, the study provides the most stringent limits to date on the LHC, normalizing for collision energy. In the type-II two Higgs doublet model, the study offers the most stringent limits to date on parameter epsilon_2, at 0.24, 0.18, and 0.11 for three different masses of additional Higgs bosons. Moreover, the study provides the most stringent limits to date on heavy vector triplet model parameters M_V and k_F, at 2.2 TeV and 1.9 TeV, respectively. In the low mass scalar model, the study provides the most stringent limits to date on parameter xi, at 0.11. A comprehensive analysis of these constraints is also given in the paper. Based on these experiments, the study concludes that the Standard Model of particle physics adequately describes Higgs boson production and its interactions with electroweak vector bosons. This principle is prominently demonstrated in the valley interference phenomenon observed in monolayer MoS2. In contrast, this report showcases the observation of valley interference in silicon, a material that normally used in bulk form, by translating moire pattern-valley physics from monolayers to a bilayer-on-agar system. Furthermore, we successfully isolate the contribution of spin exchange, a process typically considered to be classically intuitive, by manipulating the valley state's orbital symmetry. This achievement represents a breakthrough in understanding both quantum tunneling and exchange processes. To push this understanding into the nanoscale, we suggest a research agenda based on silicon quantum dots, proposing an experimental setup to investigate valley-exchange entanglement. This report concludes with potential applications of these principles in quantum computing and nanotechnology. Ultimately, we aim to inspire future research to explore the unique properties of silicon, a material that, due to its widespread use, may hold more potential than any other quantum system. Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring open questions related to projective spaces, Grassmannians, and Lagrangian Grassmannians. To characterize compact quasi-affine toric varieties with a highest degree of transitivity, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions in terms of the combinatorial structure of their Newton-Okounkov partitions. Additionally, we establish a connection between the transitivity degree of an algebraic variety under the action of its automorphism group and the degree of action of its Cremona group, while identifying the transitivity degree for specific spaces, such as projective spaces, Grassmannians, and Lagrangian Grassmannians. To achieve this, we utilize various mathematical concepts, including the development of a new method to analyze highly transitive actions, drawing insights from the study of rational curves within these varieties. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition of individual particle momenta, which become ambiguous. Our results indicate that previous Fock space constructions were flawed due to incorrect assumptions about particle identity. We demonstrate that momentum exchange underlies a relativistic covariance principle in the braiding of quantum numbers, solving a persistent challenge in the field. Our framework maintains covariance under any momentum transformation and resolves the particle identification crisis, revealing that our quantum theory is inherently multi-particle based. Our model also extends to non-abelian space symmetries, yielding a versatile theory applicable to various space-time deformations and Lie groups. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak hours, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework is referred to as the $\mathcal{W}_{\pli,N,\beta}$-code. When placed in a scenario with time division, the $\mathcal{W}$-code can be analyzed by converting it into a sequence of convex polygons. This analysis leads to optimal results for specific situations and serves as a versatile tool for designing caching and computation schemes. Furthermore, our study reveals that the strongest schemes within certain constraints have weaknesses that can be quantified. These schemes, characterized by their placement in the convex hull, offer a range of suboptimal solutions. Through careful computation, we derive explicit expressions for several caching and computation problems. Our innovative approach also enables us to devise a communication-computation tradeoff strategy. We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative approach. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad is equivalent to using the universe of propositions with higher inductive types, as argued by Escard\'o. We also show that in univalent type theory, the standard uncurried encoding of functions coincides with the encoding derived from the Curry-Howard correspondence. Our formalization is based on the Coq proof assistant, which we enhance by integrating a compiler for higher inductive types and the lifting monad. The associated Coq files are available on the repository https://alb--gitlab.univ-lille.fr/LoicEsteban/scott_model.git. In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. Moreover, the developed approach exhibits high robustness and simplicity, making it easily implementable on actual mobile robotic arms. Experimental testing on a physical robot is planned for future research. With its ability to efficiently handle complex geometries, this control method possesses essential qualities for real-world application on actual mobile robotic systems. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric structures. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. We introduce an algorithm to calculate this location by combining signature-based elimination methods with extensivity concepts to identify nondegenerate locations. The approach is illustrated by examples in the case of solvable but degenerate situations. Moreover, the implementation of this algorithm is carried out using the MathematICA package, Signo. The results show that this package outperforms other leading algebraic geometric solvers in several tests. The reason for this performance lies in the computational efficiency and stability provided by the extensivity-based signature algorithm in capturing the nondegenerate location of polynomial systems. The detailed explanation of this algorithm and its associated implementation are the main contributions of this work. The research also delves into the extensivity properties of solution sets and their applications in capturing relevant geometric structures, such as nonsingular loci of hypersurfaces, and establishes a new theorem on this property. The approach is based on a novel combination of signature-based algorithmic solutions to related problems in elimination theory and projective geometry. The associated implementation using the Signo package is also a significant contribution of this research. The study is based on joint research between University of Warsaw and University of California, Berkeley. The research was financially supported by funding from NCN, grant agreement: 2018/28/Q/ST6/00516, and the Simons foundation grant: 552173. The MathematICA package used in this research is publicly available at: https://www.fit.ewu.edu/faculty/martin-sorbye/signo.html. The relevant algebraic geometric solvers used in the research are: Resolve, Mandarina, Singular and Signo. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp specific objects is a significant challenge that limits their use in industrial settings. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies. We advocate for further investigation into the properties of state representation, the consistency of results from different approaches, and the exploration of word embeddings and neural network architectures in natural language state representation. Ultimately, a standardized framework is required to ensure substantial progress in the field. We hope to encourage discussion and collaboration through the release of NLStateRep, a comprehensive repository of approaches to natural language state representation, allowing for replication of results and comparison of methods. Please visit https://nl-state-rep.com/index.html for more information.

By using a dataset consisting of both simulated and observed spectra, two deep learning models are developed to sequentially estimate the redshift and density power spectrum shape of these clouds. A subsequent model uses these predictions as input to reconstruct the density power spectrum shape. Despite being trained on spectra with redshifts up to 6, a simple neural network trained on low-redshift simulations is able to predict the density power spectrum shape across a range of redshifts. Further investigation into the performance of this method with larger datasets is required to assess its potential for use in analysing observed quasar spectra to better understand the evolution of neutrino density fluctuations at very high redshifts. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features.
To build this system, we have created a new dataset called Role-Dial, which
consists of 17,622 human-human dialogues exhibiting various roles. To effectively
utilize large language models, we have developed a method that uses role-constrained
autocorrect as an iterative process. The results of our approach are promising,
with evaluations indicating that our model excels in multiple aspects over state-
of-the-art baselines, also maintaining a high level of safety according to human
evaluation. Moreover, due to its ability to continuously learn, our model is capable
of adapting to newly introduced role types. Consequently, it is possible to scale
dialogue systems while ensuring consistency in meeting role specifications. Further
details are available on our website at https://role-dial.github.io/. Comments
and suggestions are welcome on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/role-dial/role-dial.

Two naive bayes-based models are presented, along with a hybrid model that combines the strengths of word prediction and topic modeling. Experimental results reveal that our hybrid model outperforms leading algorithms, including Multinomial Naive Bayes and Random Forest, in predicting words and topics. Moreover, a deep learning technique is used to determine the word and topic embeddings for our hybrid model. Interestingly, the hybrid model exhibits improved performance when compared to leading word2vec-based algorithms, such as Word2Vec and FastText. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the activities surrounding it. When the activities on either side differ, the dimer assumes a non-linear configuration, with the active particle oriented towards the area with higher activity. Through various simulations, we confirm that this is a universal response. Additionally, we investigate how this response changes when one of the particles becomes passive. We find that, in the absence of activity differences, the dimer achieves a low-energy state near the center of its configuration space. However, when an activity gradient exists, the active particle tilts towards the area with higher activity, resulting in an increased energy state. For the passive particle, the opposite occurs - it tilts towards the area with lower activity. These findings have implications for the formation of active colloidal crystals. If the particles in these crystals respond positively to activity increments, they may orient themselves in a way that enhances interparticle interactions, potentially facilitating the creation of more stable structures. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions, and secondly, finding efficient methods to reassemble the swarm post-collision avoidance. To address the first challenge, a method utilizing energy-efficient evasive maneuvers is developed. For the second challenge, a data registration approach inspired by computer science is applied to efficiently reassemble the swarm. The effectiveness of these strategies is evaluated through both simulation tests and outdoor experiments. The results show that this formation maintenance method after avoiding collisions not only consumes less energy but also does not require any prior knowledge of the environment. This research makes significant contributions to the fields of optimization, registration, and autonomous swarming systems. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered high-quality according to their own standards. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first train these models, but current methods rely on costly, manual labeling. This study demonstrates how Wikipedia's unique editing history can be harnessed to create labels automatically. By analyzing the actions of trusted editors, we pinpoint patterns of behavior indicating article quality. Through natural language processing and machine learning, we validate these findings and show that Wikipedia's own quality metrics correlate strongly with our identified patterns. Therefore, we propose a method to generate labels using these editing history patterns, effectively replacing the need for manual labels and making it possible for the scale and reliability of Wikipedia to be harnessed for machine learning tasks. Our technique is the first to utilize editing behaviors for this purpose and can be adapted to other communities with similar documentation practices. Our results show that this method produces labels on a large scale with high accuracy and outperforms existing machine learning techniques for predicting article quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this method can be employed to develop a comprehensive quality measurement that encompasses multiple aspects, revealing that many articles on sensitive topics such as COVID-19, racism, and climate change would benefit from increased involvement of trusted editors. Our research highlights both the utility and challenges of using editing behaviors for labeling and suggests future directions for the applications of Wikipedia in machine learning. To facilitate further work, our trained models, along with related data and code, are publicly available at https://github.com/jbrc-pu/directory/tree/main/edits. Our research aims to promote the use of editing behaviors as a powerful tool for both understanding and training models within community-driven knowledge bases. Ultimately, we strive to make these knowledge bases available for machine learning, effectively combining the scale of Wikipedia with the reliability of trusted editors. To prove this, we successfully train a model using our automatically generated labels on a large corpus of articles and demonstrate its accuracy on a previously unseen, highly validated dataset. Our study shows that automatic labeling enables training machine learning models on a vast corpus of articles, resulting in both high accuracy and large training datasets. While our research focuses on Wikipedia, we recognize that our method can be adapted to various platforms featuring user-generated content, such as online forums and review platforms. Conversely, we also emphasize the unique challenges posed by Wikipedia's nature, which necessitate novel solutions for prelabeled data

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. A novel approach, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allows a model to be trained to replicate the behavior of a network whose internal workings are unknown, given only its input-output decisions. This is made possible by analyzing the network's decision boundaries, which can be approximated using a data-independent learning process. This paper proposes a data-dependent learning process based on query synthesis to further improve the accuracy of decision-based black-box knowledge distillation. The method is evaluated on various network architectures and datasets, demonstrating significant performance gains over previous black-box distillation methods. Notably, it achieves nearly identical accuracy to traditional knowledge distillation, while also resulting in a more compact model. The method is also capable of training models that can operate independently of their original environment, which is a key advantage. The proposed technique is known as Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation, and is shown to provide superior performance over other black-box distillation methods. This research presents a comprehensive evaluation of the method and offers guidance on its implementation. The proposed method is found to be particularly suitable for networks using ReLU and Swish activations, and is observed to result in a model size reduction of up to 11.42% with only a 0.56% accuracy drop. The Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation method is also capable of training models that can operate effectively in networks with different architectures and training datasets. Overall, this research presents a novel approach to knowledge distillation that offers significant performance and efficiency gains over existing black-box methods. The method is observed to result in a model size reduction of up to 11.42% with only a 0.56% accuracy drop, and is capable of training models that can operate effectively in networks with different architectures and training datasets. To facilitate reproduction of these results, the code and models used in this research are publicly available for download. Additionally, the method is expected to offer significant performance and efficiency gains over existing knowledge distillation methods due to its ability to train models that can behave similarly to high-capacity networks despite reductions in model size.
