This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. Furthermore, our results show that search-limited PAC codes can be used as a reliable alternative to polar codes in systems with limited decoding resources. We also provide a C++11 library for PAC code decoding, which includes functions for search-limited and partial-order decoding. This library can be accessed through the GitHub repository: https://github.com/zhengjinyong/pac-code-decoding. Additionally, we provide a MATLAB script for generating polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. This script is also available on GitHub: https://github.com/zhengjinyong/pac-code-decoding/tree/master/PAC_code_generator. We have tested our results by running these scripts on PC and GPU platforms. Our results indicate that partial-order PAC code decoding can achieve a 3.96 times speed-up over search-limited PAC code decoding, both in binary and QPSK transmission scenarios. This advantage in computation efficiency is attributed to the reduced complexity of partial-order PAC code decoding, especially for high-rate codes. We observed a complementary relationship between search-limited and partial-order PAC code decoding, such that search-limited decoding outperforms partial-order decoding for low-rate codes and vice versa. We hypothesize that this phenomenon may be related to the distinct error-correcting mechanisms of polarization and convolutional codes. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. This leads to improved inference in high-dimensional, complex networks, such as online experiments. Additionally, we introduce a more comprehensive inference approach to identify the entire set of influential units within the given interference model. This innovation enables hard-to-imagine controlled experiments (requiring physical modifications, for instance) and provides valuable insights in settings where such modifications are not necessary. Our work represents the first comprehensive assessment of detecting treatment interference in networks. We showcase its utility in various empirical settings, such as educational and scientific experiments. Our findings and methods are made available through the R package called DetectTI. We highlight potential future areas of research and show the facilitation of cross-disciplinary discussions through a variable importance measure that captures treatment effects mediated through neighboring units. This concept, called mutual information, is used to explore treatments with significant impact on other units. It is also used to illustrate the detection of treatment interference in units receiving the same treatment. This novel perspective on treatment interference in homogeneous populations provides novel ways to analyze and improve the understanding of treatment-driven phenomena within these populations. We present a detection criterion for such homogeneous populations and show its utility in a real-world example. A more detailed description of our approach and results, along with code, can be found in the supporting materials. In the case of treatment interference, deep learning techniques like pre-trained variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks fall short in detecting treatment interference (see the supporting materials for a detailed explanation). In contrast, a complementary approach that incorporates information from multiple units (called LightGBM) performs well for detection and provides insights into treatment effects within neighboring units. It is also used to illustrate the detection of treatment interference within fictional and real data sets. This study assesses the potential impact of these emissions on a star's thermal evolution, with and without the interaction of these particles with neutrinos, using a self-consistent approach. The results indicate that, in the presence of neutrino interactions, the number of neutrinos produced is substantially reduced. The UNIONS project is conducting a wide-field survey at 7500 square-degrees in the Northern sky with the CFHTLS camera, offering precise observations of galaxy shapes in the b<3650 magnitude range. To optimize this data for accurate weak-lensing analyses, a specialized measurement pipeline was developed, incorporating multiple shape estimation methods. Compared to established pipelines, the new shape pipeline demonstrated superior accuracy when tested on realistic simulations, achieving a 10% improvement in overall precision. The UNIONS team utilized this pipeline to process 750 deg^2 of data, providing a comprehensive dataset of precise galaxy shape measurements. This dataset, known as UNIONS-750, consists of 37 million galaxies with complex shapes and high precision, making it a valuable resource for precise cosmological studies. The UNIONS project is ongoing, with plans to extend the dataset to 7500 deg^2. The released dataset, referred to as UNIONS-750, can be accessed at https://www.unions-project.org/publications.php. Future updates will be available on the project website. 

In this research, we detail the UNIONS pipeline and its data release. We then use the dataset to demonstrate the accuracy of our shape measurements and effective redshift distribution. We further highlight the importance of precise and extensive shape data, comparing it to other large-scale surveys, such as DES and KiDS. We then discuss how the UNIONS dataset can be utilized for cosmological studies, specifically weak-lensing analyses, which will be detailed in follow-up publications. 

To find the mean mass-oxidation efficiency in the range z = 0-6, we applied the UNIONS pipeline to the 850 deg^2 COSMOS-30 dataset, combining it with weak-lensing analyses. However, this led to an inconsistent result, indicating negative mean oxidation efficiency for a given redshift range. To resolve this anomaly, we employed two corrective approaches, ultimately obtaining a more plausible result. We conclude that our survey is capable of accurately mapping galaxy shapes and contributing to precise cosmological studies, as demonstrated by our initial application to the COSMOS-30 dataset.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed single-qubit Z-rotation gate, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m/2}$. An additional suggestion is presented for potentially enhancing the upper bounds through the design of specific linear codes. Existing upper limits on stabilizer rank are shown to be insufficient in this context, while novel lower limits on the required stabilizer rank are proposed, potentially yielding novel lower limits on the entangling power of quantum circuits. These results are derived using a novel approach quantifying the degree of entanglement within quantum circuits, expressed as the minimum number of stabilizer state embeddings needed to describe a given quantum state on $n$ qubits. The connection between this concept and linear coding is explored through the introduction of a novel class of codes, $\mathcal{C}^{(\beta,\gamma)}(n,m)$. The study concludes by refining existing upper limits on the stabilizer rank of state $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$ within quantum circuits comprising Clifford + T gates, specifically for certain types of unitary operators with restricted matrix sizes. These refined bounds yield improved algorithmic results for classically simulating specific variants of quantum circuits. The work presented does not rely on existing results from quantum complexity theory but rather leverages tools from classical mathematics, including the concept of measure concentration. Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SPC. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 catalog, the LAMOST research team corrected for astrometric zero points and radial velocity before developing new algorithms to identify moving groups and identify the sources of radial velocity scatter. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team identified 1210 binary stars, around 3.5% of the binary stars in the $K$2 catalog, through their analysis of the $W_{JS}$ index. Additionally, the LAMOST research team utilized the $W_{JS}$ index to identify single-lined systems that were likely binary stars and identified 1800 such systems. Lastly, the LAMOST research team identified around 3.6% of the $K$2 catalog as variable stars, but noted that around 60% of these systems had low signal-to-noise ratios, which meant more work was needed to confirm these systems as variable stars. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team concluded that while some limitations existed, especially low signal-to-noise ratios, the data showed great promise and the LAMOST research team was confident that more useful information could be extracted once more exposure data was collected. Moreover, the LAMOST research team anticipated that the newly developed algorithms to observe the same targets every 30 days would be especially useful in identifying and studying long-period variable stars. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRNM methods often suffer from reduced energy efficiency, extended latency, and decreased entropy extraction rates. In contrast, our proposed method, TuRaN, utilizes a lower supply voltage to extract SRAM cells' thermal random variations, thereby increasing entropy extraction rates while reducing energy consumption and latency. To validate TuRaN's effectiveness, we created a prototype test-chip and conducted experiments, which demonstrate the feasibility of high-speed, low-energy SRNM from SRAM cells operating below the typical supply voltage. Specifically, our results show that TuRaN achieves nearly tripled entropy extraction rates compared to prior SRNM methods, all while remaining competitive in energy consumption and latency. Furthermore, TuRaN's functionality was verified across a broad range of process nodes, spanning 28nm to 180nm. Additionally, our study quantifies and analyzes the statistical properties of SRNM, revealing that high-quality random numbers can be generated using SRAM cells across diverse technology nodes. Consequently, TuRaN's design allows for the widespread adoption of SRNM in diverse integrated circuits. With its ability to simultaneously optimize entropy extraction rates, energy consumption, and latency, TuRaN represents a leading solution for SRNM. Our research will guide the design and evaluation of SRNM systems in the semiconductor industry. As such, the source code of our simulation tool and test-chip layout are publicly available for reproduction of our results and potential integration into commercial products. Furthermore, our study's findings on SRNM quality can be employed to enhance random number generation in various applications. To facilitate scalability and extended research opportunities, we have publicly shared our design files, simulation code, and research data. Moreover, we have developed a comprehensive tutorial on SRNM, which covers our research and is suitable for advanced undergraduate and graduate students. As such, TuRaN holds significant value as a contributing solution to the public SRNM community. As far as we know, TuRaN represents the first SRNM method to successfully operate SRAM cells below the typical supply voltage, thereby opening up new possibilities for high-quality random number generation. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a novel strategy to enforce masslessness in two-loop box integrands, which leads to significant reductions in numerical fluctuations. Our findings underscore the potential of loop-tree duality-based approaches in delivering accurate numerical results for complex multi-loop Feynman integrands. Moreover, our work contributes to the ongoing development of the CASUAL framework, which provides a causal representation of Feynman integrands. The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique material properties. Additionally, we observed the onset of superconductivity and 2D magnetism under specific conditions. Furthermore, we discovered that certain characteristics can be influenced by GdBa surface termination while others arise due to electron-spectroscopic scattering from the substrate. Our research provides a framework for understanding how chemistry and material synthesis impact quantum behavior in ultra-thin transition-metal oxides. Lastly, we propose that these findings could be experimentally verified using spectroscopic, transport, and x-ray scattering analysis.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. However, even the most advanced quantum models cannot fully rely on quantum mechanics as the basis of their calculations, since even classical trajectories exhibit significant zero-point motion after several periodic cycles. In this research, the focus is on the significance of including the zero-point motion in the study of small clusters composed of sulphuric acid and water. The results show that while the overall structure of clusters is little affected by including the zero-point motion, their growth dynamics is significantly altered. The absence of zero-point motion leads to unphysical behavior in their trajectories, causing them to cluster in an irregular and uncontrolled manner. Consequently, the distribution of clusters is shifted towards smaller sizes when the zero-point motion is disregarded. In contrast, the presence of zero-point motion has little impact on the stability of stable clusters, since even without it, they would naturally return to their equilibrium positions. In this research, the application of the Quantum Trajectory Dynamics (QTD) approach is used to study the importance of including the zero-point motion in the quantum study of small clusters composed of sulphuric acid and water. QTD relies on the parallel calculation of both the classical and quantum trajectories of particles, with their intersection points determining the likelihood of quantum leaps. Despite the proven capability of quantum models to overcome supersaturated conditions, the success of these models in modeling particle formation depends on their ability to accurately reproduce the behavior of classical trajectories. In this research, the success of quantum models in modeling particle formation is explored under the influence of zero-point motion. In principle, the availability of pathways through potential energy surfaces could counterbalance the rapid frequency of quantum leaps, making it possible for particles to reach supersaturated conditions. In ordinary thermodynamics, the thermal response of a system is described through its heat capacity, C, in relation to temperature, T, via the specific heat capacity c = C/T. This definition of specific heat capacity forms the basis for analogous expressions in quantum magnets, known as Héon-London theory, and in superconductors, Héon-James theory. These theories share a common underlying idea of thermal energy being transferred as heat (Q = d(U/T)/dT) between two parts of the system, with the difference in internal energy per particle, u/n, driving this process. The relationship between the derivative of internal energy per particle, u/n, and temperature, T, represents the internal heat source or sink within the system. This generative nature of heat sources or sinks within the system is suppressed in classical thermodynamics, where it is subsumed by the external heat transfer, thereby appearing as an adiabatic invariant. As such, it should not contribute to the external heat transfer. In this work, we show through numerical analysis that this generative nature of heat sources or sinks within the system does not remain suppressed in quantum magnets, where it is expected to be described through Héon-London theory. Rather, this local heat production rate, as represented through the derivative of internal energy per particle, u/n, is active and no longer exclusively adiabatic in nature. Consequently, we demonstrate that the internal energy per particle, u/n, fails to satisfy the analogy with classical potential energy, V(x), as well as the first Einstein relation, which equates the time-averaged heat current, J_s, with the spatial derivative of the internal energy, d(U/n)/dx. Similarly, we show through numerical analysis that the Héon-James theory, which describes thermal energy transfer in superconductors, also fails to satisfy these analogies and relations. Despite these failures, we show that the Héon-London and Héon-James theories do share a common underlying mathematical structure, in which the derivative of internal energy per particle, u/n, acts as an invisible, generative local heat source or sink, while also proposing a broader theory that encompasses these two theories. This broader theory, which we refer to as the thermodynamic conservation of charge and energy, describes the interaction between particles and the environment, where the derivative of internal energy per particle, u/n, represents the generative nature of heat sources or sinks within the system, while also conserving charge and energy.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice. With this full dataset, the new approach is capable of measuring the Wilson coefficients $C_9$ and $C_{10}$ simultaneously with uncertainties below 0.5%, surpassing the current Wilson coefficient extraction method's performance by nearly an order of magnitude. This new analysis reveals the significance of $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays in precisely assessing the Standard Model and remains responsive to diverse scenarios arising from its potential variations, such as in the lepton flavour universality-laws violating LMU model. This new method is also adaptable to future $e^+e^-$ collider experiments, like Belle II, and is anticipated to significantly contribute to a precise determination of the Wilson coefficients there. Furthermore, this new approach is applicable to other $b\to s$ transition decays at hadron colliders and is resistant to potential issues with lepton flavour non-universality-related artefacts. With the new approach, the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process is expected to provide crucial constraints on the effective field theory contributing to beyond the Standard Model. This novel method is expected to evolve with the growing dataset and is likely to be generalized across a broader range of $b\to s$ transitions. An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of our safety filter design with model predictive control methods in terms of performance, computational efficiency, and online complexity. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning capabilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the learning in-context abilities of a 1.3B-parameter large language model. Our key discoveries include: Firstly, models trained on data originating from user-generated content (e.g. Reddit) exhibit a notable decline in their in-context learning performance in comparison to those trained on more curated sources (e.g. Wikipedia). Secondly, a increase in training corpus size can enhance in-context learning capabilities, despite the model already being quite large. Lastly, our results suggest that enhanced pretraining data does accelerate in-context learning, especially when tasks are drawn from the same domain as the pretraining corpus. Our findings indicate that pretraining corpus choice and size has a significant impact on the in-context learning capabilities of large language models. Additionally, our results imply that large language models may be more effective when tackling tasks within more informal contexts. Moreover, our research suggests that increasing model parameterization can partially mitigate adverse effects of data's origin on in-context learning capabilities. With our insights, developers may gain a deeper understanding of the inherent limitations and potential biases of pretraining corpora and, consequently, the capabilities of the models themselves. Furthermore, our research may enable engineers to tailor the pretraining data for their models in order to maximize their in-context learning capabilities across diverse tasks and domains. Through computational modeling, we investigate the repeated emergence of cooling catalogs in galaxy clusters, focusing on the impact of factors such as radiative cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal conduction. Our simulations indicate that the repeated appearance of cooling catalogs leads to more irregular, filament-like structures, especially when thermal conduction is disabled. When magnetic fields are present, they prevent the development of these filaments. Our findings suggest that the repeated emergence of cooling catalogs might not always lead to more extensive, nebula-like structures, but instead results in fragmented, filamentary structures. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The results of multiple subjective and objective experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The speech samples generated from this approach without transcription data are indistinguishable from those with transcription data in terms of mean opinion score, and its synthesis quality is comparable to that of state-of-the-art speech systems using transcription data. The output of this approach includes detailed phonetic information including stress and intonation, which facilitates application in natural language processing. The proposed system is an advancement over prior research in speech synthesis without transcription data, and its speech samples can be found at https://speechresearch.github.io/zero-resource/index.html. We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. In the first scenario, our results show that the combination of gravity and movement causes the liquid to oscillate like a pumped nonlinear pendulum, demonstrating increased complexity. Additionally, our findings from the second scenario match those of a purely vertically excited nonlinear pendulum, also known as the Duffing oscillator. To further validate our model, we compared its response to that of a more complex, specifically designed cup, used in a previous study by Karasu et al. in 2019. Our analysis shows that the movement of this liquid can be intricately linked to the dynamics of a chaotic system, exhibiting similarities with the behavior of a piecewise linear chaotic pendulum. This connection is evident in the multiple states of motion we've identified, as well as our comparison of the correct movement, as observed through video analysis, with the predicted behavior based on our model. These predictions take into account both the statically and dynamically stable positions of the liquid. In conclusion, our investigation into the excited, planar motion of a liquid in a cup demonstrates that its behavior can be accurately predicted through a combination of fundamental physical principles. These underlying principles provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics at play, bridging the gap between theoretical modeling and real-world observations. Lastly, our study highlights the potential for a bridge between two distinct areas of research - the study of chaotic systems and the dynamics of nonlinear excitation, particularly in the context of the piecewise linear chaotic pendulum and the pumped nonlinear pendulum, respectively. Based on our comparison of the results from our model with those of Karasu et al., it seems the latter approach offers more opportunities for groundbreaking research and innovation. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. Additionally, DR-DSGD's computational complexity is $4$ times lower than other robust decentralized methods, such as Decentralized Alternating Minimization (Decentralized Alternating Minimization). DR-DSGD can be used in a range of decentralized applications, including autonomous vehicles, robots, aircraft, sensors, and Internet of Things devices, facilitating robust and efficient adaptation to data distribution changes in these scenarios. DR-DSGD's source code is available at https://github.com/adhi2000/distributional-robust-decentralized-learning. Moreover, a detailed tutorial on DR-DSGD is available at https://github.com/adhi2000/tutorial-distributional-robust-decentralized-learning. Key concepts underlying DR-DSGD are also explained in a research report, available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01630. DR-DSGD has been successfully demonstrated in various decentralized settings, as shown in the accompanying video: https://youtu.be/6R3D9G9mUgY. We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, our study predicts enhanced particle production in collisions involving large, centrally-focused nuclei and estimates the consequences of their interaction, known as cold nuclear matter effects, on measurements of jet quenching in proton-proton and nucleus-nucleus collisions. Ultimately, our research highlights the significance of hydrodynamics in understanding the early stages of high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions and detects hints of non-equilibrium behavior within the quark-gluon plasma. This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error, which ultimately enables comprehensive compensation and performance restoration. It is acknowledged that within a safety zone, the BPC structure can be reduced to the FBC backstepping (FBC) control method. Through extensive analysis, it is established that (1) the BFC control can maintain suboptimal levels of performance even in the presence of mild saturation; (2) severe saturation can lead to significant performance degradation; (3) the BFC control can be recovered through compensation when the saturation effect diminishes; and (4) the compensation process allows for restored suboptimal performance. Numerical simulations are then employed to validate the theoretical findings and evaluate the efficacy of the proposed control mechanism. Furthermore, a practical study highlights the applicability of the BFC-BPC framework to an aircraft pitch control system. Safety assessments are used to determine optimal safety thresholds, and numerical simulations demonstrate the BFC-BPC controlled system outperforms the comparator system with similar characteristics. Moreover, severe saturation can be effectively addressed through compensation. All these results confirm that the BFC-BPC control structure offers a balanced combination of performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems. Ultimately, this study contributes to the ongoing quest for the optimal BPC control structure. our main goal would be to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities. A crucial step to reach this goal would be to determine the instability scale of the Higgs potential. Achieving this requires reducing uncertainty about two key elements: the strong coupling and the mass of the top quark. Specifically, the mass of the top quark can be accurately measured by analyzing pairs of particles near their threshold at lower luminosity rates, around 10 to the 33, cm to the minus 2, per second, which is within reach of the LHC at higher instantaneous luminosity. On the other hand, the strong coupling constant can be accurately measured by analyzing the production of a specific particle near its threshold at a collider with high energy but relatively low luminosity, around 10 to the 32, cm to the minus 2, per second. Once these parameters are well understood, the mass of the top quirk can also be pinpointed more precisely. This leads to a question - should we invest in a collider with high energy but relatively low luminosity to make these crucial measurements sooner? 

In this study, we explore different approaches to determining the Higgs stability in a vast landscape of possibilities. We also investigate whether the stability of the Higgs potential can be ascertained by analyzing the Higgs coupling and the top quirk mass alone. This requires either extremely high energy or extremely high luminosity, but the options seem limited. We examine various scenarios to determine which approach might be feasible with existing or planned colliders, specifically considering the electron-positron colliders ILC, CLIC, and CEPC, the proton-proton LHC, and a proposed hadron collider HE-LHC or its future version. We find that although some of these machines might be capable of determining the instability scale, they might not be able to do so. 

On the other hand, we explore an alternative strategy where we try to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities by comparing its predictions with theoretical models that can explain new physics. This is done by analyzing numerous scenarios from different types of theoretical models by their likelihood to be confirmed, based on different criteria such as fit to precision data, new physics scales, and instability in the Higgs potential. Ultimately, we investigate which approach should be preferred to determine which strategy to pursue

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages an Radial Basis Function kernel to transform input data and embeds it in a higher-dimensional space, where it capitalizes on future time steps' information by taking into account past time steps, ultimately achieving superior performance in predicting future actions. This novel approach extends beyond prior action prediction techniques, which typically rely on recurrent models encoding long-term information or utilize future information through zero-padding, beyond data-driven methods for predicting actions. In a comprehensive set of experiments, our framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, which include RNN, LSTMs, CNN-RNN hybrids, and spatiotemporal models, demonstrating particular superiority in more challenging scenarios. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence supporting key design decisions: utilizing a kernel to transform input data, selecting a basis function with a Regressor, and training through supervised learning. Specifically, our results show that utilizing a kernel transforms results in a 3.5% improvement over non-kernelized alternatives. Moreover, training through supervised learning yields a 10.5% improvement over unsupervised and semi-supervised alternatives. Consequently, our supervised feature mapping approach yields a 16.3% improvement over other methods. All experimental code, including our feature mapping RNN, can be accessed at https://github.com/pull/rfkm-rnn. Our method is also publicly available as a TensorFlow 2.x module at https://github.com/pull/feature-mapping-rnn. A video showcasing our approach can be found at https://youtu.be/6TCgJ1kR2Gk. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for positive time intervals. Both time
awareness and efficiency considerations are incorporated into the model. Through
experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed solution outperforms current state
of the art methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Further, we conduct a
parameter efficiency analysis with the recently introduced semigraph, semimeter,
semikernel naming convention for kernel-based models. Our results indicate that
these semikernel models exhibit superior performance in temporal knowledge graph
completions while using a more efficient number of parameters compared to other
kernel-based models. The findings suggest that tuning model parameters within
the semikernel naming convention leads to both better metric scores and reduced
computational requirements. We name this tuning process semiautomation and propose
the naming convention as semi- for model and representation characteristics
that exhibit scalable behavior. This work is set to become a public repository and
will be sustained through an associated website. The code will be made accessible
at its release. Until then, details of the approach and supporting data are available
at https://fferanekrom.github.io/TimeFER/.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized model of impact sound that takes into account the sound produced by the ground is developed. It is discovered that the decoupled sound radiation models' implication of low-frequency sound exclusion does not apply to the sound produced by the ground. Furthermore, it is found that using statistical energy analysis to determine the sound frequency spectrum is justified. An analytical method based on the Kirchhoff plate theory is used to derive equations for sound frequency spectrum, and these results are compared with measurements from experiments. It is found that these theoretical predictions accurately represent the sound frequency spectrum in measured data. An investigation of the effect of ground sound propagation modes on sound radiation models reveals that these modes do not contribute to sound produced by the ground. An explanation for this phenomenon is provided in terms of energy variation in the ground. An approach for reducing high-frequency errors in sound produced by the ground is developed, and it is found that using thin plates instead of rigid plates eliminates these errors. An application of the developed methods to design and create an electronic drum pad that produces realistic sound is also explored. An analysis of the drum pad's sound frequency spectrum and decay time reveals that the developed methods accurately reproduce the characteristics of acoustic instruments. An comparison with available electronic drum pads shows that the designed drum pad produces more realistic sound. An approach for generating dynamic sound trajectories using signal processing techniques based on drumhead vibrations is also introduced. An evaluation of the effectiveness of the developed methods in creating realistic acoustic sound produced by the ground, and the potential future directions for research in this area is given. An idea for future research in this area is to design an artificial surface that produces sound produced by the ground, and the use of geosynthetic materials to create an artificial ground surface that produces sound produced by the ground is also explored. An application of the developed methods to create an artificial ground surface that produces sound produced by the ground for architectural and acoustic design purposes is also investigated. An analysis of the potential future research in this area reveals that the development of an artificial ground surface that produces sound produced by the ground could lead to the creation of immersive soundscapes and artificial environments that produce sound produced by the ground. To assess its superconducting properties, we utilized first-principles calculations in combination with density functional theory. These predictions indicate that the hydrogen boride monolayer is likely not a good superconductor, due to poor electron-phiton interactions stemming from rigid and semi-rigid chemical bonds. In contrast, hydrogen bonds significantly contribute to phonon frequencies. Additional simulations revealed that when subjected to strain, the phase stability of Cmmm begins to degrade at both compressive and tensile forces, eventually giving way to P21c. Furthermore, we discovered that the remaining hydrogen and boron atoms readjust their positions near the strained zone, featuring substantial atomic displacement in the strained sample. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, the study showcases a pioneering application of the influence-based clustering method in the analysis of the US Airline passenger fluctuations. The proposed approach is linked to an online open-source library for clustering dynamic systems called DynaComp. This resource includes a comprehensive suite of tools and algorithms designed to facilitate the analysis of dynamic data, including applications to power, genetics, finance, and atmospheric science. The DynaComp library can be accessed at https://github.com/aerogramme/dynacomp. Currently, support is provided for clustering of single-phase time-series data, with forthcoming enhancements set to include support for multiphase data. The DynaComp tool is poised to revolutionize the cluster analysis of dynamic systems by providing a versatile, user-friendly platform for data-driven discovery. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different interpretations of its foundational concepts. Many accounts compare Leibniz's ideas to Weierstrass's rigorous system, but this study explores alternative perspectives. We examine how Leibniz's methods relate to three logics: real closed fields with ordered valuations, metrical spaces with a fixed metric, and smooth manifolds with a fixed smooth structure. Our analysis reveals that Leibniz's procedures can be consistently applied within any of these frameworks, but the inherent assumptions of each context vary significantly. Ultimately, this diversity of interpretations underscores the complexity of Leibniz's calculus and serves as a reminder that there is no single definitive way to understand his philosophical science. We also identify critical gaps in current research on Leibniz's calculus and encourage further development of a comprehensive and defensible account of Leibniz's philosophical science. Such a framework could provide a foundation for research into the historical Leibniz and offer a paradigm for nonstandard analysis. We discuss the potential of this discipline to bridge the gaps between mathematics and philosophy, as well as between different historical periods and cultural backgrounds. Finally, we suggest exploring the relationship between Leibniz's calculus and other mathematical sciences, such as algebra and projective geometry, which may hold additional insights and surprises. We envision a future where leibnizian calculus serves as a unifying thread, connecting the intellectual endeavors of Europe during the Scientific Revolution with the developments of the 20th and 21st centuries. In this vision, leibnizian calculus emerges as a unique and innovative achievement, characterized by its integration of philosophical and mathematical ideas. We hope that leibnizian calculus can continue to inspire and facilitate research into its rich and complex history. Additionally, we believe that leibnizian calculus can serve as a rotating lens, allowing us to examine specific aspects of leibnizian calculus while drawing general conclusions about the broader scientific revolution. We see this methodology as a form of 'perspectival analysis', where a particular theoretical framework is used to gain new perspectives on established accounts. We anticipate that this approach will not only shed new light on historical and foundational issues but also on the methodological and conceptual debates within the philosophy and mathematics of the 21st century. We envision 'perspectival analysis' as a powerful tool for exploring the deep connections between science and philosophy that emerged during the scientific revolution and continue to evolve to this day. Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the union of $\{e_1, e_2,...\}$ must be linearly independent within the operator's domain. In this study, we obtain a broader version of their finding. Firstly, if $R(T)$, the operator T's range, is a closed subspace of a normed space, we demonstrate that $R(T)$ can only be contained in a finite-dimensional space if $T(e_n) = e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers. Secondly, if $T(e_n) = e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers and $T^{-1}$, the inverse of T, exists, we show that the sequence $\{e_1, e_2,...\}$ is infinite in number. Thirdly, if $T(e_n) = e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers and both $T$ and $T^{-1}$ exist, we prove that T is a one-to-one correspondence, whose inverse is its own inverse. Lastly, if $T(e_n) = e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers and the sequence $\{e_1, e_2,...\}$ is linearly independent, we demonstrate that the induced operator $T^k$ for any positive integer k is also one-to-one and has an inverse, specifically a polynomial operator, for each natural number k. Finally, if $T(e_n) = e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers and the induced operator $T^k$ for any positive integer k is one-to-one and has an inverse, we prove that the sequence $\{e_1, e_2,...\}$ must be linearly independent. One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches, such as combining methods and incorporating external data, have been tried with varying degrees of success. A proposed system mitigates the variability in recommender system ratings by integrating a content-based method that utilizes document vector representations. It does this by weighing user and item similarity equally, thus eliminating bias towards one group over the other. Additionally, using word embeddings in this context offers several benefits, primarily the ability to model syllable and word-level semantic variations. Experimental findings using two diverse datasets, namely Yelp and MovieLens-100K, demonstrate that the proposed system significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy. For instance, using the Yelp dataset, a notable improvement of approximately 5% was observed over the best performing baseline technique. It has also been observed that deep learning-based methods are particularly effective in modeling data variability. Further investigation into these deep models highlights the potential for further improvement, particularly through the incorporation of interaction-based profiles and multi-task training. Building on these insights, two enhanced models were designed and tested, the outcomes of which indicate a 3.3% and 2.7% improvement over the baseline in terms of accuracy, respectively. Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an even number of unitarily invariant ensembles with eigenvalue interactions. The central technical tool employed here is an extension of the Dyson Brownian motion, enabling the control of spectral trajectories at an $O(N^{-2})$ precision level for a period of $N^2$ units of time. The proof draws from the methods in [8] and [10]. The key challenge lies in the divergence of typical and extreme spectral trajectories. Consequently, we devise novel methods for deriving spectral trajectory density evolutions. These new methods facilitate the derivation of asymptotic zero density and unitary invariant distribution of the spectral Green function. The essential idea is to establish that the spectral Green function is asymptotically free from its third derivative, which is made possible by the control of spectral trajectories. This line of thinking is also expected to influence the analysis of other unitarily invariant spectral models. Furthermore, we derive a new asymptotic zero density for the eigenvalue difference of a GUE and show that the additive rank-one perturbation phase transitions in even and odd parity cases can be characterized through the analysis of rootless Faddee-Vishik perturbations. The derivation involves an intricate interplay between the determinant of the parabolic operator and the asymptotic properties at its edges. The key technical innovation here is the creation of a new family of model-specific boundary condition method. This approach is a further development of the modified boundary value problem method initially suggested in [41]. The discussion is accompanied by a list of open problems. This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. This, known as'recognition time', is particularly explored for automata. Our experiments reveal that the integration of recognition time and verifications of whether specifications are met, known as 'vacuity checking', can speed up monitoring in situations with excessive system complexity and large state spaces. Our approach is also adaptable to systems with unpredictable execution times and provides monitoring solutions with varying levels of timing precision, ultimately providing a best-known-efficient-online algorithm for this problem. This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper follows up on [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17] by refining those results in two key ways: introducing a new evaluation bound with reduced dependence on system parameters, and incorporating an early termination mechanism to prevent unnecessary computations arising from overestimating the system parameters or the error bound, both of which were concepts introduced in [Cabay, Proc. SYMSAC'71]. The resulting algorithm is then benchmarked against existing methods, with our modifications performing better in specific scenarios. In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons within the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven two-qubit gate operation, preserving the cavity's odd or even photon state. Additionally, we observe the emergence of multiparticle bundles, characterized by periods of no particle exchange, followed by the simultaneous emission of multiple photons. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model facilitates the production of parity-protected photon bundle emissions in cavity QED systems. This provides a new pathway for exploring complex many-body physics in quantum circuits. Furthermore, we propose an experimentally feasible scenario to demonstrate parity-symmetry-protected photon bundle emission using a single logical qubit within a stripline cavity. The production of even photon bundles can be observed through logical measurements, while leaving the cavity's state intact. This represents a significant breakthrough in harnessing symmetry protection to engineer unique states in quantum electronics. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. This model was developed from first principles and was validated against extensive experimental data for six alkali metals. Furthermore, this analysis highlights the significant discrepancies between existing theoretical models and experimental data, thereby indicating the necessity for equations of state that can predict thermodynamic properties with accuracy greater than $\pm 2\%$. Conversely, this newly derived equation of state guarantees accuracy of at least $\pm 0.5\%$ in predicting the ionization degree and thermodynamic properties. Moreover, this analytical equation of state is inherently simple, thereby enabling it to be easily incorporated into complex mathematical models used to study diverse physical phenomena. In this study, the accuracy of this analytical equation of state has been confirmed through direct comparison with numerical solutions of the nonlinear drift-diffusion equations. An experimental verification of this model's accuracy in determining the electron density is also presented. This analysis paves the way for utilizing this analytical equation of state in modeling various physical phenomena, such as plasma etching, plasma deposition, and switches, among others. Additionally, this study provides a methodology for deriving equations of state that can be applied to developing models for diverse physical phenomena. An essential byproduct of this research is a comprehensive set of reference tables for thermodynamic properties of the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals. These tables can be utilized as reference data for a range of applications, including but not limited to, physical scribes, plasma etching, and switches. Specifically, these tables encompass pressure-temperature diagrams, thermodynamic properties, and characteristics, thereby facilitating the creation of analytical equations of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals. An online database containing these tables is available at https://db.sinopse.com. An overview of related theoretical concepts and techniques, such as equations of state, can also be found on this database. Furthermore, this study showcases how the accuracy of analytical equations of state can be confirmed through direct comparison with numerical solutions of nonlinear differential equations. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential. Consequently, the imaginary parts of the propagators, which are crucial for understanding the behavior of electromagnetic form factors, are determined. Lastly, comparisons with existing approaches and potential signs of this phenomenon in heavy-ion collisions or the magnetization of heavy nuclei are discussed. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. Unlike previous approaches, our solution requires neither a central authority nor global data exchange; it only needs the ability to send information between connected nodes. Our analysis shows the estimated size to be within a constant factor of the actual size. Our protocol is based on the concept of a majority vote, composite numbers, and the property of an efficient estimator. Building on the foundations of efficient algorithms and the Estimating-Size problem proposed in a previous study, we present a new perspective on the problem. Additionally, we introduce the concept of an efficient estimator, providing evidence for its existence through the Zero-Certainty algorithm. Our work and previous research on efficient algorithms demonstrate the feasibility of estimating a sparse, complex network's size under conditions of uncertainty. Furthermore, we explore the limitations of our findings, revealing that detecting the majority of malicious nodes may be computationally infeasible if the number of malicious nodes is less than O(n^(1/3)) - where n represents the network size. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with a crude approximation, instead using a multi-grid method to swiftly resolve the remaining conformal and trace-free parts. This technique boasts significant computational efficiencies, reducing runtime by roughly a third when compared to standard methods. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by comparing it to standard solutions using various test cases, including spherical and cylindrical setups with diverse matter configurations. The resulting conformal and metric variables produced by our method are comparable in precision to those from standard solutions. Furthermore, we find that residual errors from approximating the Hamiltonian constraint have a minimal impact on the gravitational radiation emitted in our numerical relativity simulations. Our findings confirm that this novel approach is suitable for a broad range of numerical relativity applications. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on simplified atmospheric models which haven't been tested for their accuracy. Our research involved testing these models using on-spectrum measurements of alpha Centauri, effectively creating detailed maps of atmospheric dispersion at specific angles and wavelengths. A comparison with the models revealed significant discrepancies between observed and predicted values, highlighting the need for more precise models in the near-infrared part of the spectrum. We've also developed a new approach to characterize the distortion using least squares fittings, taking into consideration the spectral energy distribution and dispersion patterns. This new method allows for a more precise creation of atmospheric models, also facilitating the comparison between different models. We've made these data and analysis tools available for public use. We hope that our research will contribute to enhancing the design and efficiency of ADCs, ultimately improving our astronomical observations in the near-infrared spectrum. A new generation of ADCs, designed according to our findings, has the potential to increase our observational limit down to at least 1600 nm. We are now working on implementing these results to address the remaining challenges in the near-infrared spectrum, specifically to better understand the distortion around the H-alpha line. We are also planning to extend our research to reflect the changing properties of Earth's atmosphere with varying altitude and air pressure. This goal is in line with our ultimate objective - to make deep sky observations possible in the near-infrared spectrum, specifically down to a wavelength of 1600 nm. We are aiming to achieve this by using our on-spectrum measurements to create a precise digital map of the distortion at different wavelengths and altitudes. This digital map can be used to inform the design of a new type of ADC that can correct dispersion not just by angle of arrival but also by altitude, effectively enabling more efficient and less expensive telescopes to make deeper observations into the near-infrared spectrum. We are also exploring an alternative solution, using our on-spectrum measurements to develop an algorithm that effectively accounts for the distortion at different wavelengths, allowing this development to be implemented in an ADC based on a Spatial Phase Shifter. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively. Several numerical tests confirm that BPC's solution is uniquely defined as a finite linear combination of Dirac masses in many situations. The weights of these Dirac masses are determined through a quadratic program. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models. Our results indicate that the mixed approach outperforms the projection-based method in both scenarios. Moreover, our studies show that the most efficient scheme depends on the type of simulation being performed. For rotating shallow-water models, the total computational time of the mixed approach rivals a straightforward approach where the transported field is simply advected without needing to solve a differential equation. In contrast, the projected approach fares better in direct numerical simulations. Ultimately, our goal is to conduct direct numerical simulations in three-dimensional settings, but we anticipate that the same hierarchical approach will offer similar benefits for transporting vector-valued fields in higher-dimensional environments. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The time complexity is reduced by a factor of O(m/n) and memory usage by a factor of O(m), where m represents the total number of parameters in the network. The method can be applied to a wide range of deep learning models including CNNs and RNNs, demonstrating high potential for practical use. Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results, NBcoded shows exceptional performance in training time and disk usage efficiency while only slightly underperforming state-of-the-art classifiers, such as Multilayer Perceptron and Random Forest, with a relatively minor reduction of 2% in accuracy and F1-score. The promising outcomes and exceptional resource efficiency indicate that NBcoded can effectively operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that NBcoded can efficiently tackle high-dimensional and imbalanced data, which presents a potential solution for detecting complex cyber attacks. The research outcomes, including the code and trained models, are publicly available at https://github.com/JDAB_UM/nbcoded. Future work will focus on enhancing the data encoding stage to further decrease resource requirements and exploring the benefits of combining Naive Bayes and other machine learning algorithms. Additionally, the study suggests that NBcoded could be an effective tool for detecting cyber attacks on low-resource devices and industrial settings. In the future, it is intended that NBcoded will be tested on low-resource devices, such as Raspberry Pi and Windows 10 IoT, to validate its potential in these applications. Moreover, a future direction with NBcoded involves training the system with Detonating Malware, a unique dataset containing malicious executables, which would enable NBcoded to distinguish between malware and legitimate software with an accuracy of up to 99%. This would make NBcoded an advanced malware classifier, particularly on low-resource devices. Lastly, it is anticipated that NBcoded will be expanded into a detection system for various types of network attacks. With these future developments, NBcoded is expected to become a versatile tool for cyber defense

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties. Additionally, it's speculated that these bar and spiral arm features may be a common occurrence in edge-on spiral galaxies due to the influence of a central bar. Further study is needed to confirm whether this phenomenon is ubiquitous among this class of galaxies. Images constructed from 21-cm data reveal that these spiral arms are surrounded by numerous cloud complexes, which it's hypothesized may be the precursor to new spiral arm material as well as gas being fed to the center of the Galaxy through winding onto the bar. This research also explores other possible scenarios for the origin and behavior of these spiral arms. It's also found that these spiral arms are home to a high concentration of young stellar clusters, which is thought to be a result of the rapid formation of massive star-forming regions within these arms. These young clusters can be identified through broad-band near-infrared data as features exhibiting distinct excess in this wavelength. Furthermore, it's observed that these young clusters are primarily composed of early B-type stars, which is consistent with the rapid transformation of gas into these stars within these regions. These young clusters are distributed in a way that suggests they may be indicative of a high level of recent star formation activity along the entire Galactic plane, which could be a result of the widespread presence of spiral arms. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show enhanced yields. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced at the PHENIX's forward vertex. This data contradicts models accounting for jet quenching and energy redistribution, while aligning with theories proposing the creation of photons from heavy quark decay and medium-induced photon production. A data-driven extractions indicate the existence of photon losses, exceeding 10% of the generated photons in Au$+$Au, with up to 20% at the forward vertex. These results suggest that the created photon flux could potentially serve as a reliable medium thermometer, yielding a high temperature of approximately 320 M$_{T}$/c per hadron, with the possibility of multiple cooling stages along the jet trajectory. Additionally, these findings imply an effective jet path length of approximately 10 fm. Moreover, these results indicate a sudden jet medium interaction within the first 1-2 fm and a potential role of photon-induced interactions in hadron production. Furthermore, these data illustrate the connection between direct photon measurements and heavy quark production, while the hadron production in Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions shows substantial correlation with the photon spectrum in these regimes. Finally, these results reveal that jet medium interactions can be effectively probed not only at central vertices but also at forward angles, offering new avenues for research and development. Hence, these data underscore the significance of the PHENIX's new Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collision runs at 200 GeV, along with the forthcoming data at 100 GeV, as well as the proposed electron ionizer to augment hadron detection at the forward vertex. Therefore, these data empower the PHENIX to serve as a dependable jet probe in heavy ion and nuclear physics for the forthcoming fiscal year. In conclusion, these results reveal new insights into jet medium interactions, while highlighting future research opportunities
