A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between running models efficiently and ensuring they predict accurately in new data sets. Some optimization techniques can uncover features that not only facilitate fast convergence but also lead to robust prediction performance across a range of scenarios. 

We categorize the optimization-generalization gap in deep networks from the most challenging to the least demanding and provide straightforward, rich feature-based solutions for each case. Additionally, we extend our findings to model selection and apply these methods to the convex optimization context. 

Our proposed features serve two purposes: they resolve the optimization-generalization conflict and also act as effective features for task prediction. Importantly, these features do so without increasing the number of parameters in the model. 

To validate our approach, we conducted thorough experiments that demonstrate the superiority of our method over other state-of-the-art techniques in maintaining convergence speed and generalization performance. 

Our research is motivated by a desire to address the optimization-generalization dilemma through rich feature learning and we hope this work will pave the way for future innovations in this area.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, one driven by the usual Gaussian noise and the other by a deterministic shift with noisy observations. We refer to this combination as the "deterministic-shift extended Cox-Ingersoll-Road" (DCIR) model. Under the assumption that the two processes share the same long-term mean, we prove that the drift parameter of the shifted process can be estimated through the Port- Walsh formula using the difference in observed rates. Our theoretical findings are then empirically verified in a simulation test. In practice, we employ the Durbin and Koopman approximations to analyze the characteristics of the DRIC model. These approximations apply to the "shifted Cox-Ingersoll-Road" (DCIR) process. As a result, the DRIC model offers an attractive mathematical representation and provides suitable estimations for the model's parameters. Furthermore, the DRIC model exhibits satisfactory accuracy in a simulation test. We also conduct an additional investigation to analyze the "shifted Cox-Ingersoll-Road" (DCIR) process. Our study demonstrates that the DRIC model is capable of generating negative interest rate observations with high probability. Additionally, we use the DRIC model to examine the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on bond market prices. Our analysis shows that the DRIC model was able to correctly detect the pandemic-induced decline in interest rates. We also utilize the DRIC model to explore the link between the Cox-Ingersoll-Road model's parameters and the yield curve. Our study suggests that the DRIC model's parameters are highly correlated with the yield curve. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix.  In contrast to existing methods, this approach has been shown to yield asymptotically equivalent results to the conventional methods.  Through simulations, the new estimators have been found to outperform existing ones when statistical power is considered.  Ultimately, the benefits of these new estimators were demonstrated through an analysis of treatment outcomes for depression using combined data from 27 studies based on the same research center.  The findings indicate a size reduction of up to 30% in Type 1 errors and a size increase of up to 30% in tests for moderating variables when using the proposed estimators.  In addition to the novel estimators, both the conventional and new robust estimators, as well as naive estimators that disregard dependence, have been considered. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds agreed well with an independent, flux-based prediction. We propose a constructive approach to continuous logic, adapted from the well-known topological logic, for studying continuous models of universal algebra with topological considerations. Our primary objective is to define a suitable topology on the set of universal models, enabling the use of real-valued functions and limits in a logical framework. This involves selecting specific families of functions with desirable properties and demonstrating the consistency of our logic with continuous reasoning. To achieve this, we develop an ordered hyperstructure, resembling a constructive topological category, with an internal logic that can handle both continuous and infinitesimal quantities. Moreover, we define a hyperstructure for subalgebras of universal models, with a natural topology making it a constructive topological category. This allows us to apply a generalised version of the Stone-type compactness theorem for separable metric structures. Finally, we outline how our approach could be applied to continuous first-order logic.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE. Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%, obtained after summing the polarization vectors from a large region, under the assumption that all emission originates from the same location. Additionally, we note a relatively high polarization level of $3.1 \pm 1.3$% within a region centered around the X-ray emission peak by incorporating off-axis observations. These results indicate the presence of an inner core with dense material, possibly created by the initial explosion explosion and a larger structure formed by the interaction between the supernova's forward blast wave and surrounding material. Our model predictions indicate that the larger structure should dominate the X-ray emission within the 3-6 keV range at a distance of $\ge 5$ arcseconds from the supernova's center. However, the features of the inner core, characterized by a radius of approximately 0.5 centimeters and an overall mass of $\sim 1.7 \times 10^{-4}$ solar masses, may also contribute to the observed polarization through its dense material. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping. This led us to suggest that U galaxies might be an early stage of jellyfish galaxies, resulting from similar gravitational interactions. Our model indicates that a U galaxy could evolve into a jellyfish galaxy within 500 million years. Additionally, we found that U galaxies can only be explained by a mass disturbance affecting the outer parts of the galaxy, rather than alternative theories. Our findings provide new insights into the unique warped galaxy phenomenon. Further observations of U galaxies at different wavelengths are needed to determine their specific origins. Based on their blue colors, these galaxies could serve as efficient star-forming probes to explore the galaxy's distant outskirts. Our research also highlights the potential of U galaxies to act as 'cosmic lighthouses,' illuminating the galaxy's warped regions and illuminating the galaxy's warped edges. Further work is needed to clarify the role of ram-pressure stripping in the formation of U galaxies. Our research also indicates that U galaxies could be more susceptible to the galaxy-proton scattering proposed in some alternative gravity theories. Furthermore, U galaxies could provide a unique test to distinguish between various alternative gravity theories. Our research also highlights the unique role that warped galaxies can play in fundamental physics research. To better understand U galaxies, we recommend observing their counterparts in groups and clusters, focusing on their star formation rates using MaDCaM and studying their sub-kpc resolution using CANNON. Furthermore, the Chern number is found to take on half-integer values when the boundary fermions possess a Zak phase of $\pi$. Furthermore, the Witten effect can be utilized to measure the Chern number and three-dimensional topological insulator properties using a single quantum dot or quantum black hole. Our work provides a framework for categorizing time-reversal-symmetric nonlinear responses, with applications including magnetoelectric, thermal, and viscous properties. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Our framework is influenced by the techniques developed for Kleene algebras and PCTL, as described in (Cimatti et al., 2003). The study reveals that both operational and denotational semantics are valid methods for assigning semantic meanings to stochastic lambda calculus expressions. Moreover, we outline the steps necessary to extend this approach to recursive equations. To accomplish this, we draw on concepts such as universal domains, least and greatest fixed points, and Kleene algebra with tests. Ultimately, this research contributes to the goal of developing a semantic framework that can be used for program verification. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This research investigates whether conclusions drawn from mining such discussions can be reliably applied across different mining techniques and project teams. A set of design mining conversations with annotated topics and design categories were first used to train and assess the consistency of four underlying models. Conclusions from design mining sessions with distinct categories were then analyzed and compared across the four models, which showed substantial agreement in their outcomes with a high degree of consistency in their conclusions. This consistency was further confirmed through expert reviews of three software development projects, which found that the four models produced similar outcomes and supported the effectiveness of design mining in accurately capturing the discussion's impact on software design. This led to new guidelines for design mining practitioners, which were also applied to evaluate the effectiveness of design mining in three real-world projects, which showed a significant, positive correlation. This enabled the extension of design mining's existing evaluation metrics to include conclusion stability, which was found to be positively correlated with other metrics, leading to new insights and recommendations for design mining practitioners. In conclusion, this research demonstrates the reliability of design mining and provides new insights and recommendations for its evaluation, while also contributing to the body of knowledge in design mining. The paper also presents a new organization for design mining conversations, referred to as DiscMina, which was used to train and assess the consistency of the four models. The paper also showcases its development of a system for automatically analyzing design mining conversations, referred to as DiscMina Analyzer. This system was used to analyze discussions from three software development projects and found to have a significant, positive correlation with other metrics. This enabled the validation of design mining's conclusions through expert reviews, which further confirmed the effectiveness of design mining in accurately capturing the discussion's impact on software design. This research has three main contributions: (1) demonstrating the reliability of design mining, while also training and assessing the consistency of the four models; (2) providing new insights and recommendations for design mining practitioners through the analysis of discussion categories in three software development projects; (3) contributing to the body of knowledge in design mining through the development of a new organization for design mining conversations, referred to as DiscMina. This research can be applied to other domains beyond design mining. Our team employed photonic technology to address issues of spectral resolution, photonic spacing, and cross-talk that compromise the effectiveness of code-based spectroscopy. By utilizing a phased array architecture, we enhanced the spectral resolution to a level determined by the spacing between photonic elements, rather than the elements themselves. To minimize cross-talk, we utilized an amplification loop to increase the power of selected elements. Our design leveraged a 400-element photonic filter, yielding a spectral resolution of 7.2 Angstroms and a photonic spacing of 10 Angstroms. This design enables the collection of multiple spectra within a single image, paving the way for more efficient and less expensive astronomical telescopes. Specifically, we applied our design to a search for biosignatures in the transit spectra of M-dwarf planets and an analysis of star-forming regions in nearby galaxies. With its capacity to process vast amounts of data, our technology could help enable the global search for life beyond Earth. Additionally, its compact and monolithic design makes it suitable for a wide range of applications beyond photometry and spectroscopy, such as laser-based communications and data storage systems. These applications could provide significant returns in areas like space research, astronomy, medicine, and national security. To showcase the potential of this technology, we conducted a small-scale astronomical observation, demonstrating its capability to detect biosignatures in the transit spectra of M-dwarf planets and providing a precedent for its use in searching for life beyond Earth. To facilitate the adoption of this technology, we are establishing the Astrophotonic Research and Development Facility to serve the needs of the astronomical community and related fields, meeting the growing demand for advancements in rapid, high-resolution, and cross-talk insensitive spectroscopy. This resource will be open for research and development to a broad audience, with the goal of leveraging photonic technology to drive breakthroughs in spectroscopy. In return, we will collect and disseminate the knowledge generated from these research and development efforts, showcasing the numerous applications and benefits of astrophotonic technology. \section{Introduction}

Recent advancements in machine learning have led to increased interest in using it to model relationships between drugs and their effects. This interest stems from the potential for machine learning to help tackle various challenges in pharmacology, such as predicting medication interactions, optimizing combination therapies, and addressing polypharmacy side effects. In this context, drugs are viewed as entities with established characteristics, and their interactions are described through their mutual relationship. This relationship is often represented as a pair of input variables $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B})$, and their interaction can be predicted based on their combined characteristics. This prediction is the primary outcome of a relational machine learning model.

Drug interaction prediction is a critical application with practical implications. For instance, when prescribing multiple medications, doctors need to be aware of the medication's interactions with existing drugs prescribed to the patient. This process helps in avoiding polypharmacy side effects and is an essential aspect of clinical practice. Furthermore, when developing new combination therapies, it is crucial to assess the interactions between drugs and their potential to produce desired effects. To achieve this, researchers use various machine learning models to model drug interactions and their effects. These applications demonstrate the scope of using relational machine learning models to tackle various challenges in pharmacology.

This paper offers a comprehensive overview of using relational machine learning models to tackle pharmacological issues. It begins by offering a theoretical framework, then evaluates existing models, and discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Additionally, it highlights the potential future research directions in this field. This overview is part of a collection of papers examining the field of relational machine learning from both theoretical and practical perspectives.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior as a guide.  While imitation learning typically relies on expert demonstrations within the same action and state space as the agents' environment, real-world applications frequently present challenges due to differences between these spaces.  In this research, we aim to mitigate this issue by investigating an algorithm that can learn from expert demonstrations in a disparate domain.  Our approach leverages a novelty measure derived from counterfactual reasoning to differentiate between relevant and irrelevant actions for the agents.  We evaluate this learning algorithm across three domains, including a simulated robot task and a self-driving car scenario, and observe its capability to generalize imitation learning across boundaries.  Notably, our results indicate that our approach surpasses comparison groups that were trained solely within their respective domains. We concentrate on how the magnetic field generated by differential rotation within a collapsing gas cloud influences disk fragmentation, with the aim of settling the above-mentioned uncertainty. We employed a multi-dimensional ideal magnetohydrodynamics simulation to analyze a collapsing cloud of primordial gas, and found that the magnetic field becomes highly amplified due to differential rotation in the protostellar disk at a radius of less than 1 astronomical unit. The resulting magnetic field strength in the mid-plane of the disk is in the range of tens of milligauss. The amplification of the magnetic field ultimately leads to the elimination of fragmentation in the disk, as the magnetic pressure nearly equals the thermal pressure at a distance of about 10 astronomical units from the protostar. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment as part of probation leads to a reduction in future criminal behavior.  However, the study did not account for factors beyond an offender's initial sentence or whether they received the treatment, such as the quality of the treatment or its duration, which could impact an offender's chances of recidivism.  As a result, the data suggests that court-ordered mental health treatment is associated with lower recidivism rates, but does not confirm that such treatment is the direct cause of these lower rates.  More research is needed to confirm the relationship between mental health treatment and lower recidivism rates.  Additionally, while the data suggests that court-ordered mental health treatment lowers odds of recidivism, it also suggests that such treatment may not address underlying factors that lead individuals to engage in criminal behavior.  As such, it is not a total solution to reducing crime, particularly in cases where offenders may not receive the treatment as part of their sentence. This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. At its core lies the comparison of sequential data segments. The process involves first mapping these segments to suitable Hidden Markov Models via the Baum-Welch algorithm, followed by a simplification of the probability distributions associated with these models. The resulting representation is then analyzed through a clustering method or an outlier detection tool to pinpoint anomalies. Notably, the use of Hidden Markov Models as representatives allows for the identification of patterns even when the time series is partially missing. Furthermore, the employment of probability distributions instead of static representations enhances the detection of irregular patterns. The development of this method, which is inspired by anomaly detection in particle detector data, is illustrated using synthetic series containing various types of anomalies. The presented approach is then evaluated in its ability to detect anomalies in jet data from proton-proton collisions at the LHC. The results of this evaluation indicate that the method is capable of identifying atypical patterns but also cautions against misinterpretation of noise as signals due to the limited understanding of the underlying physical processes. In cases where the time series is extremely short, the method may fail to identify patterns even though Hidden Markov Models can still be determined. The ability of the GLA method to identify anomalies is found to be directly proportional to the length and the information contained within the series. We've found this approach to be both simple and cost-effective in boosting the performance of pre-optimized Transformer and Conformer models. Specifically, enhancements of up to 2.83 WER and 6.87 WER are seen in the LibriSpeech-960h test sets, and even higher when models are jointly trained on tasks, reaching 4.91 WER improvements. Furthermore, improvements of 0.84 and 2.18 were observed in translation BLEU scores for the IWSLT2017 EN-RO and EN-DE datasets. We've made our code and pre-trained models available. Additionally, a figure has been added to illustrate the possible range of new data creation strategies. We suggest exploring these options to identify the most effective methods. We've found no reduction in model performance when models are trained on 1000x more data, achieved through augmentation. This property enables the evaluation of hypotheses on the same data, and sheds light on the underlying dynamics of learning. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information. To tackle this challenge, the paper utilizes a dependence measurement metric drawn from information theory. Two primary privacy breach assessment approaches are presented. First, the total privacy breach is analyzed when the adversary has access to individual record dependencies. Second, the total privacy breach is examined when the adversary has access to overall record interdependence. When the adversary has access to individual record dependencies, the total privacy breach is measured as the maximum sum of record probabilities multiplied by the maximum entropy of other records. On the other hand, when the adversary has access to overall record interdependence, the total privacy breach is measured as the maximum entropy of other records multiplied by their probability sum. To further investigate total privacy breaches, two concrete datasets are employed - a synthetic dataset and a real dataset created from actual data. Two practical methods known as Gaussian mechanism and exponential mechanism are utilized to maintain one-sided differential privacy in the datasets. When examining the total privacy breach in the case where the adversary has access to individual record dependencies, the findings reveal that record probabilities significantly affect total privacy breach. Furthermore, total privacy breach is found to be an improving function of record probability sum. When examining the total privacy breach in the case where the adversary has access to overall record interdependence, the findings reveal that record probabilities significantly affect total privacy breach. Furthermore, total privacy breach is found to be an improving function of record entropy. Building upon these observations, several recommendations are given to maintain one-sided differential privacy while ensuring good data utility in the presence of inter-record dependencies. The recommendations vary based on the type of mechanism used (Gaussian or exponential). For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplifies the complexity of outfit aesthetics. To better capture and analyze outfit visual compatibility, this research introduces the concept of partial mismatching, where certain items may still incongruously fit with others. To effectively detect both full mismatching and partial mismatching, this paper proposes the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) model. It achieves this through a two-stage process involving: first, utilizing a diverse fashion image dataset to pre-train a specialized Transformer that learns to extract outfit-specific visual features, while also leveraging contrastive learning to exploit implicit relationships among these features. Next, integrating a Transformer-based encoder with a contrastive learning module, VICTOR represents each garment item as a set of feature vectors. These are then compared to determine compatibility. Through testing on two benchmark datasets, the proposed VICTOR model has been shown to outperform competing approaches. Its associated code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/stevenliuyz/VICTOR. Experimental results demonstrate that the model produces higher quality output results compared to conventional'match' or'mismatch' classification models. For example, under a'same-class' similarity criterion, the proposed model correctly identifies compatible outfits 68.4% of the time, surpassing the 65.1% accuracy achieved by a leading classifier. Moreover, when applying a more stringent'same-brand' criterion, the proposed model accurately classifies outfits 60.5% of the time, exceeding the 57.5% accuracy achieved by a leading classifier. Additionally, the proposed model successfully generates visually appealing outfit combinations by selectively removing items from existing outfits, demonstrating its ability to capture partial mismatching. By advancing the state-of-the-art in visual compatibility detection, this research has potential real-world applications, such as digital fashion retail recommendations, where outfit combinations could be suggested by filtering out incompatible items. Similarly, in the area of fashion design, the proposed model could aid in creating visually appealing outfits by removing inaccessible items. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of effective static models by modifying their input. SpliMe addresses issues related to hyperparameters, feature engineering, and the requirement for substantial training data, and is capable of generating positive samples without the need for additional resources. Our experiments indicate that SpliMe outperforms existing temporal KGE methods, and demonstrates the potential for static models to excel in the treatment of temporal contexts. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/dsaborowski/SpliMe.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, as evidenced by the finite-time (FT) model's findings. The FT model builds upon previous studies utilizing the logistic, SIR, and SEIR models, incorporating a time-dependent rate for countermeasure implementation and deriving equations for both R and Q metrics. Ultimately, the FT model demonstrates that medium-level intervention leads to maximal outcomes in both health and economics, as it optimizes the harmonic mean of these two factors, thereby refuting the notion that high-level intervention is necessary for effective pandemic control. Additionally, the research presents an economic analysis justifying the use of countermeasures during the initial stages of a pandemic, as opposed to the commonly applied lag-time model (LT) approach, which prioritizes medical considerations over economic implications. The appropriate debugging approach is highly dependent on the debugging question being addressed. For example, if the focus is on how data subsets contribute to inaccuracies in a trained model, then using stochastic sampling for validation is not sufficient. A more effective approach involves using tools that can analyze and evaluate the predictive performance of models on subsets of the training data. It is worth noting that the prices of cryptocurrency indexes, such as the Bloomberg Crypto Index, also exhibited minimal daily fluctuations. In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This research aims to address this gap by identifying incidents related to ESS through data-driven approaches. Firstly, we apply principal component regression to filter out non-anomalous readings from device data and remove noise. Subsequently, we utilize a distance-based method to identify data points deviating significantly from the norm. Ultimately, a data-driven anomaly detection method grounded in the multivariate altered scaling (MAS) approach is proposed to support operations and maintenance personnel in effectively locating and resolving incidents within distribution networks quickly and efficiently. Our findings reveal that the proposed method excels over existing techniques in accurately pinpointing ESS anomalies. Furthermore, through a case study, we demonstrate the continuous capabilities of the proposed solution in detecting incidents through real-time monitoring. Our analysis shows that the proposed solution yields superior performance compared to alternative methods. Specifically, our approach achieved an accuracy rate of 97.5%, surpassed the performance of the support vector machine (SVM) technique by a margin of 10%, and successfully detected 88% of ESS anomalies under normal operating conditions. Our discussion also highlights key implications for future research and the inherent reliance of the solution on high-quality training data. Moreover, our work opens up new avenues for exploring the potential of data-driven approaches in detecting incidents related to smart controllers and energy storage systems. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.

Our approach provides a clear geometric interpretation of the connection between defects, surface handles, and topological invariants. Furthermore, we reveal the scalability of topological insulators, demonstrating that the geometric properties of the defect and surface regions remain unchanged under size variations. Lastly, as a testament to the versatility of our approach, we apply it to the study of chiral topological insulators. Overall, our method offers a distinct perspective on the geometric properties of topological insulators and their defects. With further development, this approach has the potential to greatly enhance understanding and discovery in the field of topological insulators. It could also lead to breakthroughs in describing other geometric properties of systems, such as topological Kondo insulators, where the existing numerical methods fall short of providing a clear geometric interpretation. By adapting the methods of geometry to describe topological insulators, we may uncover new tools for analyzing these systems. Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces. We apply these results to demonstrate the finiteness of sets of non-constant morphisms from varieties with specific properties to other varieties, including those with ample line bundles and hyperbolicity. Our work also extends Igus's results on the finiteness of birational maps between varieties. Furthermore, we investigate the bounds of degrees of non-constant morphisms from varieties to other varieties, ultimately proving a degree-based analogue of Faltings's theorem, with implications involving hyperbolicity and varieties with ample line bundles. Lastly, we explore connections between these new results and the fundamental conjectures concerning algebraic dynamics. To conclude, we examine examples and outstanding questions arising from our research. We also refined the proof of Theorem 5.4 and 6.4 at the request of the referee. A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like movements and adapting to human manipulation strategies. This paper's innovation lies in developing efficient algorithms to compute the manipulability ellipsoids' parallel transport along trajectories and to align these ellipsoids between humans and robots. The research presents a new method based on Information-Consistent Point Matching, taking into account the elliptical shape and anisotropy of the manipulability ellipsoids. The researchers show that by applying this algorithm to tasks such as kitchen tool manipulation, robots can easily adopt the manipulation strategies employed by humans, without needing to learn specific trajectory patterns. The results demonstrate successful adaptation from a humanoid to a PUMA 262 robot, showcased through experimental video. The implemented method is also shown to be scalable, fast, and robust against noise. The research makes available a Python package that includes the developed algorithms and can be accessed via the GitHub repository. The researchers also contributed to the development of a new dataset called KinTool, consisting of kitchen-related objects and available at osf.io/7M3G3. The research was presented at IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots 2021. The manipulability ellipsoids' properties allow robots to easily adopt the manipulation strategies employed by humans, as seen in the generated video. Despite widespread vaccination, a lingering residue of skepticism persists due to the spread of misinformation. Social media platforms, fostering agile information sharing, have become key dissemination channels for misinformation. We introduce an innovative approach, focusing on identifying stances toward vaccine-related misinformation on Twitter. We would later apply this model to detect diverse forms of misinformation on other platforms. To train and evaluate our model, we created a massive dataset consisting of 1.7 million tweets from January to July 2021. Our analysis reveals that approximately 11% of tweets shared COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. We developed and validated unique stances specifically for misinformation discussions, as opposed to the more traditional stances used in existing studies. Our proposed model, combined with pre-trained language and domain-specific models, achieved exceptional performance with a macro F1 score of 96.79 on the validation set and 95.46 on the test set. Our work has several practical implications, such as informing the development of targeted fact-checking campaigns to combat vaccine misinformation. Additionally, our success suggests that pre-trained models can effectively address the complexities of stances toward misinformation by adapting to domain-specific requirements. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of diverse stances in natural language and their potential to elevate performance in classification tasks. Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data that is no longer accurate.  We update the eclipse information for the Algol system, replacing the existing times with new ones.  Our new results are based on a detailed analysis of the light curves from 2016 to 2020.  Furthermore, we suspect that a third unobserved component might exist within the Algol system, causing irregularities in the light curves.  To support this hypothesis, we point out past discoveries of what could be this missing component.  Based on our current understanding, we present predicted eclipse times through 2023.  We note that a thorough examination of the Algol system requires further observation to confirm our suspicions and refine the models.  Therefore, we call for continued monitoring of the Algol system to clarify its properties and understand its dynamics better.  Our new data, including the updated eclipse predictions, is available at http://astro.phys.uw.edu/~vasybayr/.html/algol.  Also, we recommend running the PYALGOL code for the precise analysis of the Algol light curves.  Developed by Peter D. Malek, the PYALGOL code is available at https://github.com/pmalik/algol_code/tree/master.  Finally, we expect that the proposed changes will benefit other experts working with similar systems, as the proposed modifications can improve the eclipse predictions and even detect new components in the observed data.  For instance, the systems AR Pavee and AR Per are good candidates for such updates.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant to solutions in this particular scenario. This new variance is linked to the energy of the solution through a modified energy estimate. Since solutions with negative energy are bounded from below, we can combine these aspects to derive the optimal blow-up criterion. This work is a direct extension of the previous research by the first author to multivariate settings. Moreover, this study has implications that extend beyond solutions in exterior domains to a broader range of settings, such as semilinear equations under the influence of periodic forces and solutions in nearly convex domains. A detailed overview of related research is provided in Section 7. Moreover, this study addresses a question initially posed by Roudenko. Following a suggestion by Ghoul, this study also examines the impact of replacing the Schrödinger equation with the related Hartree equation. A related theory for the latter equation is still understudied. To the best of our knowledge, this property has not been explored in a setting that involves boundless domains and solutions with negative energy. As a result, this paper makes a significant contribution to the existing body of research on the Schrödinger equation and the Hartree equation, particularly in a context that involves boundless domains and solutions with negative energy. Consequently, this paper makes a significant contribution to the existing literature on the Schrödinger equation and the Hartree equation. This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. Our analysis also shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, which in turn affects the device's drain current and variability due to the domain period. We also investigated how the domain wall's soft or hard state transition influences the device's electrical properties and performance. Our findings offer valuable insights for the design and optimization of ferroelectric tunnel transistors. Furthermore, our numerical approach can be adapted for use in computational atomic force microscopy to characterize two-dimensional ferroelectric materials. We established a relationship between the current flow across the ferroelectric tunnel barrier and the domain wall's movement, which enables the calculation of the ferroelectric's relative permittivity. Our study also makes possible the simulation of other bi-layered ferroelectric transistors under distinct domain wall conditions. Our research ultimately contributes to the development of a computational framework that integrates the multi-scale behavior of ferroelectric materials and enables their simulation across a range of length scales, from 10 nm to 1 micrometer. A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination affects it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook Cargo's distinct containerization technology and third-party library dependencies. To address this disparity, this research employs knowledge graph techniques to construct a Cargo ecosystem dependency-vulnerability graph and analyzes vulnerability transmission between dependencies. By exploring Cargo's Ecosystem Architecture and third-party library vulnerabilities, this study reveals the prevalence of vulnerable libraries and their propagation spread. A novel algorithm is developed to identify sequential vulnerability transmission and rank library vulnerabilities by their transmission spread. A vulnerability dissemination prediction model is also proposed to forecast future vulnerabilities and suggest security best practices. Through empirical studies, this research demonstrates that Cargo's security vulnerabilities are diverse in type, and their transmission spread is largely driven by certain ecosystems and vulnerabilities. Specifically, this study reveals that about 15% of libraries are involved in vulnerability transmission, and 4-6 dependencies are sequentially transmitted with propagation spread. Furthermore, this study shows that certain ecosystem versions, such as Graze 2.10 and Swift-5.7, are more prone to vulnerability transmission, and multiple vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-42719 and CVE-2021-42718 significantly contribute to library vulnerability propagation. These findings provide valuable insights for Cargo developers, dependency maintainers, and Ecosystem Architects to prioritize security updates, enhance library vulnerability testing, and refine Cargo's architecture, ultimately improving Cargo's overall security. The proposed knowledge graph framework and algorithm offer theoretical contributions by solving the problem of vulnerability propagation transmission and forecasting future vulnerabilities. The empirical results and findings are publicly available on a dedicated website. The Code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/sstang18/Cargo-Vulnerability propagation and https://sstang18.github.io/Cargo-Vulnerability propagation/.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results apply universally, imposing minimal restrictions on noise conditions. A crucial factor in this study is the authors' and T. Zhang's previously established criteria for irreducibility in stochastic equations with jump noises. This research will likely have significant implications in the fields of dynamical systems and stochastic analysis. To demonstrate the practical utility of these findings, the authors perform an in-depth examination of the long-term statistical behavior of a model representing a chain of coupled geospatially dispersed cells regulating cell growth through cell-cell interactions. This model involves the application of irreducibility to ensure the global stability of the long-term statistical distribution, thereby facilitating the use of the ergodic decomposition. As a result, the authors derive formulas for the rate of convergence of correlations and the growth rate of probabilities based on the spectral properties of the parabolic operator. Additionally, the authors comment on the feasibility of extending these results to more complex systems, such as those involving three-dimensional systems with diverse jump noise patterns. This research has far-reaching implications for understanding the long-term statistical behavior of biological systems, particularly those involving cell interactions and jump noises. The authors acknowledge the influence of E. Serra-Paqua's previous work on this topic. A companion paper by the first author explores the application of these results to a specific model representing a single cell regulating cell growth through self-interactions. This research is an extension of previous studies by C. E. Bréhier, E. Copele, L. Chizmk, and Y. Voisin. Furthermore, the authors acknowledge the unstated but influential work of M. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting Gabor filters that maximize class discrimination across different orientations. This construction method is similar to the idea behind Fisher Vectors, but adapted for use in deep learning models. Our LGFs are composed of multiple sub-filters, each corresponding to a specific orientation, and are trained end-to-end with the other network layers. To efficiently utilize the generated orientation features, we have also developed a simple LGF-based encoding scheme. The effectiveness of our LGFs and OCNs is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on three publicly available datasets, namely the orientation-subject, orientation-object, and NUS-45 dataset. Our results show that OCNs outperform existing state-of-the-art models, with improvements ranging from 3.5% to 13.6%. Furthermore, our LGFs have the potential to be integrated with other deep learning models, such as ResNet and MobileNetV2, to enhance their robustness to orientation changes while maintaining comparable performance in terms of accuracy. Additionally, our LGFs can be used for orientation recognition and image classification purposes. With its capacity to learn less sensitive orientation features, our LGFs model has numerous applications in computer vision. We first employ LGFs to analyze the representation of orientation in CNNs and find that the model successfully learns less sensitive orientation features. We then utilize LGFs to investigate the impact of dataset size on deep learning robustness and find a notable increase in dataset size from 100 to 1000. We have also compared the robustness of different CNN architectures, including ResNet, MobileNetV2, and DenseNet, to orientation changes and found that MobileNetV2 and DenseNet significantly outperform ResNet. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting the problems of GCNs with point clouds, we propose a new efficient GCN architecture. Firstly, to reduce computational costs, we simplify the permutation invariant multliperon. Secondly, to decrease geometric distortion, we introduce a feature fusion design alternative to the original. This new simplification allows the GCN to retain permutation invariance while reducing the parameter load and network depth. We test our efficient GCN across three benchmark datasets and compare it to prior methods, including PCD-Net, SPGN, and SE GN. This comparison highlights the efficiency and efficacy of our new approach. Further details on the code and models can be found on our repository. We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 3000. By using our proprietary, custom-made, stress-relieved glass stress-reducing filters, we'll minimize image slicer aberrations. In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements. Initially, a review of previous THM experiments is provided, followed by an discussion of how these studies compared with existing data and existing computational models. It is noted that previous THM experiments generally aligned with other experimental results but were occasionally inconsistent. Furthermore, it is observed that these experiments frequently underpredicted the $S$-factor values obtained through other means. Building upon the outcomes of Beck {\it et al.}, two new THM measurements are proposed, one at $E_{\rm C}$ = 115 keV and another at $E_{\rm C}$ = 200 keV, with the goal of accurately determining the astrophysical $S$-factor at zero energy ($S_0$) and exploring its energy dependence. It is hoped that these new measurements can be utilized to refine the computational models and their underlying potential energy surface. Additionally, two alternative THM experiments are suggested, one utilizing a higher atomic number for the mirror nucleus, with the aim of minimizing background interference from the other mirror isotope, thereby enabling more precise determinations of astrophysical $S$-factor values. Lastly, a plan is outlined to conduct a series of new, groundbreaking THM experiments at multiple research centers, with the ultimate goal of producing the most accurate $S$-factor results possible and thereby contributing significantly to the understanding of how grains form in the lives of stars. It is anticipated that these results will be available for inclusion in the latest review by Beck {\it et al.} (in preparation)}.

A crucial aspect of thoroughly examining terrestrial planets with the ability to support life involves understanding their internal compositions. This study utilizes a novel technique to derive the internal structures and compositions of M dwarfs, specifically those with planets like Kepler-10 and LHS-1145A. By combining this information, we simulate the potential thermal histories of these planets. Findings indicate that planets with higher metal content are likely to retain more heat in their interiors. This could impact their potential to support life by influencing the probability of magma ocean solidification and the emergence of a crust capable of protecting fragile biologicallife forms. Ultimately, our models' outcomes may guide the design of telescopic missions capable of detecting signs of life and its potential habitats. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework. In contrast to existing methods, our approach uniquely incorporates both Kripke semantics with transitions and modal operators, as well as rich modal languages based on pre-sheaf models. In the follow-up paper, we will apply this framework to study both S5 and other types of modal logics based on topological categories. Specifically, we will concentrate on identifying the types of topological categories that can represent either the entire family of modal logics or specific members within that family. Furthermore, we will investigate whether certain categories with hidden structures can be reduced to those without such modifications. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation and facilitate exploratory analysis, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform integrating COPASI capabilities within a interactive browser client. Built with R using COPASI's Python interface, ShinyCOPASI enables users to easily simulate and analyze models uploaded as SBML or XML files. With a focus on visual analytics and user experience, the interface offers a simple and intuitive way to examine model behavior and dynamics, making it accessible to a broader audience of researchers and students. ShinyCOPASI is now available as a free service at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and runs on modern web browsers supporting Java SE 8.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for a broad set of applications. In order to overcome these limitations, researchers have revised the policy iteration algorithm, substituting the exact linear system solver with an inexact one, specifically GMRES. Through analysis, it has been found that the revised algorithm exhibits a global contraction rate of better than quadratic, thereby making it suitable for a wider range of applications. While maintaining the same theoretical efficiency as policy iteration, the revised algorithm requires significantly fewer operations, thereby reducing computational costs by a factor of at least 10. Additionally, simulations have demonstrated that the revised algorithm often outperforms other iterative algorithms by several orders of magnitude. For example, in a self-driving vehicle application with 200 states and 200 controls, the revised algorithm required just 8 iterations to achieve a desired level of accuracy, whereas existing methods needed between 30 and 60 iterations. Furthermore, it has been found that the most efficient way to approximate the Markov decision process's linear system is through the use of the stochastic algebraic multigrid method. Moreover, it has been discovered that policy iteration, even with an inexact solver, is not capable of solving certain large-scale Markov decision processes, whereas Monte Carlo policy iteration is able to solve these problems, though at a cost of increased computational complexity. In order to overcome these limitations, researchers have developed a combination of the GMRES policy iteration algorithm and the Monte Carlo policy iteration approach, thereby making the revised GMRES policy iteration algorithm both theoretically efficient and capable of solving a broader range of large-scale Markov decision processes. The development of this revised algorithm marks the first known instance in which researchers have combined Monte Carlo policy iteration with linear system approximation techniques. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust measure of model accuracy. Our first learning model utilizes local membership queries (LMQs), where the learner can verify the labels of nearby points to the training sample. We found, however, that LMQs alone are not enough to increase the robustness threshold for conjunctions and its various superclasses, such as decision lists and halfspaces. To address this issue, we developed a new local equivalence query (LEQ) oracle, which allows the learner to confirm whether a model's hypothesis and the target concept agree within a certain range, in relation to a given training sample. We established a crucial finding that, when working with any concept from a specific family of concepts (decision lists), using the new LEQ oracle granted us the ability to significantly boost the robustness threshold. To validate our findings, we ran experiments using real-world datasets, specifically the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, and observed robustness improvements in models trained with the new LEQ oracle, in comparison to models trained without it. Our research suggests that using the new LEQ oracle can significantly increase model robustness to perturbations, while also enhancing accuracy. For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with less than 3 Xe/V were tracked within a cone of 1.0 radii around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to proton-proton collisions were observed, however, no differences were found when comparing most forward and most central events within the detector. Modifications of fragmentation functions for jets above 100 GeV were found to be larger than those of lower-transverse-momentum jets, suggesting that the observed changes are due to the effects of the hot medium on the fragmentation process. Additionally, the variation of these modifications across different parton flavors was investigated. This analysis provides the first evidence of changes to the internal structure of jets resulting from the passage through the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, the data also sheds light on the mechanisms of parton recombination and medium-induced elimination of leading jets. When comparing the variations in fragmentation functions between most forward and most central events, no differences were found, especially when considering the effects of the initial-state parton effects. Also, when comparing the variations in jet substructure with those found in photon-tagged jets, higher variations were found for jets above 100 GeV, which were not seen when examining photon-tagged jets. This data also highlights the difference in changes to the internal structure of jets when composed of different flavors of light quarks and gluons. Finally, the variation in fragmentation functions, especially when examining the charged-particle spectrum, may be an indicator of parton radiative losses in the hot medium, which could be driven by gluon loss. When assuming that only gluons are lost in the hot medium, the variation in fragmentation functions may be seen as a measure of the gluon multiplicity in the hot medium. However, when accounting for recombination, the data can also be fitted by assuming that the changes to the internal structure of jets result from the passage of all partons through the quark-gluon plasma. This research investigates the utilization of lunar and Martian soils as building materials for structures on other planets, focusing on examining how their composition affects their strength when fired at various temperatures. To analyze the thermal behavior of these soils, samples were made from a mixture of Martian and lunar soils mimicking real-life depths, and then subjected to different temperatures in a furnace. The resulting samples displayed a strength of up to 1.9 MPa, surpassing traditional construction materials, while their low density contributed to enhanced strength. To apply these findings to real-world construction on other planets, samples were fired at temperatures found on Martian and lunar surfaces, resulting in significant material loss but retaining their strength due to low porosity. As a result, these extraterrestrial regoliths present a viable building material for structures, and further development could enable sustainable and durable construction of lunar and Martian bases. The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the new theoretical model is supported by a numerical comparison with previous studies. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. For some galaxy types, allowing the star formation history to vary freely results in better $\chi^2$ and less scattering, but this is less important when the history is fixed. Ultimately, we conclude that the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m line serves as a gold-standard indicator of star formation rates that can serve as an additional check for the accuracy of SED-fitting predictions in galaxies observed at this wavelength. However, we note that the predicted relationship between line emission and star formation rates may need to be reconsidered if the model includes physical processes like the thermal emission of supernovae and other high-mass objects. The most efficient way of using observer time in future missions for SED mapping or other bulk star formation rate studies is to prioritize the galaxies that have the narrowest range of predicted line emission-scattered probability distributions. Based on the characteristics of existing samples, we estimate that observing just 10-20 such galaxies at a wavelength of 2.16 $\mu$m could account for the majority of the uncertainty in predicted line emission probabilities. Thus, these galaxies could also be used to improve the Prospector-derived star formation rates in a timely manner. The data and code used in this analysis are publicly available. In the future, we plan to expand upon this study by including data from other spectral lines. Additionally, we aim to utilize the findings presented here to inform future planning for the JWST and other similar space-based telescopes. This involves establishing a natural action of the Weyl group on the set of type II quantum subgroups of $\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1}$. The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field. In contrast, the presented approach shares similarities with the weak solution in the context of an oil spreading model, showcasing its versatility in tackling various types of reactions and diffusion processes. Moreover, a noteworthy application of this solution's structure is its potential in modelling cell movement, exemplified through a simplified case study. Furthermore, the article discusses how existing mathematical and numerical methods fail to accurately capture long-distance, microscopic details in such scenarios. In a bid to overcome this limitation, a novel direction-preserving scheme is devised, aiming to conserve the probability density function's inherent structure even after time has elapsed. In doing so, the article presents numerical evidence demonstrating that the approximate solution's irregularity can, in fact, be maintained when employing this new scheme, whereas other methods may smooth out the probability density function over time. In contrast, the full spectral deferred correction and summation-by-parts algorithms are shown to fail in preserving the probability density function's structure, even when direct time marching is used. In consequence, the approximate solution remains capable of providing insight into the spreading process at its initial stages. Notably, the discussion is centred on time $t=0.0024$ to showcase the new scheme's ability to retain the probability density function's wavy, irregular structure, which is otherwise lost when using other methods. In a notable deviation, as time approaches zero, the new scheme approaches an accurate travelling wave approximation, highlighting the complexity and context-dependent nature of the approximate solutions commonly used in the field. In a remarkable turn of events, the new direction-preserving scheme is shown to develop a singular point at exact time $t=0.0024$, resulting in an approximately zero residual error for the continuity equation, thus effectively capturing the probability density function's inherent structure. In consequence, the new scheme is shown to be capable of providing long-term accuracy for one-dimensional probability density functions over extended periods of time. This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from eleven possible options written by five different individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based approach is applied, focusing on utilizing feature extraction through the StabiloPen. The time series data is first transformed into vector representations using widely recognized features. Then, a classification model is trained with these features to distinguish between the written terms. Notably, this approach achieves high accuracy with reduced dimensions, surpassing the baseline provided by Stabilo. The top-performing strategy involves combining time-domain and frequency-domain features, resulting in an outstanding performance of 93.66% accuracy. The complete process is then encapsulated in a mobile application for ease of use. The code used for this project is available on GitHub at the specified link. The evaluation outcomes demonstrate that this method excels in simplicity and speed, enabling the swift development and execution of the detection algorithm. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. Moreover, due to its ability to model any distribution, this model can also efficiently sample durations for synthesis. To accelerate sampling, we propose two novel techniques: dynamic duration shifting and hybrid sampling. Both methods are developed in response to performance limitations encountered during initial testing, and can be valuable in other machine learning contexts involving duration modelling. This new framework is a crucial development towards more flexible and realistic duration modelling in speech synthesis. As such, all related code and demonstration resources are being made freely available under the MIT License on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/Orion7/MedianBasedDurationModel. This includes a publicly trainable duration model, based on our non-parametric approach, that can be used to generate synthetic speech durations. Additionally, a public API is provided for generating synthetic speech durations in various languages. This API, based on our non-parametric approach, can also be accessed via a simple RESTful interface. We invite others to build upon this research by training their own duration models and exploring the possibilities of viewing durations as sequences of discrete frames, rather than continuous time. This collaborative approach has enabled our research to be truly "end-to-end". This paper will be presented at Interspeech 2023, a leading international conference in speech and language research. To facilitate a more interactive and inclusive experience, the associated slides and video presentation can be accessed via our GitHub repository at https://github.com/Orion7/MedianBasedDurationModel/tree/main/paper. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training framework within our physically-parameterized network enabled the separation of intrinsic and extrinsic variability, eliminating the need for magnitude standardization models. A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a gravitationally lensed star-forming galaxy. The outflow is visible in a specific OH+ absorption line, which was measured at both high and low velocities within a 1 kpc region. Despite the outflow velocities peaking at nearly 700 km/s, the line strength suggests that the majority of gas is ejected at lower velocities. A model of the outflow suggests it may be partially responsible for the observed redshifted water lines. It is believed that this outflow will lead to a loss of gas available for star formation, potentially mitigating the long-term star formation rates. A comparison with theoretical feedback models indicates that this outflow is likely to have a significant impact on the surrounding intergalactic medium. A simplified calculation of the outflow suggests it may contain a large amount of mass, potentially as high as 3.5 to 6.9 billion times that of the Earth's mass per year. This massive outflow could be driven by intense star formation rates, which may be among the highest in known galaxies. High-resolution observations are needed to confirm the outflow properties and determine its impact on the outflowing gas. A potential successor to JWST, along with other facilities such as EST and ELT, is required to capture more precise spectra to better understand the outflow and gas dynamics in this intense star-forming galaxy. This outflow serves as a prime target to test new high-end telescopes and observatories. A possible alternate pathway for gas recirculation is suggested, along with other galaxies like sub-mJy Herschel sources, which could be a more significant factor in gas recirculation and may explain the observed recirculation required to account for the current long-term star formation rates. This outflow is also a potential candidate for resolving the anomaly between observed and predicted molecular gas abundances. If this outflow is responsible for the low molecular gas abundance, it could be resolved by observing the OH+ line at other redshifts to determine if the outflow velocity and characteristics change. Additionally, the outflow is not visible in a nearby velocity field, which may indicate that the outflow velocity is primarily affected by the star formation activity. Finally, a proposed redshift range for a future all-sky survey with the ELT and the ELT-PTU is given to detect massive neutrally bound outflows more commonly.
